docs.title: MCPA Preparation Course
docs.text:
A complete, self-paced course for the Linux Foundation Model Context Protocol Associate (MCPA) certification.

Exam at a glance

Certification Model Context Protocol Associate (MCPA) Format Online, proctored, multiple choice Duration 90 minutes Price $250 USD (one retake included) Level Beginner / associate Prerequisites None formal Validity 2 years Eligibility window 12 months from purchase Spec version referenced MCP 2026-07-28

Source: Linux Foundation certification page

docs.title: The five domains
docs.text:
# Domain Weight 1 MCP Fundamentals 16% 2 Architecture & Components 14% 3 Interactions & Execution 26% 4 Security & Governance 24% 5 Use Cases & Ecosystem 20%

Half the exam is Domains 3 and 4. That is where most of your study time should go.

docs.title: Read this before anything else
docs.text:
The exam targets a protocol that changed fundamentally in July 2026

The Linux Foundation page links the exam to MCP specification revision 2026-07-28. That revision redesigned the protocol:

  • The initialize handshake is gone. MCP is now stateless. Every request carries its own protocol version and client capabilities in _meta.
  • Protocol-level sessions are gone (no more Mcp-Session-Id).
  • Servers no longer send requests to clients. When a server needs input, it returns an InputRequiredResult and the client retries the request (Multi Round-Trip Requests).
  • Sampling, Roots and Logging are deprecated.
  • Tasks moved out of the core protocol into an extension.
  • ping was removed. A mandatory server/discover RPC was added.

Most blog posts, tutorials, YouTube videos and older AI answers describe the previous protocol (2025-11-25 and earlier). If you learned MCP from those, some of what you know is now wrong in ways the exam can test.

Start with What Changed in 2026-07-28. This whole course is written against the 2026-07-28 specification. Legacy behavior is covered only where you need to recognize it.

docs.title: How to use this course
docs.text:
1. Read the blueprint so you know what each domain covers.
  2. Read What Changed even if you already use MCP.
  3. Follow the study plan.
  4. Work the chapters in order. Each builds on the previous one, and each domain ends with a quiz.
  5. Do the labs. MCP is a wire protocol. Watching the actual JSON-RPC messages move is the fastest way to make it concrete. Every lab was run against SDK mcp 2.2.0, which implements 2026-07-28.
  6. Take the mock exams under timed conditions.

docs.title: What the exam tests
docs.text:
The Linux Foundation describes it as focusing on “MCP internals, including architecture, message flow, client-server interactions, capabilities, tools, resources, prompts, transports, and security considerations.”

In practice that means three kinds of question:

  • Recognition. What is server/discover for? What does resultType: "input_required" mean? Which primitive is user-controlled?
  • Mechanics. A server needs the user to confirm an action halfway through a tool call. What goes over the wire, and in what order?
  • Judgement. A remote MCP server receives a token whose audience is a different service. What must it do? Which transport fits a local, single-user integration?

The recommended background the exam assumes is: JSON-RPC basics, experience calling LLM APIs, familiarity with agents and tool use, and basic security literacy (API keys, OAuth 2.1, tokens). Where this course relies on those, it explains them from scratch.

Disclaimer

Unofficial study material. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the Linux Foundation, the Agentic AI Foundation or the MCP project. All practice questions are original and are not real exam questions.

docs.title: Domain 1 — MCP Fundamentals 16%
docs.text: The conceptual foundation: what problem MCP solves, the vocabulary it introduces, and why a shared protocol is worth having. The weight is modest, but everything in the other four domains assumes you have this vocabulary.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
Competency: Core MCP Concepts.

This chapter introduces MCP’s whole vocabulary in one pass. Domain 2 goes deeper into architecture and messages, and Domain 3 into each primitive. The goal here is a correct mental model you can hang every later detail on.

docs.title: 1. Three participants
docs.text: MCP has three participants. The distinction between the first two confuses nearly everyone at first, so take it slowly.

docs.title: Host
docs.text:
The host is the AI application the user actually interacts with: Claude Desktop, Claude Code, VS Code with Copilot, Cursor, ChatGPT, or a custom agent you wrote.

The host is the coordinator. The specification lists its responsibilities:

  • Creates and manages multiple client instances
  • Controls client connection permissions and lifecycle
  • Enforces security policies and consent requirements
  • Handles user authorization decisions
  • Coordinates AI/LLM integration
  • Manages context aggregation across clients

Notice that the host is where the user, the model and policy all live. It talks to the LLM, shows the UI, asks the user for permission, and decides what goes into the model’s context.

docs.title: Client
docs.text:
A client is a protocol component inside the host that maintains the connection to one server. It is not an application the user sees. It is a connector object.

  • Communicates with exactly one server
  • Attaches protocol version and capabilities to every request
  • Routes protocol messages
  • Manages subscriptions and notifications
  • Maintains security boundaries between servers

docs.title: Server
docs.text:
A server is a program that exposes capabilities through MCP: a GitHub server, a filesystem server, a Postgres server, a Sentry server.

  • Exposes resources, tools and prompts
  • Operates independently with focused responsibilities
  • Can request client input (elicitation) by returning an InputRequiredResult
  • Must respect security constraints
  • Can be a local process or a remote service

docs.title: Putting them together
docs.text:
graph LR
    User((User)) --- Host
    subgraph Host["Host: e.g. VS Code"]
        LLM[LLM integration]
        C1[Client 1]
        C2[Client 2]
        C3[Client 3]
    end
    C1 --- S1["Filesystem server<br/>(local, stdio)"]
    C2 --- S2["Database server<br/>(local, stdio)"]
    C3 --- S3["Sentry server<br/>(remote, Streamable HTTP)"]

The rule to memorize: a host creates one client per server connection; each client talks to exactly one server. VS Code connecting to three servers means three client objects inside VS Code.

Why one client per server?

Isolation. If one client served several servers, a message from one server could leak into another’s context. One client per server gives the host a clean boundary to enforce: server A never sees server B’s traffic. It is the mechanism behind the design principle that servers “should not be able to read the whole conversation, nor ‘see into’ other servers.”

"Server" means the program, not the machine

An MCP server is a program that serves context, wherever it runs. The filesystem server launched by Claude Desktop on your laptop is a local server. The Sentry MCP server running on Sentry’s infrastructure is a remote server. Both are MCP servers.

docs.title: 2. Three server primitives
docs.text:
Primitives are the most important concept in MCP. They define what a server can offer.

Primitive What it is Example Tools Executable functions the AI can invoke to perform actions create_issue, run_query, send_email Resources Data identified by a URI, provided as context A file, a database schema, a calendar Prompts Reusable templates that structure interactions with the model “Review this code”, “Plan a vacation”

Each primitive has discovery (*/list), retrieval (*/get or resources/read) and, for tools, execution (tools/call).

A single server usually offers more than one. A database server might expose:

  • Tools to run queries
  • A resource containing the schema
  • A prompt with few-shot examples of good queries

docs.title: The control model: who decides when each is used
docs.text:
This is the most examinable idea in Domain 1. Each primitive has a different controller:

Primitive Controlled by Meaning Typical UI Prompts User The user explicitly chooses to invoke it Slash commands, menu items Resources Application The host decides what context to attach File picker, automatic inclusion Tools Model The LLM decides when to call it The model’s tool calls, with confirmation

Why does this distinction exist? Because the three primitives carry different risks and fit different interactions.

Tools are model-controlled because the whole point is agency: the model notices it needs the weather and calls get_weather without the user naming the tool. That is powerful and risky. A tool can write to databases or send emails, so the spec says there SHOULD always be a human in the loop able to deny tool invocations.

Resources are application-controlled because they are context, and context is the host’s decision. The host might let the user pick files, include them automatically, or search them with embeddings. The model does not “call” a resource.

Prompts are user-controlled because they are workflows a person chooses to start. Note the subtlety the spec calls out: user-controlled refers to who decides when the prompt is used, not who authors its content. Prompt content is defined by the server.

The mapping, as an exam reflex

  • “The user types /review” → prompt
  • “The app attaches the open file as context” → resource
  • “The model decides to look something up / take an action” → tool

Control model is guidance, not enforcement

The protocol does not force any UI. The spec repeats that implementations are “free to expose [primitives] through any interface pattern that suits their needs.” The control model describes intent, and exam questions test the intent.

docs.title: 3. Client features
docs.text:
Clients can also offer features to servers, so servers can build richer interactions.

Feature What it lets a server do Status in 2026-07-28 Elicitation Ask the user for information or confirmation during a request Active Sampling Ask the client’s LLM for a completion Deprecated Roots Learn which filesystem directories the client considers relevant Deprecated

Elicitation is the one to know in depth. A booking server might need the user to confirm a $3,000 purchase before completing a tool call. Rather than failing, it elicits confirmation.

How it works has changed. In 2026-07-28, a server does not send a request to the client. It returns an InputRequiredResult saying what it needs, and the client retries the original request with the answers. This is Multi Round-Trip Requests, covered in MRTR & Elicitation.

docs.title: 4. The message format: JSON-RPC 2.0
docs.text:
MCP messages are JSON-RPC 2.0. JSON-RPC is a tiny, well-established standard for remote procedure calls encoded as JSON. It has three message shapes:

Request: “please do this”, with an id so the answer can be matched:

{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "tools/list", "params": { } }

Response: carries the same id and either a result or an error:

{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "result": { "resultType": "complete", "tools": [ ] } }

Notification: “FYI”, with no id, and no response allowed:

{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "notifications/tools/list_changed" }

Why JSON-RPC? It is simple, language-neutral, human-readable, transport-independent and already understood by a huge amount of tooling. LSP uses it too.

MCP adds its own rules on top. Two matter immediately:

  • Request ids MUST NOT be null (base JSON-RPC allows null).
  • Only clients send requests. Servers send responses and notifications, never requests.

Full detail: JSON-RPC Messages & _meta.

docs.title: 5. Capabilities
docs.text:
Not every client and server supports every feature. Capabilities are how each side declares what it supports, so neither attempts something the other can’t handle.

  • Server capabilities are returned by server/discover:
"capabilities": {
  "tools": { "listChanged": true },
  "resources": { "subscribe": true },
  "prompts": {}
}
  • Client capabilities travel in every request’s _meta:
"_meta": {
  "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities": { "elicitation": { "form": {}, "url": {} } }
}

The rules follow directly:

  • A server that implements a feature must advertise it.
  • A server MUST NOT rely on a client capability the client did not declare. If it needs one, it returns MissingRequiredClientCapabilityError (-32021).
  • A server MUST NOT send an elicitation request to a client that did not declare elicitation.

This design lets features be added progressively. A minimal server can implement only tools. A minimal client can declare no capabilities at all.

docs.title: 6. Statelessness
docs.text:
In 2026-07-28 MCP is a stateless protocol:

All the information needed to process a request is contained in the request itself. A server processes each request independently; no state should be inferred from previous requests, even those on the same connection or stream.

Concretely:

  • There is no initialize handshake and no session.
  • Every request carries its protocol version and client capabilities in _meta.
  • An open connection, even a stdio process, is not a conversation.
  • State that must span requests uses an explicit identifier passed on each request, such as a handle returned by a tool.

Why? So that any server instance can handle any request. Remote MCP servers can then scale horizontally behind an ordinary load balancer with no sticky sessions or shared session store.

If you learned MCP before July 2026

The initialize / notifications/initialized handshake no longer exists in the current protocol. See What Changed.

docs.title: 7. Two layers
docs.text:
MCP is described as two layers.

Data layer (inner). The JSON-RPC protocol itself: discovery (server/discover), the primitives, client features, notifications and utilities. This is what is said.

Transport layer (outer). How messages travel: connection setup, framing, authorization. This is how it is carried. Two standard transports exist:

Transport Where How stdio Local Client launches server as a subprocess; newline-delimited JSON over stdin/stdout Streamable HTTP Remote Each client message is an HTTP POST; replies are JSON or an SSE stream

The layers are independent. The same JSON-RPC messages work over either transport, and custom transports are allowed if they preserve the message format and patterns.

docs.title: 8. A complete interaction, end to end
docs.text:
Everything above, in one flow. A user asks a host, “What’s the weather in Seattle?”

sequenceDiagram
    actor User
    participant Host as Host (incl. LLM integration)
    participant Client
    participant Server as Weather server

    opt Discovery (optional, cacheable)
        Client->>Server: server/discover
        Server-->>Client: versions, capabilities {tools}, serverInfo
    end
    Client->>Server: tools/list
    Server-->>Client: [get_weather + inputSchema]
    User->>Host: "What's the weather in Seattle?"
    Host->>Host: Send message + tool definitions to the LLM
    Host->>Host: LLM decides: call get_weather({location: "Seattle"})
    Host->>User: Confirm tool call?
    User-->>Host: Allow
    Host->>Client: call get_weather
    Client->>Server: tools/call (with _meta)
    Server-->>Client: result: complete, content [text]
    Client-->>Host: tool result
    Host->>Host: Add result to context, LLM writes answer
    Host->>User: "It's 12°C and raining in Seattle."

Note what each participant did:

  • The server never talked to the model or the user. It answered two requests.
  • The client only moved protocol messages.
  • The host did everything involving the user, the model and the decision to allow the call.

That division of labor is MCP’s architecture in miniature. Domain 2 examines it in detail.

docs.title: 9. Recap
docs.text:
• Host = the AI application (coordinates, enforces consent, talks to the LLM). Client = one connector per server inside the host. Server = program exposing capabilities, local or remote.
  • One client per server, for isolation.
  • Server primitives: tools (actions, model-controlled), resources (data by URI, application-controlled), prompts (templates, user-controlled).
  • Client features: elicitation (active); sampling and roots (deprecated).
  • Messages are JSON-RPC 2.0: requests (with non-null id), responses, notifications (no id). Only clients send requests.
  • Capabilities declare support: server’s via server/discover, client’s in every request’s _meta.
  • MCP is stateless: no handshake, no session; version and capabilities ride on each request.
  • Two layers: data (JSON-RPC messages) and transport (stdio or Streamable HTTP).

docs.title: Interoperability & Value
docs.text: Competency: Interoperability & Value.

docs.title: 1. What “interoperability” means for MCP
docs.text:
Interoperability means that independently built software works together without prior coordination. An MCP server written in Go by one company works with an MCP client written in TypeScript by another, even though the two teams never spoke, because both followed the same specification.

That is the value proposition in one sentence, and the official documentation expresses it as “build once and integrate everywhere.” A server author implements MCP one time and becomes usable from Claude, ChatGPT, VS Code, Cursor, MCPJam and every other MCP host. A host developer implements MCP one time and gains access to every MCP server.

Interoperability depends on three properties working together:

  1. A precise specification. Normative language (MUST, SHOULD, MAY), a TypeScript schema as the source of truth, and a generated JSON Schema. Two implementations built from the same spec produce compatible messages.
  2. Capability negotiation. Implementations support different subsets, and each side declares what it has, so a rich client and a minimal server still work together on their common ground.
  3. Versioning and compatibility rules. Every request names its protocol version, and there are defined rules for mismatches and for talking across protocol eras.

docs.title: 2. Value for each stakeholder
docs.text: The documentation frames MCP’s benefits by where you sit in the ecosystem.

docs.title: Developers
docs.text:
MCP reduces development time and complexity when building, or integrating with, an AI application or agent.

Consider a team that wants its internal ticketing system usable from AI tools. Without MCP, it writes a plugin for each AI application it cares about, each in that application’s plugin format, and maintains all of them. With MCP, it writes one MCP server. Every current and future MCP host can use it.

SDKs lower the cost further. With the Python or TypeScript SDK, a basic server exposing a couple of tools is a few dozen lines. You write the function; the SDK produces the JSON Schema, the protocol messages and the transport handling.

docs.title: AI applications and agents
docs.text:
MCP gives them access to an ecosystem of data sources, tools and apps, which enhances their capabilities and improves the end-user experience.

An AI application that supports MCP does not need its own integration team for each service. Its capability grows as the ecosystem grows. When a new service ships an MCP server, every MCP host can use it the same day.

docs.title: End users
docs.text:
MCP results in more capable AI applications or agents that can access user data and take actions on the user’s behalf when necessary.

Users get assistants that can actually do things: read their calendar, file a ticket, query a dashboard. They also get portability: a server they configured in one host can be configured in another.

docs.title: Organizations
docs.text:
Not listed separately in the docs, but a direct consequence, and relevant to the governance roles the exam targets:

  • Reuse: an internal MCP server in front of a system of record serves every AI application in the company.
  • Central control: one place to apply authorization, logging and rate limiting for AI access to that system, instead of scattered custom integrations.
  • Vendor neutrality: the protocol is open and governed by a neutral foundation, so switching AI vendors does not mean rewriting integrations.

docs.title: 3. Composability
docs.text:
The specification’s third stated goal is to “build composable integrations and workflows.”

Composability means small, focused pieces that combine into something larger without modification. MCP achieves it structurally: a host connects to many servers simultaneously, each through its own client, and the model can use capabilities from all of them in a single task.

The documentation’s travel-planning example shows it. A host connects three independent servers:

  • a travel server (flights, hotels),
  • a weather server (forecasts),
  • a calendar/email server (schedules, messages).

The user invokes a plan-vacation prompt (from the travel server), attaches their calendar as a resource (from the calendar server), and the model calls searchFlights and checkWeather tools from two different servers, then createCalendarEvent and sendEmail. No server knows the others exist. The host composes them.

Composition happens in the host

Servers do not talk to each other in MCP. Cross-server interactions are controlled by the host. This keeps servers simple, and it keeps the security boundary in one place.

docs.title: 4. The design principles behind the value
docs.text: The specification states four design principles. Each one explains why MCP delivers interoperability and composability, and they are good exam material.

docs.title: Principle 1: Servers should be extremely easy to build
docs.text:
• Host applications handle complex orchestration responsibilities
  • Servers focus on specific, well-defined capabilities
  • Simple interfaces minimize implementation overhead
  • Clear separation enables maintainable code

Why it matters: the ecosystem’s value scales with the number of servers. Complexity was deliberately pushed into hosts, of which there are few and which are built by well-resourced teams, and away from servers, of which there are many and which are often built by one person in an afternoon. The 2026-07-28 statelessness redesign continues this: a stateless server is simpler to write, deploy and scale.

docs.title: Principle 2: Servers should be highly composable
docs.text:
• Each server provides focused functionality in isolation
  • Multiple servers can be combined seamlessly
  • Shared protocol enables interoperability
  • Modular design supports extensibility

Why it matters: a server that does one thing well can be combined with any other.

docs.title: Principle 3: Servers should not be able to read the whole conversation, nor “see into” other servers
docs.text:
• Servers receive only necessary contextual information
  • Full conversation history stays with the host
  • Each server maintains isolation
  • Cross-server interactions are controlled by the host
  • Host process enforces security boundaries

Why it matters: this is the security principle hidden inside the architecture. You can connect a third-party server without handing it your entire chat history or letting it read what another server returned. It is the reason for one-client-per-server, and it is foundational to Trust Boundaries.

docs.title: Principle 4: Features can be added to servers and clients progressively
docs.text:
• Core protocol provides minimal required functionality
  • Additional capabilities can be negotiated as needed
  • Servers and clients evolve independently
  • Protocol designed for future extensibility
  • Backwards compatibility is maintained

Why it matters: it lets the ecosystem grow without lockstep upgrades. A server adding resource subscriptions does not break clients that never subscribe. Optional extensions (Tasks, MCP Apps, Skills) extend this principle beyond the core.

docs.title: 5. How MCP keeps interoperating as it evolves
docs.text:
A protocol that changes risks fragmenting its ecosystem. MCP has explicit mechanisms against that.

Date-based versions. A version is a string like 2026-07-28, meaning the last date backward-incompatible changes were made. Backward-compatible improvements do not change the version.

Per-request version declaration. Every request states its version. A server that doesn’t support it responds with the versions it does support, and the client retries.

Revision states. A revision is Draft (in progress), Current (ready, may still receive compatible changes) or Final (complete, frozen).

Feature lifecycle. A feature is Active, Deprecated (still works; new implementations shouldn’t adopt it; at least twelve months before removal eligibility) or Removed. A public deprecated features registry lists every deprecation with its migration path.

Cross-era compatibility. Implementations may be dual-era, supporting both modern (2026-07-28) and legacy (initialize-based) peers, with defined detection rules on each transport.

Extensions. New capabilities can be incubated as optional extensions, negotiated via capabilities, without touching the core, and graduate through the SEP process.

docs.title: 6. Where interoperability stops
docs.text:
A standard protocol guarantees that messages are understood. It does not guarantee identical behavior everywhere. Being precise about this helps with judgement questions.

Hosts implement different subsets. One host may support elicitation and MCP Apps; another may support tools only. A server that depends on elicitation won’t get it from a client that doesn’t declare the capability, and must not assume it. Servers SHOULD degrade gracefully, for example returning meaningful text for a host that can’t render an MCP App.

Hosts use primitives differently. One host exposes prompts as slash commands, another as a menu, another not at all. The protocol does not mandate UI.

Tool names can collide. Tool names are only unique within a server. Two servers can both expose search. Hosts that aggregate tools SHOULD disambiguate, for example by prefixing with a server identifier. They SHOULD NOT rely on serverInfo.name for this, because server names are not guaranteed unique.

Model behavior varies. The same tools produce different results with different models. MCP standardizes the interface to the tool, not the reasoning that decides to call it.

Configuration formats are host-specific. How you register a server with a host (claude_desktop_config.json, VS Code settings, and so on) is not part of the specification. The MCP Registry’s server.json format helps here by standardizing installation metadata, but each host still has its own configuration.

docs.title: 7. Recap
docs.text:
• Interoperability = independently built clients and servers work together because they follow one spec. “Build once, integrate everywhere.”
  • It rests on a precise spec, capability negotiation, and versioning rules.
  • Developers build one server instead of N plugins; AI applications gain an ecosystem; end users get capable, portable assistants; organizations get reuse, central control and vendor neutrality.
  • Composability: a host connects many focused servers and composes them itself. Servers never talk to each other.
  • Four design principles: servers easy to build; servers composable; servers isolated from the conversation and each other; features progressive.
  • Evolution is managed with date versions, per-request negotiation, revision states, a deprecation lifecycle, dual-era compatibility and extensions.
  • Interoperability does not guarantee identical features, UI or model behavior across hosts, and tool names can collide across servers.

docs.title: Why MCP Exists
docs.text: Competency: MCP Purpose & Scope.

docs.title: 1. The problem: models are isolated
docs.text:
A large language model on its own knows only what was in its training data. It cannot see your files, query your database, read today’s tickets, check a calendar or take any action in the world. Every useful AI application therefore needs a way to connect the model to external systems, both to read context and to act.

This is not a new observation, and before MCP every AI application solved it the same way: by writing custom integration code.

Picture an organization in 2024:

  • A chat assistant needs GitHub, Jira, Slack and the internal wiki.
  • An IDE assistant needs GitHub, the filesystem, the build system and Jira.
  • A customer-support agent needs Jira, the CRM, Slack and the knowledge base.

Each application wrote its own GitHub integration, its own Jira integration, its own Slack integration. Each used different code, different auth handling, different error handling and different ways of describing tools to the model. When Jira changed its API, three teams fixed three integrations.

docs.title: The M × N problem
docs.text:
Count the work. With M AI applications and N external systems, point-to-point integration needs up to M × N connectors:

        Without a shared protocol                  With MCP

   App 1 ──┬── GitHub                      App 1 ─┐          ┌─ GitHub server
           ├── Jira                        App 2 ─┼── MCP ───┼─ Jira server
           └── Slack                       App 3 ─┘          ├─ Slack server
   App 2 ──┬── GitHub                                        └─ Wiki server
           ├── Jira
           └── Filesystem
   App 3 ──┬── Jira                        Each app implements MCP once (M).
           ├── CRM                         Each system gets one server (N).
           └── Slack                       Total work: M + N.

   Total work: up to M × N

Make it concrete. 10 AI applications and 50 data sources:

  • Point to point: up to 10 × 50 = 500 integrations to write and maintain.
  • Shared protocol: 10 + 50 = 60 implementations: each application speaks MCP once, and each system has one MCP server.

That arithmetic is the entire economic argument for MCP. It turns a multiplicative problem into an additive one.

docs.title: The same problem, solved before
docs.text:
The pattern should look familiar, because it has been solved this way repeatedly:

USB-C. Before universal ports, every device had its own connector and every computer needed the matching port. The official MCP documentation uses exactly this analogy: “Think of MCP like a USB-C port for AI applications.” A standard port means any device works with any computer.

The Language Server Protocol (LSP). The analogy the specification itself cites. Before LSP, adding support for a programming language meant writing a plugin for every editor: Go for VS Code, Go for Vim, Go for Emacs, then Rust for each of them. LSP defined one protocol between editors and “language servers”. Now a language implements one server, an editor implements one client, and they all interoperate. The spec says MCP “takes some inspiration from the Language Server Protocol” and standardizes “how to integrate additional context and tools into the ecosystem of AI applications” in a similar way.

Exam-ready framing

MCP solves the M×N integration problem by giving AI applications and external systems a shared, open protocol, the way USB-C did for devices and LSP did for editors and languages. Its inspiration, per the spec, is LSP.

docs.title: 2. What MCP is
docs.text:
The specification’s own definition:

MCP is an open protocol that enables seamless integration between LLM applications and external data sources and tools.

And the three things it standardizes. MCP provides a standardized way for applications to:

  1. Share contextual information with language models
  2. Expose tools and capabilities to AI systems
  3. Build composable integrations and workflows

Unpack the key words, because each one is load-bearing.

Open. The specification, SDKs and reference implementations are public and permissively licensed (Apache 2.0 for code and specifications). Anyone can implement MCP without permission. In December 2025 Anthropic donated MCP to the Agentic AI Foundation, a directed fund under the Linux Foundation, so it is also governed neutrally rather than by one vendor. See Roles & Adoption.

Protocol. MCP is a wire protocol: a definition of the messages two programs exchange, what they mean, and the rules for exchanging them. It is not a library, a product, a hosted service or a framework. SDKs implement the protocol; the protocol is the specification.

LLM applications on one side, data sources and tools on the other. MCP sits in the middle.

docs.title: 3. What MCP covers
docs.text:
The specification is organized into layers. All implementations MUST support the base protocol, versioning and the message patterns. Everything else is optional and implemented as needed.

Component What it defines Required? Base protocol JSON-RPC message types, errors, _meta, statelessness MUST Versioning & compatibility Per-request version, extension negotiation, legacy interop MUST Message patterns Request/response, Multi Round-Trip Requests, subscribe/notify MUST Authorization OAuth 2.1-based framework for HTTP transports Optional Server features Tools, resources, prompts Optional (per need) Client features Elicitation (plus deprecated sampling and roots) Optional Utilities Caching, pagination, completion, progress, cancellation, (deprecated) logging Optional

Beyond the core, extensions add optional, opt-in functionality such as Tasks, MCP Apps and Skills.

The MCP project is broader than the specification. It also includes:

  • SDKs in many languages (TypeScript, Python, C#, Go and Rust are Tier 1)
  • Development tools, notably the MCP Inspector
  • Reference server implementations
  • The MCP Registry for discovering public servers

docs.title: 4. What MCP deliberately does not cover
docs.text: Scope boundaries are as examinable as scope, and several are stated explicitly.

docs.title: MCP does not dictate how the LLM is used
docs.text:
From the architecture documentation:

MCP focuses solely on the protocol for context exchange — it does not dictate how AI applications use LLMs or manage the provided context.

MCP says nothing about which model you call, how you build the prompt, how many tool definitions you put in context, how you rank resources, or how the agent loop works. A host could hand every tool to the model, search for the right three, or let a smaller model choose. All of those are compliant.

This matters in exam scenarios. If a question asks how a host should choose which tool definitions to include in a prompt, the answer is a host design decision, not a protocol rule.

docs.title: MCP does not enforce security
docs.text:
This is stated plainly in the specification:

While MCP itself cannot enforce these security principles at the protocol level, implementors SHOULD build robust consent and authorization flows into their applications…

The protocol defines requirements (for example, that hosts must obtain consent before invoking tools) but cannot enforce them. A malicious or careless host can ignore them, and nothing in the wire format stops it. Consent, confirmation UI, sandboxing and access control are implementation responsibilities. Domain 4 builds on this.

docs.title: MCP does not mandate user interfaces
docs.text: Every primitive page in the spec includes a variant of: “implementations are free to expose [this] through any interface pattern that suits their needs — the protocol itself does not mandate any specific user interaction model.” Slash commands for prompts, a file picker for resources, confirmation dialogs for tools are all suggestions.

docs.title: MCP does not provide the connection to the model
docs.text: MCP connects the application to external systems. The application’s own connection to its LLM (an Anthropic, OpenAI or local-model API call) is outside MCP. This is exactly why sampling was deprecated: it pulled the client’s model connection into MCP, and the recommended migration is for servers to “integrate directly with LLM provider APIs”.

docs.title: MCP does not replace existing APIs
docs.text: An MCP server is typically a thin adapter in front of an existing API, database or file system. GitHub keeps its REST API. The GitHub MCP server translates between MCP messages and that API, and presents the result in a form an AI application can use.

docs.title: 5. What MCP enables
docs.text:
The official documentation gives concrete examples of what becomes possible when AI applications can reach external systems through a standard interface:

  • Personal assistants that access your Google Calendar and Notion.
  • Coding agents that generate a whole web app from a Figma design.
  • Enterprise chatbots that connect to multiple databases across an organization so people can analyze data by chatting.
  • Creative and physical workflows, such as a model creating a 3D design in Blender and sending it to a 3D printer.

The common thread: the AI application gains context (reading calendars, designs, database schemas) and agency (creating events, writing code, starting a print) without the application developer writing a bespoke integration for each system.

docs.title: 6. A short history
docs.text:
Date Event Nov 2024 Anthropic open-sources MCP. First spec revision 2024-11-05; stdio and HTTP+SSE transports Mar 2025 2025-03-26: Streamable HTTP replaces HTTP+SSE; OAuth-based authorization framework; tool annotations Jun 2025 2025-06-18: structured tool output, elicitation, resource links, servers classified as OAuth resource servers, MCP-Protocol-Version header Sep 2025 MCP Registry launches in preview Nov 2025 2025-11-25: URL-mode elicitation, tasks (experimental), Client ID Metadata Documents Dec 2025 MCP donated to the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation Jul 2026 2026-07-28: stateless redesign, MRTR, server/discover, subscriptions/listen; sampling, roots and logging deprecated

You will not be asked to recite dates. The history matters because it explains why so much existing material is out of date, and why the specification version is part of every request.

docs.title: 7. Recap
docs.text:
• LLMs are isolated from data and tools. Before MCP, every AI application wrote custom integrations: the M×N problem.
  • A shared protocol makes it M + N: each application implements MCP once, each system has one server.
  • MCP is an open wire protocol built on JSON-RPC, inspired by the Language Server Protocol, often explained as USB-C for AI applications.
  • It standardizes three things: sharing context, exposing tools, building composable integrations.
  • Required of every implementation: base protocol, versioning, message patterns. Everything else is optional.
  • Out of scope: how the LLM is used, enforcement of security (implementors must build it), UI patterns, the application’s own model connection, and replacing existing APIs.

docs.title: Domain 1 Quiz — MCP Fundamentals
docs.text:
15 exam-style questions. Answer before expanding. Target: 13/15.

Note

Original questions written against the 2026-07-28 specification. They are not real exam items.

1. With 8 AI applications and 40 external systems, how many integrations does a shared protocol like MCP require, compared to point-to-point integration?

  • A. 48 instead of 320
  • B. 320 instead of 48
  • C. 40 instead of 8
  • D. 8 instead of 320
Answer

A. Point to point is up to M×N = 320. With MCP each application implements the protocol once (8) and each system has one server (40), giving M+N = 48.

2. Which existing protocol does the MCP specification explicitly name as its inspiration?

  • A. gRPC
  • B. The Language Server Protocol
  • C. GraphQL
  • D. OpenAPI
Answer

B. The spec says MCP “takes some inspiration from the Language Server Protocol”, which standardized how editors integrate language support, much as MCP standardizes how AI applications integrate context and tools.

3. A user types /summarize-meetings in their AI assistant to start a workflow defined by an MCP server. Which primitive is this?

  • A. Tool
  • B. Resource
  • C. Prompt
  • D. Elicitation
Answer

C. Prompts are user-controlled, and slash commands are the canonical example. Tools are model-controlled; resources are application-controlled.

4. Which statement about hosts and clients is correct?

  • A. A host and a client are the same thing
  • B. A client can connect to many servers to reduce overhead
  • C. A host creates one client per server connection, and each client talks to exactly one server
  • D. Servers create clients to call back into the host
Answer

C. The 1:1 client–server relationship isolates servers from each other. The host is the application; clients are connector components inside it.

5. Which of the following is outside the scope of the MCP specification?

  • A. The JSON-RPC message format
  • B. How a host decides which tool definitions to put in the LLM’s context
  • C. How a client declares its capabilities
  • D. How a server reports a tool execution error
Answer

B. MCP “does not dictate how AI applications use LLMs or manage the provided context.” Tool selection strategy is a host design decision. The other three are defined by the spec.

6. The specification says MCP “cannot enforce” its security principles at the protocol level. What does this imply?

  • A. MCP has no security requirements
  • B. Consent, authorization and access controls must be built by implementors, especially hosts
  • C. Security is handled automatically by JSON-RPC
  • D. Only remote servers need security
Answer

B. The spec defines requirements (such as obtaining consent before invoking tools) but relies on implementors to build consent and authorization flows. Nothing on the wire forces compliance.

7. Which component set MUST every MCP implementation support?

  • A. Tools, resources and prompts
  • B. Authorization, elicitation and logging
  • C. The base protocol, versioning, and the message patterns
  • D. Streamable HTTP and OAuth 2.1
Answer

C. “All implementations MUST support the base protocol, versioning, and the message patterns.” Server features, client features, utilities and authorization are optional.

8. Which design principle is the direct reason a server cannot see results returned by another server?

  • A. Servers should be extremely easy to build
  • B. Servers should not be able to read the whole conversation, nor “see into” other servers
  • C. Features can be added progressively
  • D. Servers should be highly composable
Answer

B. Full conversation history stays with the host; each server is isolated and cross-server interactions are controlled by the host.

9. In the 2026-07-28 protocol, how does a server learn which protocol version and client capabilities apply to a request?

  • A. From the initialize handshake at the start of the connection
  • B. From the Mcp-Session-Id header
  • C. From _meta fields carried on that request
  • D. From the previous request on the same connection
Answer

C. MCP is stateless. io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion and io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities are required on every request. A and B describe the legacy protocol; D is explicitly forbidden.

10. Where does composition of multiple MCP servers happen?

  • A. Servers call each other directly over MCP
  • B. In the host, which connects to each server through its own client
  • C. In a central MCP broker required by the spec
  • D. In the MCP Registry
Answer

B. The host composes servers. Servers never talk to each other in MCP, and no broker is required.

11. An MCP server is best described as:

  • A. A physical machine running MCP software
  • B. A hosted service operated by the MCP project
  • C. A program that exposes capabilities through MCP, whether it runs locally or remotely
  • D. A library that must be embedded in the host
Answer

C. “MCP server refers to the program that serves context data, regardless of where it runs.”

12. Two connected servers both expose a tool named search. What should an aggregating host do?

  • A. Refuse to connect the second server
  • B. Rely on serverInfo.name to tell them apart
  • C. Implement a disambiguation strategy such as prefixing tool names with a server identifier
  • D. Nothing; the protocol guarantees global tool-name uniqueness
Answer

C. Tool names are unique only within a server. Hosts SHOULD disambiguate, and SHOULD NOT rely on serverInfo.name, which is not guaranteed unique.

13. What does a protocol version string such as 2026-07-28 represent?

  • A. The release date of the latest SDK
  • B. The last date backward-incompatible changes were made
  • C. The date the exam was published
  • D. The expiry date of the revision
Answer

B. Versions follow YYYY-MM-DD and indicate the last backward-incompatible change. Compatible improvements do not bump the version.

14. Which best describes what a deprecated feature means in MCP?

  • A. It has been removed and no longer works
  • B. It still works and remains in the spec, but new implementations should not adopt it
  • C. It is experimental
  • D. It is available only as an extension
Answer

B. Deprecated features remain part of the spec for at least twelve months before becoming eligible for removal. Sampling, Roots and Logging are deprecated, not removed.

15. Which statement about interoperability is TRUE?

  • A. Every MCP host supports every MCP feature
  • B. The protocol mandates how hosts display prompts
  • C. Capability negotiation lets implementations with different feature sets work together on their common ground
  • D. Server configuration files are standardized across all hosts
Answer

C. Implementations support different subsets and declare them via capabilities. UI and host configuration formats are not mandated by the spec.

Score Verdict 14–15 Solid. Move on. 11–13 Re-read Core Concepts. < 11 Rework the domain before continuing; everything later builds on it.

docs.title: Domain 2 — Architecture & Components 14%
docs.text: How MCP is put together: the participants and their boundaries, the message format, the data structures, how messages travel, how versions are agreed, and how a request moves from the user through the model to a server and back.

docs.title: Competencies
docs.text:
Competency Chapter Schemas & Structured Data Schemas & Structured Data MCP Hosts, Clients and Servers Hosts, Clients & Servers Model Interaction Flow Model Interaction Flow

The exam focus statement also names message flow, capabilities and transports, which are architectural. They are covered in JSON-RPC Messages & _meta, Transports and Versioning & Discovery.

  • Hosts, Clients & Servers: responsibilities, the 1:1 rule, local vs. remote, isolation.
  • JSON-RPC Messages & _meta: requests, results, errors, notifications, resultType, reserved metadata.
  • Schemas & Structured Data: JSON Schema 2020-12, tool schemas, content blocks, annotations.
  • Transports: stdio and Streamable HTTP in full, headers, Origin validation.
  • Versioning & Discovery: server/discover, version negotiation, extensions, dual-era compatibility.
  • Model Interaction Flow: the full path from user prompt to tool result, and where the model sits.
  • Quiz: 16 questions.

docs.title: Hosts, Clients & Servers
docs.text:
Competency: MCP Hosts, Clients and Servers.

Core Concepts introduced the three participants. This chapter examines each in depth: exactly what it is responsible for, what it is not allowed to do, and why the boundaries sit where they do.

docs.title: 1. The architecture in the specification’s words
docs.text:
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) follows a client-host-server architecture where each host can run multiple client instances. MCP is a stateless protocol: every request is self-contained and carries its own protocol version and capabilities. This architecture enables users to integrate AI capabilities across applications while maintaining clear security boundaries and isolating concerns.

Two phrases carry the design: clear security boundaries and isolating concerns. Every responsibility below is assigned to keep those true.

graph LR
    subgraph HostProcess["Application host process"]
        H[Host]
        C1[Client 1]
        C2[Client 2]
        C3[Client 3]
        H --> C1
        H --> C2
        H --> C3
    end
    subgraph Local["Local machine"]
        S1["Server 1<br/>Files & Git"]
        S2["Server 2<br/>Database"]
        R1[("Local resource A")]
        R2[("Local resource B")]
    end
    subgraph Internet
        S3["Server 3<br/>External APIs"]
        R3[("Remote resource C")]
    end
    C1 --> S1 --> R1
    C2 --> S2 --> R2
    C3 --> S3 --> R3

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: The host is the application process the user runs, and the container and coordinator for everything MCP-related inside it. Examples: Claude Desktop, Claude Code, VS Code, Cursor, ChatGPT, Goose, a custom agent.

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text: Responsibility What it means in practice Creates and manages clients Reads its configuration, starts a client per configured server, restarts them if they crash Controls connection permissions and lifecycle Decides which servers may be connected, and when to connect or disconnect them Enforces security policies and consent requirements Confirmation dialogs before tool calls, blocking disallowed servers Handles user authorization decisions Runs OAuth flows in a browser, stores tokens, asks the user to approve access Coordinates AI/LLM integration Calls the model, passes it tool definitions, routes its tool calls to the right client Manages context aggregation Merges tools, resources and prompts from all servers into what the model sees

docs.title: Why these all sit in the host
docs.text:
Look at what the host has that nobody else has:

  • The user. Only the host has a UI, so only the host can ask for consent.
  • The model. Only the host calls the LLM, so only the host knows what the model is trying to do.
  • The whole conversation. Only the host holds the full history.
  • Every server. Only the host sees all connected servers at once.

Consent, policy and context aggregation require all four. No other participant is in a position to do them, which is why the specification puts security enforcement in the host.

Exam-ready consequence

When a question asks who should confirm a tool call, obtain consent before sharing data, decide what enters the model’s context, or aggregate tools across servers, the answer is the host. Servers and clients are not in a position to do these things.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: A client is a connector created by the host. It holds the protocol relationship with one server. It is an object inside the host process, not an application.

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
Responsibility What it means in practice Communicates with exactly one server One client, one server, always Attaches protocol version and capabilities to every request Builds the _meta block on each outgoing request Routes protocol messages Sends requests; receives responses and notifications and hands them to the host Manages subscriptions and notifications Opens subscriptions/listen streams; correlates notifications by subscriptionId Maintains security boundaries between servers Never forwards one server’s messages to another

Because MCP is stateless, the client also does work the old handshake used to do once per connection: it declares its capabilities on every request, and handles version errors by retrying with a supported version. It may cache server/discover results and list results according to their ttlMs.

It is also the client that carries out the Multi Round-Trip retry: on an InputRequiredResult, it (with the host’s help for anything involving the user) gathers the input and re-sends the original request with a new id, the inputResponses and the echoed requestState.

docs.title: Why exactly one server
docs.text:
If a single client multiplexed several servers, the boundary between servers would depend on bookkeeping inside that client. One client per server makes isolation structural: server A physically has no channel to server B.

A single server can, however, have many clients. A remote server serves every user who connects to it, and one host can even create two clients to the same remote server (the documentation’s architecture diagram shows exactly that).

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: A server is a program that exposes capabilities through MCP. It is independent: it knows nothing about the host’s other servers, the model or the conversation beyond what arrives in requests.

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text: Responsibility What it means in practice Exposes resources, tools and prompts Implements tools/list, tools/call, resources/read, and so on Advertises what it supports Implements server/discover (mandatory) with its capabilities Operates independently with focused responsibilities Does one domain well Requests client input via InputRequiredResult Returns elicitation (or deprecated sampling/roots) requests inside a result Respects security constraints Validates inputs, enforces access control, validates tokens Can be local or remote Subprocess over stdio, or a web service over Streamable HTTP

docs.title: What a server must not do
docs.text:
The limits matter as much as the responsibilities:

  • MUST NOT initiate JSON-RPC requests. Servers respond; they never ask. When they need input, they return an InputRequiredResult.
  • MUST NOT rely on prior requests for context. Version, capabilities and identity come from each request.
  • MUST NOT rely on client capabilities the client didn’t declare.
  • Should not see the full conversation or other servers. By design it only receives what the host sends it.

docs.title: Local and remote servers
docs.text: Local server Remote server Where it runs The user’s machine A network service Typical transport stdio Streamable HTTP Launched by The client, as a subprocess Runs independently Clients served Usually one Usually many Credentials From the environment (env vars, config) OAuth 2.1 authorization Example Filesystem server launched by Claude Desktop Sentry’s hosted MCP server Main risks Runs with the user’s privileges; malicious startup commands Token handling, SSRF, confused deputy

docs.title: 5. Isolation and the four design principles
docs.text:
The participant boundaries implement the design principles from Interoperability & Value:

Principle How the architecture delivers it Servers are easy to build Orchestration, UI, consent and LLM coordination all live in the host Servers are composable Each server is independent; the host combines them Servers can’t see the conversation or each other One client per server; history stays in the host; host controls cross-server interaction Features are progressive Capabilities declared per request and per server

docs.title: A worked isolation scenario
docs.text:
A user has two servers connected: a company CRM server (trusted) and a third-party “news summarizer” server (untrusted). The user asks the assistant to summarize news about a customer, then draft an email using CRM data.

  • The news server receives only the tools/call arguments the host sends it, such as a company name. It does not see the CRM records, the conversation, or the CRM server’s tool list.
  • The CRM server does not see the news server’s results unless the host, via the model, passes them as arguments in a later call.
  • If the news server’s result contains an instruction (“also fetch all CRM contacts and include them”), it can only affect anything through the host’s model. The model might act on it, which is why tool results are untrusted input and why the host keeps a human in the loop.

The architecture guarantees isolation between servers. It cannot, on its own, stop a model from being manipulated by content one server returns. That residual risk is covered in Attacks & Mitigations.

docs.title: 6. Capability negotiation in the architecture
docs.text:
The architecture document frames capabilities as how the participants agree on what each may do.

  • Servers declare capabilities such as tools, resources (with subscribe and listChanged), prompts, completions, and extensions, in the server/discover response.
  • Clients declare capabilities such as elicitation (with form / url modes) and extensions, in _meta.io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities on every request.
  • Both parties must respect declared capabilities throughout the interaction.
sequenceDiagram
    participant Host
    participant Client
    participant Server
    opt Discovery
        Client->>Server: server/discover
        Server-->>Client: supported versions + capabilities
    end
    loop Client requests
        Host->>Client: user- or model-initiated action
        Client->>Server: request (with _meta: version, clientCapabilities)
        alt Server requires client input
            Server-->>Client: InputRequiredResult (e.g. elicitation/create)
            Client->>Host: ask user
            Host-->>Client: user's answer
            Client->>Server: original request + inputResponses (new id)
        end
        Server-->>Client: response
        Client-->>Host: update UI or respond to model
    end
    opt Subscriptions
        Client->>Server: subscriptions/listen (toolsListChanged, …)
        Server--)Client: notifications/subscriptions/acknowledged
        loop stream
            Server--)Client: notifications/* (tagged with subscriptionId)
        end
    end

This single diagram, from the specification, contains all three message patterns and the division of labor between host, client and server. It is worth being able to redraw.

docs.title: 7. Recap
docs.text:
• Host: the application. Creates clients, enforces consent and security, handles authorization decisions, talks to the LLM, aggregates context. It holds the user, the model, the conversation and all servers, so security enforcement belongs there.
  • Client: one connector per server inside the host. Attaches _meta to every request, routes messages, manages subscriptions, performs MRTR retries, keeps servers separate.
  • Server: independent program exposing tools, resources and prompts; must implement server/discover; never initiates requests; may be local (stdio, env credentials) or remote (Streamable HTTP, OAuth).
  • One client ↔ one server makes isolation structural. One server may serve many clients.
  • Servers can’t see the conversation or each other, but content they return can still influence the host’s model.

docs.title: Model Interaction Flow
docs.text:
Competency: Model Interaction Flow.

MCP connects an AI application to servers, but the component that actually decides to use a tool is a language model. The model is not an MCP participant: it never sends or receives an MCP message. This chapter traces exactly how a user’s message becomes model reasoning, then MCP traffic, then an answer, and where each responsibility sits.

The recommended experience for the exam includes “LLM API interaction experience” and “agentic AI concepts (ReAct patterns, tool-use, chain-of-thought)”. This is where MCP meets both.

docs.title: 1. Where the model sits
docs.text:
graph LR
    User((User)) <--> Host
    subgraph Host["Host application"]
        Orch["Orchestrator<br/>(agent loop, policy, UI)"]
        C1[Client A]
        C2[Client B]
    end
    Orch <-->|"LLM provider API<br/>(not MCP)"| LLM[(Language model)]
    C1 <-->|MCP| S1[Server A]
    C2 <-->|MCP| S2[Server B]
    Orch --- C1
    Orch --- C2

Two different protocols meet inside the host:

  • Host ↔ model: the model provider’s API (Anthropic Messages, OpenAI Chat Completions or Responses, a local model server). Not MCP.
  • Host ↔ servers: MCP, through one client per server.

The host translates between them. The model only ever sees tool definitions and tool results in its provider’s format; servers only ever see MCP requests. The model never talks to a server, and a server never talks to the model.

The consequence exam questions probe

Because the host is the only bridge, the host is the only place that can:

  • decide which tool definitions the model sees,
  • inspect and approve a tool call before it reaches a server,
  • inspect and filter a tool result before it reaches the model,
  • keep one server’s data away from another server.

docs.title: 2. Phase 1: startup and discovery
docs.text:
Before any conversation, the host prepares.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Host
    participant Client
    participant Server
    Host->>Host: Read config: which servers to connect
    Host->>Client: Create one client per server
    opt stdio server
        Client->>Server: Launch subprocess
    end
    opt Up-front discovery (optional)
        Client->>Server: server/discover
        Server-->>Client: versions, capabilities, serverInfo, instructions (ttlMs)
    end
    Client->>Server: tools/list (paginate with cursor if needed)
    Server-->>Client: tools + ttlMs + cacheScope
    Client->>Server: prompts/list, resources/list (if supported)
    Server-->>Client: prompts, resources
    opt Wants change notifications
        Client->>Server: subscriptions/listen {toolsListChanged: true}
        Server--)Client: notifications/subscriptions/acknowledged
    end
    Client-->>Host: Register tools, prompts, resources in host registry

What the host now holds:

  • A registry of tools from every server, disambiguated if names collide.
  • Prompts to offer the user (for example, as slash commands).
  • Resources to offer as attachable context.
  • Cached results, fresh until their ttlMs expires or a list_changed notification invalidates them.

docs.title: 3. Phase 2: a conversation turn
docs.text: The user types: “Is it going to rain in Seattle tomorrow? If so, add ‘bring umbrella’ to my todo list.”

docs.title: Step 1: The host builds the model request
docs.text:
The host sends the conversation plus the available tools to the model, in the provider’s format. MCP tool definitions map almost one-to-one onto provider tool definitions:

MCP tool definition                      Anthropic Messages API tool      OpenAI tool (function)
─────────────────────                    ───────────────────────────      ──────────────────────
name          ────────────────────────►  name                          ►  function.name
description   ────────────────────────►  description                   ►  function.description
inputSchema   ────────────────────────►  input_schema                  ►  function.parameters

{
  "model": "…",
  "max_tokens": 1024,
  "tools": [
    { "name": "weather__get_forecast", "description": "Get the forecast for a city and date",
      "input_schema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "city": {"type":"string"}, "date": {"type":"string","format":"date"} }, "required": ["city","date"] } },
    { "name": "todo__add_item", "description": "Add an item to the user's todo list",
      "input_schema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "text": {"type":"string"} }, "required": ["text"] } }
  ],
  "messages": [
    { "role": "user", "content": "Is it going to rain in Seattle tomorrow? If so, add 'bring umbrella' to my todo list." }
  ]
}

Notice the weather__ and todo__ prefixes. The host added them to disambiguate tools from different servers and to know where to route each call. MCP doesn’t mandate a scheme; it only says hosts SHOULD disambiguate.

Also notice what is not here: nothing about stdio, JSON-RPC, _meta, capabilities or which server hosts the tool. The model sees a flat list of functions.

docs.title: Step 2: The model decides to call a tool
docs.text:
This is the model-controlled part. The model reasons (the “Reason” step of a ReAct loop) and emits a tool call instead of a final answer:

{
  "role": "assistant",
  "stop_reason": "tool_use",
  "content": [
    { "type": "text", "text": "Let me check tomorrow's forecast." },
    { "type": "tool_use", "id": "toolu_01", "name": "weather__get_forecast",
      "input": { "city": "Seattle", "date": "2026-09-16" } }
  ]
}

docs.title: Step 3: The host applies policy
docs.text:
Before anything reaches a server, the host decides whether the call may proceed. The specification says there SHOULD always be a human in the loop able to deny invocations, and that clients SHOULD show tool inputs to the user before calling the server, to avoid accidental or malicious data exfiltration.

In practice hosts combine:

  • Per-call confirmation (“Allow get_forecast with city=Seattle?”)
  • Pre-approval for tools the user has marked safe, possibly informed by readOnlyHint from a trusted server
  • Policy (organization-blocked tools, blocked servers)
  • Validation of arguments against inputSchema

docs.title: Step 4: The client sends tools/call
docs.text:
The host strips its routing prefix, finds the client for the weather server, and the client sends MCP:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 41,
  "method": "tools/call",
  "params": {
    "name": "get_forecast",
    "arguments": { "city": "Seattle", "date": "2026-09-16" },
    "_meta": {
      "io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion": "2026-07-28",
      "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities": { "elicitation": { "form": {} } },
      "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo": { "name": "MyHost", "version": "2.3.0" },
      "traceparent": "00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01"
    }
  }
}

The server receives only the tool name and arguments, never the user’s message, the conversation, or the fact that a todo server exists.

docs.title: Step 5: The server executes and returns
docs.text:
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 41,
  "result": {
    "resultType": "complete",
    "content": [ { "type": "text", "text": "Seattle, 2026-09-16: 90% chance of rain, high 16°C." } ],
    "structuredContent": { "precipitationChance": 0.9, "highC": 16 },
    "isError": false
  }
}

docs.title: Step 6: The host feeds the result back to the model
docs.text:
The host translates the MCP result into the provider’s tool-result format and calls the model again with the whole conversation so far:

{
  "role": "user",
  "content": [
    { "type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "toolu_01",
      "content": "Seattle, 2026-09-16: 90% chance of rain, high 16°C." }
  ]
}

Before doing so, the spec says clients SHOULD validate tool results before passing them to the LLM. The host may also use annotations here, for example keeping audience: ["user"] content out of the model’s context.

docs.title: Step 7: The loop continues
docs.text:
The model observes the result (the “Observe” step) and decides it needs a second tool:

{ "type": "tool_use", "id": "toolu_02", "name": "todo__add_item", "input": { "text": "bring umbrella" } }

The host routes this to the todo server’s client (steps 3–6 again). After that result, the model returns a final text answer with stop_reason: "end_turn":

“Yes, there’s a 90% chance of rain in Seattle tomorrow. I’ve added ‘bring umbrella’ to your todo list.”

docs.title: The whole turn
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    actor User
    participant Host
    participant LLM
    participant CW as Client (weather)
    participant SW as Weather server
    participant CT as Client (todo)
    participant ST as Todo server

    User->>Host: message
    Host->>LLM: messages + tool definitions
    LLM-->>Host: tool_use get_forecast
    Host->>User: approve? (policy)
    User-->>Host: allow
    Host->>CW: call get_forecast
    CW->>SW: tools/call
    SW-->>CW: result (complete)
    CW-->>Host: result
    Host->>LLM: tool_result
    LLM-->>Host: tool_use add_item
    Host->>CT: call add_item
    CT->>ST: tools/call
    ST-->>CT: result (complete)
    CT-->>Host: result
    Host->>LLM: tool_result
    LLM-->>Host: final answer (end_turn)
    Host->>User: answer

Two MCP servers, one model, zero direct contact between any of them. The host is the agent loop.

docs.title: When a tool needs user input: MRTR inside the loop
docs.text:
Suppose todo__add_item on a shared list needs the user to pick which list. The server returns resultType: "input_required" with an elicitation/create request:

sequenceDiagram
    participant LLM
    participant Host
    actor User
    participant Client
    participant Server
    LLM-->>Host: tool_use add_item
    Host->>Client: call add_item
    Client->>Server: tools/call (id 50)
    Server-->>Client: input_required: elicitation "Which list?" + requestState
    Client->>Host: needs user input
    Host->>User: form: Which list?
    User-->>Host: "Personal"
    Host->>Client: answer
    Client->>Server: tools/call (id 51) + inputResponses + requestState
    Server-->>Client: result (complete)
    Client-->>Host: result
    Host->>LLM: tool_result

Note what the model saw: one tool call and one result. The elicitation happened entirely between host, user, client and server. The server asked the user, not the model.

docs.title: When a tool fails
docs.text:
Tool execution error (bad input the model can fix, API failure, business rule): the server returns a result with isError: true, and the host SHOULD give it to the model so it can self-correct:

{ "resultType": "complete", "isError": true,
  "content": [ { "type": "text", "text": "Invalid date: must be in the future. Today is 2026-09-15." } ] }

The model reads this, fixes the date, and retries.

Protocol error (unknown tool, malformed request): a JSON-RPC error. Hosts MAY pass these to the model, but recovery is less likely. See Error Handling.

docs.title: Parallel tool calls
docs.text: Models can request several tools in one turn (for example forecasts for Paris and London). The host can issue the tools/call requests concurrently, each with its own JSON-RPC id, and return all results together. Since MCP is stateless and each request is independent, nothing in the protocol requires ordering.

docs.title: Resources: application-driven context
docs.text:
Resources enter the flow before the model call, chosen by the application:

User attaches "Q3-report.pdf" from the resource picker
      → Host: resources/read { uri: "file:///reports/Q3-report.pdf" }
      → Server returns contents
      → Host places contents in the model's messages as context
      → Model answers using it

The model did not “call” anything. That is what application-controlled means.

docs.title: Prompts: user-driven templates
docs.text:
User types /code_review and pastes code
      → Host: prompts/get { name: "code_review", arguments: { code: "…" } }
      → Server returns messages [{role: "user", content: …}]
      → Host inserts those messages into the conversation
      → Model responds

The user triggered it, the server authored the message content, the host placed it in context.

docs.title: Long-running operations
docs.text:
For operations that take minutes, the host may:

  • request progress by putting a progressToken in _meta and showing notifications/progress to the user;
  • cancel if the user gives up (close the HTTP stream, or send notifications/cancelled on stdio);
  • use the Tasks extension, if both sides support it, to get a durable handle and poll with tasks/get instead of holding a connection open.

docs.title: 5. Scaling the flow: context economy
docs.text:
Every tool definition the host puts in the model request costs tokens, on every turn. With a handful of tools this is irrelevant. With dozens of servers exposing hundreds of tools, definitions alone can consume most of the context window before the model reads the user’s message, and too many options also degrade tool selection.

The official Client Best Practices describe two host-side patterns. Neither changes the MCP protocol; both change what the host shows the model:

  • Progressive tool discovery. Fetch everything with tools/list, but give the model only a lightweight search_tools meta-tool, and load full definitions when needed. Suggested trigger: when definitions exceed roughly 1–5% of the context window.
  • Programmatic tool calling (“code mode”). Generate a typed API from tool schemas (including outputSchema), let the model write a script that calls several tools in a sandbox, and return only the final output to the model, so intermediate data never passes through its context.

Both are covered in Operational Use Cases.

Deterministic ordering helps prompt caching

Servers SHOULD return tools/list in a deterministic order. Model providers cache the prompt prefix, which includes the tools array. A server that shuffles its tools on every call silently defeats that cache.

docs.title: 6. Recap
docs.text:
• The model is not an MCP participant. Host ↔ model uses the provider API; host ↔ servers uses MCP. The host translates and runs the agent loop.
  • Startup: create a client per server → optional server/discover → tools/list / prompts/list / resources/list → register → optionally subscriptions/listen.
  • A turn: host sends messages + tool definitions → model returns tool_use → host applies policy/consent → client sends tools/call → server returns result → host validates and returns a tool_result → loop until the model gives a final answer.
  • MCP name / description / inputSchema map directly to provider tool definitions. Hosts disambiguate names across servers.
  • Servers see only the call arguments: never the conversation, other servers, or the model.
  • MRTR elicitation happens between host, user, client and server; the model sees one call and one result.
  • isError: true results go back to the model for self-correction; protocol errors rarely help it.
  • Resources enter context by application choice; prompts by user choice.
  • At scale, use progressive discovery and code mode; servers should return tools in deterministic order.

docs.title: JSON-RPC Messages & _meta
docs.text:
Supports the competency Schemas & Structured Data and the exam focus on message flow.

Every MCP interaction is a sequence of JSON-RPC messages. If you can read a raw message and say what kind it is, who sent it and what it is doing, most message-flow questions become easy.

docs.title: 1. Why JSON-RPC
docs.text:
MCP needed a message format that is:

  • language-neutral (servers are written in every language),
  • transport-independent (the same messages over stdio and HTTP),
  • human-readable (debugging a protocol by reading its traffic is invaluable),
  • simple and already widely implemented.

JSON-RPC 2.0 fits all of these. It is a tiny specification (a few pages) defining how to encode a remote procedure call as JSON. The Language Server Protocol uses it for the same reasons.

JSON-RPC defines requests, responses and notifications. MCP adopts all three, and adds rules on top.

All MCP messages MUST follow JSON-RPC 2.0 and MUST be UTF-8 encoded.

docs.title: 2. Requests
docs.text:
A request asks the receiver to perform an operation and expects exactly one response.

{
  jsonrpc: "2.0";
  id: string | number;
  method: string;
  params?: { [key: string]: unknown };
}

A real one:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 7,
  "method": "tools/call",
  "params": {
    "name": "get_weather",
    "arguments": { "location": "New York" },
    "_meta": {
      "io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion": "2026-07-28",
      "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities": {},
      "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo": { "name": "ExampleClient", "version": "1.0.0" }
    }
  }
}

docs.title: MCP’s rules for requests
docs.text:
1. The id MUST be a string or an integer.
  2. Unlike base JSON-RPC, the id MUST NOT be null.
  3. The id MUST NOT match any other request the sender has issued and not yet received a response for.
  4. In MCP, requests are sent only by clients. Servers MUST NOT initiate JSON-RPC requests.
  5. Every request MUST carry the required _meta fields (section 6).

Rule 3 is subtle. IDs need only be unique among in-flight requests. Once a request is answered its ID could, in principle, be reused, though most implementations just increment a counter.

Why null IDs are forbidden

In base JSON-RPC, a null id is legal but ambiguous: error responses to unparseable requests also use a missing/null id. Forbidding null on requests means an id-less error can only ever refer to a malformed message, never to a real request.

MRTR retries need a new id

A Multi Round-Trip retry is a brand-new request, so it MUST use a different id from the original, even though the method and arguments are the same.

docs.title: 3. Responses
docs.text: A response answers a request. It carries the same id and exactly one of result or error.

docs.title: Result responses
docs.text:
{
  jsonrpc: "2.0";
  id: string | number;
  result: {
    resultType: string;
    [key: string]: unknown;
  };
}
  • MUST include the same id as the request.
  • MUST include a result field, which may follow any JSON object structure.
  • The result MUST include a resultType field. 2026

docs.title: resultType: polymorphic results
docs.text:
In 2026-07-28 a request can end in more than one way, so the result declares its own shape:

resultType Meaning Shape "complete" Finished successfully The method’s normal result (tools, content, contents, …) "input_required" Needs more input first InputRequiredResult: inputRequests and/or requestState Extension-defined (e.g. "task") Defined by a negotiated extension Per extension

The rules:

  • The set of valid values is the core set plus values from extensions advertised via capabilities.
  • A resultType the client does not recognize MUST be considered invalid.
  • An absent resultType (from a server implementing an earlier protocol version) MUST be treated as "complete".

Think about why the last two rules differ. An absent value can only come from an older server that predates the field, and its results were always complete, so treating them as complete is safe. An unrecognized value means the server believes it is saying something specific that the client cannot interpret. Guessing would be dangerous.

docs.title: Error responses
docs.text:
{
  jsonrpc: "2.0";
  id?: string | number;
  error: {
    code: number;
    message: string;
    data?: unknown;
  };
}
  • MUST include the same id as the request, except when the request was so malformed its id could not be read.
  • MUST include error with an integer code and a message.
  • MAY include data with additional detail of any type.

The codes, and when to use an error response versus a result with isError: true, are covered in Error Handling.

docs.title: 4. Notifications
docs.text:
A notification is a one-way message. It has no id, and the receiver MUST NOT respond.

{
  jsonrpc: "2.0";
  method: string;
  params?: { [key: string]: unknown };
}

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "method": "notifications/progress",
  "params": { "progressToken": "abc123", "progress": 50, "total": 100 }
}

Notifications in the core protocol:

Notification Sender Where it travels notifications/progress Server On the response stream of the request it relates to notifications/message (deprecated logging) Server On the response stream of the request that set logLevel notifications/subscriptions/acknowledged Server First message on a subscriptions/listen stream notifications/tools/list_changed Server On a subscriptions/listen stream notifications/prompts/list_changed Server On a subscriptions/listen stream notifications/resources/list_changed Server On a subscriptions/listen stream notifications/resources/updated Server On a subscriptions/listen stream notifications/cancelled Client (stdio); server only to end a listen stream stdio channel

How to classify a raw message in two seconds

  • Has method and id → request (so the sender is a client)
  • Has id and result → result response
