  • Has id (or none, if malformed) and error → error response
  • Has method and no id → notification

docs.title: 5. Direction: who sends what
docs.text:
The message patterns page states it flatly:

Servers MUST NOT initiate JSON-RPC requests, and clients do not send JSON-RPC responses.

Message type Client sends Server sends Request ✅ ❌ Result / error response ❌ ✅ Notification ✅ (only notifications/cancelled, stdio) ✅

This is one of the most important facts about 2026-07-28, and it simplifies every transport: messages only ever flow as client-request → server-response, plus server notifications.

docs.title: 6. _meta
docs.text: _meta is a reserved property on params and result objects for protocol-level metadata. Arguments describe what to do; _meta describes the request itself.

docs.title: Key naming rules
docs.text:
A _meta key has an optional prefix and a name: prefix/name.

Prefix

  • If present: dot-separated labels followed by /.
  • Labels start with a letter, end with a letter or digit, and may contain hyphens.
  • Implementations SHOULD use reverse DNS (com.example/, not example.com/).
  • Any prefix whose second label is modelcontextprotocol or mcp is reserved for MCP.
Prefix Reserved for MCP? Why io.modelcontextprotocol/ Yes second label modelcontextprotocol dev.mcp/ Yes second label mcp org.modelcontextprotocol.api/ Yes second label modelcontextprotocol com.mcp.tools/ Yes second label mcp com.example.mcp/ No second label is example

Name

  • Unless empty, begins and ends with an alphanumeric character.
  • May contain hyphens, underscores, dots and alphanumerics in between.

Implementations MUST NOT make assumptions about values at reserved keys they don’t understand.

docs.title: Reserved keys
docs.text:
Key Purpose progressToken Opts a request into progress notifications io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion Protocol version for the request 2026 io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo Client name and version 2026 io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities Client capabilities for the request 2026 io.modelcontextprotocol/logLevel Minimum log level for the request (deprecated logging) 2026 io.modelcontextprotocol/subscriptionId Correlates a notification with its subscription 2026 traceparent, tracestate, baggage OpenTelemetry trace context (an explicit exception to the prefix rule) 2026

Official extensions add more keys under io.modelcontextprotocol/; third-party extensions use their own vendor prefix.

docs.title: Per-request fields (client → server)
docs.text:
Key Type Required io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion string Yes io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities ClientCapabilities Yes io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo Implementation No (but clients SHOULD include it) io.modelcontextprotocol/logLevel LoggingLevel No

Missing a required field → the request is malformed → the server MUST reject it with -32602 (Invalid params), and on HTTP with 400 Bad Request.

Needing an undeclared capability → the server MUST return MissingRequiredClientCapabilityError (-32021), with data.requiredCapabilities listing what is missing, and on HTTP 400 Bad Request.

docs.title: Per-response fields (server → client)
docs.text:
Key Type Required io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo Implementation No (but servers SHOULD include it on every result)

On notifications delivered via a subscriptions/listen stream, the server MUST include io.modelcontextprotocol/subscriptionId.

clientInfo and serverInfo are unverified

Both are self-reported and not verified by the protocol. They exist for display, logging and debugging. Implementations SHOULD NOT change behavior based on them and SHOULD NOT use them for security decisions. A client claiming {"name": "TrustedCorpAgent"} proves nothing. Identity for security comes from authorization.

docs.title: OpenTelemetry trace context
docs.text:
traceparent, tracestate and baggage are reserved for OpenTelemetry and must follow W3C Trace Context and W3C Baggage formats. They let a trace flow from the host, through the MCP call, into the server and beyond, so one distributed trace covers the whole operation. See Auditability & Observability.

"_meta": { "traceparent": "00-0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c-00f067aa0ba902b7-01" }

docs.title: icons
docs.text:
Tools, resources, prompts and implementations may carry icons, an array of { src, mimeType?, sizes?, theme? }. src is an HTTPS URL or a data: URI.

The requirements are mostly security rules, because icons are fetched and rendered by the client from server-supplied URLs:

  • Treat icon metadata and bytes as untrusted.
  • Accept only https: or data: URIs; reject javascript:, file:, ftp:, ws: and local app schemes; disallow scheme changes and cross-origin redirects.
  • Fetch without credentials (no cookies, no Authorization header).
  • Verify icons come from the same origin as the server.
  • Beware SVG with embedded JavaScript; validate content type by magic bytes, not by the declared MIME type.
  • Defend against oversized images and excessive GIF frames.
  • Clients that render icons MUST support image/png and image/jpeg, and SHOULD support image/svg+xml and image/webp.

docs.title: title vs. name
docs.text: Tools, resources and prompts have a name (programmatic identifier) and an optional title (human-readable display name). Use name in protocol calls and title in UI.

docs.title: 8. A complete exchange, annotated
docs.text:
A client lists tools, then calls one, over stdio. Each line is one message.

// C→S  REQUEST (method + id)
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/list","params":{"_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion":"2026-07-28","io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities":{}}}}

// S→C  RESULT (id 1, resultType complete, cache hints)
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"result":{"resultType":"complete","tools":[{"name":"get_weather","inputSchema":{"type":"object","properties":{"location":{"type":"string"}},"required":["location"]}}],"ttlMs":300000,"cacheScope":"public","_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo":{"name":"weather","version":"1.0.0"}}}}

// C→S  REQUEST (progressToken opts into progress)
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"get_weather","arguments":{"location":"Oslo"},"_meta":{"progressToken":"p-2","io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion":"2026-07-28","io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities":{}}}}

// S→C  NOTIFICATION (no id), scoped to request 2 via its token
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"notifications/progress","params":{"progressToken":"p-2","progress":1,"total":2}}

// S→C  RESULT (id 2)
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"result":{"resultType":"complete","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Oslo: 4°C, snow"}],"isError":false}}

// C→S  REQUEST with a missing required _meta field
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"method":"tools/list","params":{}}

// S→C  ERROR (malformed: missing protocolVersion/clientCapabilities)
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"error":{"code":-32602,"message":"Missing required _meta field: io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion"}}

Lab 1 has you type messages like these into a real server by hand.

docs.title: 9. Recap
docs.text:
• MCP uses JSON-RPC 2.0, UTF-8 encoded: requests, responses (result or error), notifications.
  • Request ids are string or integer, never null, unique among in-flight requests; an MRTR retry uses a new id.
  • Only clients send requests; servers send responses and notifications.
  • Every result has resultType: complete, input_required or an extension value. Absent → complete; unrecognized → invalid.
  • Error responses carry integer code, message, optional data, and the request id unless unreadable.
  • Notifications have no id and get no response.
  • _meta keys: optional reverse-DNS prefix; prefixes whose second label is modelcontextprotocol or mcp are reserved.
  • Required on every request: protocolVersion and clientCapabilities. Missing → -32602 / HTTP 400. Undeclared capability needed → -32021.
  • clientInfo and serverInfo are self-reported; never use them for security decisions.
  • traceparent / tracestate / baggage carry OpenTelemetry context.
  • Icons are untrusted: HTTPS or data: only, no credentials, same origin, beware SVG scripts.

docs.title: Domain 2 Quiz — Architecture & Components
docs.text:
16 exam-style questions. Target: 14/16.

1. Which participant is responsible for enforcing consent requirements before a tool is invoked?

  • A. The server
  • B. The client
  • C. The host
  • D. The LLM
Answer

C. The host “enforces security policies and consent requirements” and “handles user authorization decisions”. It is the only participant with the user, the model and all servers in view.

2. A raw message reads {"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"notifications/progress","params":{...}}. What is it?

  • A. A request from the client
  • B. A notification; the receiver must not respond
  • C. A result response
  • D. A malformed message because it lacks an id
Answer

B. A message with method and no id is a notification. Notifications MUST NOT include an id, and the receiver MUST NOT respond.

3. Which statement about request IDs in MCP is correct?

  • A. They may be null, as in base JSON-RPC
  • B. They must be globally unique forever
  • C. They must be a string or integer, not null, and not match any other in-flight request from the sender
  • D. They must be UUIDs
Answer

C. MCP forbids null ids (unlike base JSON-RPC) and requires uniqueness only among requests still awaiting a response.

4. A client receives a result with resultType: "task" but has not negotiated any extension defining that value. What must it do?

  • A. Treat it as "complete"
  • B. Treat the result as invalid
  • C. Retry the request with a new id
  • D. Ignore the resultType field
Answer

B. An unrecognized resultType MUST be considered invalid. Only an absent resultType (from a legacy server) is treated as "complete".

5. Which _meta fields are required on every client request?

  • A. clientInfo and logLevel
  • B. protocolVersion and clientCapabilities
  • C. progressToken and traceparent
  • D. serverInfo and subscriptionId
Answer

B. io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion and io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities are required. clientInfo is SHOULD. A request missing a required field is rejected with -32602 (HTTP 400).

6. Which _meta prefix is NOT reserved for MCP?

  • A. io.modelcontextprotocol/
  • B. dev.mcp/
  • C. com.example.mcp/
  • D. org.modelcontextprotocol.api/
Answer

C. A prefix is reserved when its second label is modelcontextprotocol or mcp. In com.example.mcp/ the second label is example.

7. A security team wants to grant elevated access to requests whose clientInfo.name is "CorpApprovedAgent". What is wrong with this?

  • A. Nothing, clientInfo is verified by the protocol
  • B. clientInfo is self-reported and unverified, and must not be relied on for security decisions
  • C. clientInfo is only available over stdio
  • D. clientInfo is deprecated
Answer

B. clientInfo and serverInfo are for display, logging and debugging. Implementations SHOULD NOT rely on them for security decisions. Identity for security comes from authorization.

8. A tool takes no arguments. Which inputSchema does the specification recommend?

  • A. null
  • B. {}
  • C. { "type": "object", "additionalProperties": false }
  • D. { "type": "array" }
Answer

C. inputSchema must be a valid JSON Schema object, not null. The recommended form accepts only an empty object; { "type": "object" } is also valid but accepts any properties.

9. A tool defines an outputSchema. Which is required?

  • A. The server MUST return structuredContent conforming to the schema
  • B. The client MUST reject any content array
  • C. The server MUST omit text content
  • D. The output schema MUST use draft-07
Answer

A. With an output schema, servers MUST return conforming structured results; clients SHOULD validate them. For compatibility the server SHOULD also return the JSON serialized in a text block.

10. A tool has no annotations. How should a careful client interpret its behavior?

  • A. Read-only and closed-world
  • B. Not read-only, potentially destructive, not idempotent, open-world
  • C. Idempotent and safe to retry
  • D. Annotations are required, so the tool is invalid
Answer

B. The defaults are conservative: readOnlyHint false, destructiveHint true, idempotentHint false, openWorldHint true. And annotations are untrusted anyway unless the server is trusted.

11. A server launched over stdio prints Server started! using print(). What happens?

  • A. Nothing; stdout is ignored
  • B. The client receives a non-JSON line on stdout and fails to parse it; logs belong on stderr
  • C. The client treats it as a notification
  • D. The server is automatically restarted
Answer

B. The server MUST NOT write anything to stdout that is not a valid MCP message. Logging goes to stderr.

12. On Streamable HTTP, how does a client cancel an in-flight request?

  • A. POST a notifications/cancelled message
  • B. Send HTTP DELETE with the session id
  • C. Close the SSE response stream for that request
  • D. Send ping with a cancel flag
Answer

C. Closing the response stream is the cancellation signal on Streamable HTTP. notifications/cancelled is used on stdio. Sessions and ping no longer exist.

13. A Streamable HTTP request has header Mcp-Name: read_report but the body says "name": "delete_reports". What must a server that processes the body do?

  • A. Execute the body’s tool, since the body is the source of truth
  • B. Execute the header’s tool
  • C. Reject with 400 Bad Request and -32020 HeaderMismatch
  • D. Ignore the header
Answer

C. Servers MUST reject header/body mismatches. Otherwise a gateway authorizing by header and a server executing by body would act on different things.

14. A local MCP server uses Streamable HTTP on the user’s laptop. Which measures does the spec require or recommend against DNS rebinding?

  • A. Enable CORS for all origins
  • B. Validate the Origin header (403 if invalid) and bind to 127.0.0.1 rather than 0.0.0.0
  • C. Use Mcp-Session-Id
  • D. Require HTTP GET for all requests
Answer

B. Servers MUST validate Origin and SHOULD bind locally to loopback, and SHOULD authenticate connections.

15. Which is TRUE about server/discover?

  • A. Clients must call it before any other request
  • B. Servers must implement it, clients may call it, and the result carries caching hints
  • C. It establishes a session
  • D. It replaces tools/list
Answer

B. Servers MUST implement it. Clients MAY call it up front, or send any request directly and handle version errors. It establishes no state and its result is cacheable.

16. A dual-era client on stdio sends server/discover and receives error -32601 (Method not found). What should it conclude?

  • A. The server is modern but misconfigured; retry
  • B. The server is legacy; fall back to the initialize handshake
  • C. The server supports no versions
  • D. The client must switch to Streamable HTTP
Answer

B. On stdio, a DiscoverResult or a recognized modern error means modern. Any other error, or a timeout, means legacy. The fallback must not be keyed to one specific code, but -32601 is a typical legacy response.

Score Verdict 15–16 Strong. 12–14 Re-read Messages and Transports. < 12 Rework the domain. Domain 3 depends on it.

docs.title: Schemas & Structured Data
docs.text:
Competency: Schemas & Structured Data.

MCP is a protocol between programs and a language model. Both sides need to know the shape of the data: what arguments a tool accepts, what a result looks like, what a form should ask for. MCP uses JSON Schema for this, and a small set of content types for everything that flows back.

The recommended experience for the exam includes the “ability to read MCP server manifests and capability definitions”. This chapter is where that ability comes from.

docs.title: 1. The source of truth
docs.text:
The specification states that the protocol is defined by a TypeScript schema:

  • schema.ts is the source of truth for all protocol messages and structures.
  • A JSON Schema (schema.json) is generated automatically from it for use by tooling.

When the prose specification and the schema appear to disagree, the schema is authoritative for message structure.

docs.title: 2. JSON Schema in MCP
docs.text:
JSON Schema is a vocabulary for describing and validating JSON. MCP uses it in three places:

  1. Tool inputSchema — the arguments a tool accepts
  2. Tool outputSchema — the structure of a tool’s structuredContent
  3. Elicitation requestedSchema — the form a user fills in

docs.title: Dialect rules
$ref resolution: a security rule
docs.text:
JSON Schema lets $ref point at another schema, including one at an absolute network URI. A validator that follows such references automatically would fetch arbitrary URLs chosen by whoever wrote the schema. When the schema comes from an MCP server, that is a server-side request forgery vector aimed at the client.

So the specification says:

  • Implementations MUST NOT automatically dereference $ref values that resolve to a network URI.
  • An opt-in mode that fetches non-local $refs MAY exist, but MUST be disabled by default and SHOULD enforce a host allowlist, or at minimum reject loopback, link-local and private addresses, apply timeouts and size limits, and log dereferenced URIs.
  • A schema that fails because of an unresolved external $ref SHOULD be rejected, not silently treated as permissive.

That last point closes a quieter hole. If an unresolvable reference were treated as “accept anything”, an attacker could disable validation just by pointing at a URL that never resolves.

docs.title: Composition keywords: a denial-of-service rule
docs.text: anyOf, oneOf, allOf, if/then/else and $defs are expressive, and pathological schemas can make validation exponentially expensive. Implementations SHOULD apply bounds, such as maximum schema depth, a cap on total subschemas, or a per-validation time budget, so a malicious schema cannot be used as a denial-of-service vector against the validator.

docs.title: 3. Tool schemas
docs.text:
A tool definition is the “manifest” most exam questions ask you to read:

{
  "name": "get_weather_data",
  "title": "Weather Data Retriever",
  "description": "Get current weather data for a location",
  "inputSchema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "location": { "type": "string", "description": "City name or zip code" }
    },
    "required": ["location"]
  },
  "outputSchema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "temperature": { "type": "number", "description": "Temperature in celsius" },
      "conditions": { "type": "string" },
      "humidity": { "type": "number" }
    },
    "required": ["temperature", "conditions", "humidity"]
  },
  "annotations": { "readOnlyHint": true, "openWorldHint": true }
}

docs.title: inputSchema
docs.text:
• Defines the expected arguments; follows the dialect rules above.
  • MUST be a valid JSON Schema object, not null.
  • In 2026-07-28 it may use any JSON Schema 2020-12 keyword. 2026
  • Properties MAY carry an x-mcp-header annotation to mirror the value into an HTTP header (see Transports).

For a tool with no parameters, the spec gives two valid options:

Schema Behavior { "type": "object", "additionalProperties": false } Recommended. Accepts only an empty object { "type": "object" } Accepts any object, including one with properties

The recommended form is stricter, so a model that invents arguments gets a validation error instead of having them silently ignored.

docs.title: Why descriptions matter
docs.text:
The model never sees your code. It chooses tools and fills arguments entirely from name, description, and the property descriptions inside inputSchema. A vague description (“does weather stuff”) produces wrong calls. A precise one (“City name or zip code, e.g. ‘Paris’ or ‘94103’”) produces right ones. The schema is the model’s documentation.

That same fact is a security consideration: text in descriptions goes straight into the model’s context, which is why hidden instructions there (tool poisoning) work. See Attacks & Mitigations.

docs.title: Tool names
docs.text:
Rule Level 1–128 characters inclusive SHOULD Case-sensitive SHOULD Only A–Z a–z 0–9 _ - . SHOULD No spaces, commas or other special characters SHOULD NOT Unique within a server SHOULD

Valid examples: getUser, DATA_EXPORT_v2, admin.tools.list.

Names are unique only within one server. A host aggregating several servers SHOULD disambiguate collisions (for example, prefixing with a server identifier), and SHOULD NOT rely on serverInfo.name, which is not guaranteed unique.

docs.title: outputSchema and structuredContent
docs.text:
A tool result can carry two kinds of content:

  • Unstructured: a content array of text, images, audio and resources, for the model and user to read.
  • Structured: a structuredContent field, a JSON value for programs to consume.

If a tool declares an outputSchema:

  • The server MUST return structuredContent that conforms to it.
  • Clients SHOULD validate structuredContent against it.
{
  "resultType": "complete",
  "content": [
    { "type": "text", "text": "{\"temperature\": 22.5, \"conditions\": \"Partly cloudy\", \"humidity\": 65}" }
  ],
  "structuredContent": { "temperature": 22.5, "conditions": "Partly cloudy", "humidity": 65 }
}

Three details:

  1. structuredContent may be any JSON value: object, array, string, number, boolean or null. The spec’s list_users example returns an array. 2026
  2. Backward compatibility: a tool returning structured content SHOULD also return the serialized JSON in a text content block, so clients that ignore structuredContent still get the data.
  3. structuredContent is not “structured outputs.” It is server-produced result data, unrelated to LLM structured outputs (schema-constrained model generation). The spec calls this out explicitly because the names are easy to confuse.

Why output schemas matter: they enable strict validation, give clients type information, and let hosts generate typed APIs from tools, which is exactly what programmatic tool calling (“code mode”) relies on. See Operational Use Cases.

docs.title: 4. Tool annotations
docs.text:
Annotations describe behavior as hints:

Annotation Meaning Default Meaningful when title Human-readable title — always readOnlyHint Tool does not modify its environment false always destructiveHint Tool may perform destructive updates (vs. only additive) true readOnlyHint == false idempotentHint Repeating the call with the same args has no additional effect false readOnlyHint == false openWorldHint Tool interacts with an open world of external entities true always

Read the defaults carefully. They are conservative: absent any hint, a tool is assumed to be not read-only, possibly destructive, not idempotent, open-world. A host that uses hints to decide whether to auto-approve therefore errs toward caution when a server says nothing.

Examples: a web search tool is open world; a memory tool is closed world. delete_file is destructive; append_log is additive (destructiveHint: false); set_status("done") is idempotent.

Annotations are untrusted

The specification: “clients MUST consider tool annotations to be untrusted unless they come from trusted servers.” A malicious server can label delete_everything as readOnlyHint: true. Hints can make UX better for trusted servers; they can never be the basis of a security decision for untrusted ones.

docs.title: 5. Content blocks
docs.text:
Tool results, prompt messages and (deprecated) sampling messages share a common set of content types.

type Carries Key fields text Plain text text image Image data (base64), mimeType audio Audio data (base64), mimeType resource_link A pointer to a resource uri, name, description?, mimeType? resource An embedded resource, inline resource: { uri, mimeType, text \| blob } 
{ "type": "text", "text": "Tool result text" }
{ "type": "image", "data": "iVBORw0KG...", "mimeType": "image/png" }
{ "type": "audio", "data": "UklGRiQA...", "mimeType": "audio/wav" }
{ "type": "resource_link", "uri": "file:///project/src/main.rs", "name": "main.rs", "mimeType": "text/x-rust" }
{ "type": "resource", "resource": { "uri": "file:///project/src/main.rs", "mimeType": "text/x-rust", "text": "fn main() {}" } }

docs.title: Resource link vs. embedded resource
docs.text:
The distinction is examinable:

resource_link Embedded resource Contains A URI and metadata The contents themselves Client must Fetch it (or subscribe) if it wants the data Nothing, the data is already there Good for Large or optional data; letting the host decide Small data the model definitely needs Listed in resources/list? Not guaranteed Not applicable Server should declare resources? — SHOULD

A link keeps the result small and leaves the decision to the application, consistent with resources being application-controlled.

Binary data (images, audio, resource blob) MUST be base64-encoded with a valid MIME type.

docs.title: Content annotations
docs.text:
All content types, resources and resource templates accept annotations that help the client decide how to use them:

Annotation Values Use audience Array of "user", "assistant" Who it is for. ["user"] might be shown but not sent to the model priority 0.0–1.0 Importance. 1 ≈ effectively required; 0 = entirely optional lastModified ISO 8601 timestamp When it last changed; sort or show recency 
{
  "type": "image",
  "data": "base64-encoded-data",
  "mimeType": "image/png",
  "annotations": { "audience": ["user"], "priority": 0.9 }
}

audience is useful for context economy. A server can return a large human-readable report tagged ["user"] and a compact summary tagged ["assistant"], and a host can keep the report out of the model’s context window.

docs.title: Resource
docs.text:
{
  "uri": "file:///project/src/main.rs",
  "name": "main.rs",
  "title": "Rust Software Application Main File",
  "description": "Primary application entry point",
  "mimeType": "text/x-rust",
  "size": 1024
}

uri and name identify it. title, description, icons, mimeType and size (bytes) are optional. Contents come back from resources/read as text or blob.

docs.title: Resource template
docs.text:
{
  "uriTemplate": "weather://forecast/{city}/{date}",
  "name": "weather-forecast",
  "title": "Weather Forecast",
  "mimeType": "application/json"
}

uriTemplate follows RFC 6570 URI templates. Arguments can be autocompleted with completion/complete.

docs.title: Prompt
docs.text:
{
  "name": "code_review",
  "title": "Request Code Review",
  "description": "Asks the LLM to analyze code quality and suggest improvements",
  "arguments": [ { "name": "code", "description": "The code to review", "required": true } ]
}

Prompt arguments are not JSON Schema. They are a simple list of { name, description?, required? }. prompts/get returns messages, each with a role (user or assistant) and a content block.

docs.title: Elicitation requestedSchema
docs.text:
Form-mode elicitation uses a deliberately restricted subset of JSON Schema: a flat object with primitive properties only, so any client can render it as a simple form.

Allowed property type Options string minLength, maxLength, format (email, uri, date, date-time), default number / integer minimum, maximum, default boolean default enum (single select) enum: [...], or oneOf: [{const, title}] for titled options enum (multi select) type: array with items.enum or items.anyOf: [{const, title}], minItems, maxItems

Not supported: nested objects, arrays of objects (beyond enums) and other advanced keywords. Every primitive supports default, and clients that support defaults SHOULD pre-populate fields with them.

This is a useful contrast for the exam. Tool inputSchema accepts any 2020-12 keyword (programs and models fill it). Elicitation requestedSchema is restricted (humans fill it, through a generic UI).

docs.title: 7. Reading a server’s “manifest”
docs.text:
Put it together. Given this server/discover result and one tool definition, what can you say?

{
  "resultType": "complete",
  "supportedVersions": ["2026-07-28"],
  "capabilities": {
    "tools": { "listChanged": true },
    "resources": { "subscribe": true },
    "extensions": { "io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks": {} }
  },
  "_meta": { "io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo": { "name": "deploy-server", "version": "3.1.0" } },
  "ttlMs": 3600000,
  "cacheScope": "public"
}

{
  "name": "deploy_service",
  "description": "Deploy a service version to an environment",
  "inputSchema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "service": { "type": "string" },
      "environment": { "type": "string", "enum": ["staging", "production"], "x-mcp-header": "Environment" },
      "version": { "type": "string" }
    },
    "required": ["service", "environment", "version"],
    "additionalProperties": false
  },
  "annotations": { "destructiveHint": true, "idempotentHint": true }
}
  • Speaks only 2026-07-28; a legacy client cannot use it.
  • Offers tools and will send tools/list_changed to clients that subscribe via subscriptions/listen.
  • Offers resources with per-resource update subscriptions, but not resource listChanged.
  • Offers no prompts and no completions.
  • Supports the Tasks extension: deploy_service might return a task handle instead of blocking.
  • The discovery result can be cached for one hour and shared across users (public).
  • deploy_service needs three strings, rejects extra arguments, and restricts environment to two values.
  • Over Streamable HTTP, the client must send Mcp-Param-Environment: production alongside the body.
  • It is not read-only, may be destructive, but is idempotent: deploying the same version twice has no additional effect. Those hints are untrusted unless this server is trusted.
  • A careful host should confirm before calling it, especially for production.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• schema.ts is the source of truth; schema.json is generated.
  • JSON Schema default dialect is 2020-12; others via $schema; 2020-12 support is mandatory.
  • Never auto-dereference network $refs; reject schemas with unresolved external refs; bound composition keywords against DoS.
  • inputSchema must be an object schema, not null; for no parameters prefer {"type":"object","additionalProperties":false}.
  • outputSchema present → server MUST return conforming structuredContent; clients SHOULD validate. structuredContent can be any JSON value, and should be mirrored as text for compatibility.
  • Tool annotations readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, openWorldHint have conservative defaults and are untrusted unless the server is trusted.
  • Content types: text, image, audio (base64), resource_link (pointer), resource (embedded).
  • Content annotations: audience, priority (0–1), lastModified.
  • Prompt arguments are a simple list, not JSON Schema. Elicitation schemas are flat primitives only.

docs.title: Transports
docs.text:
Part of the exam focus on transports.

The data layer defines what is said. A transport defines how it travels: framing, delivery, where metadata lives, how cancellation is signaled. The specification is explicit that this separation is strict:

Protocol semantics are identical on every transport. A transport is a binding: it defines how messages are framed and delivered, how request metadata is carried, and how cancellation and termination are signaled. It does not define what the messages mean.

MCP defines two standard transports, stdio and Streamable HTTP, and allows custom ones.

docs.title: 1. What every transport must do
docs.text:
A transport binding MUST deliver:

  • client-sent requests and notifications to the server, and
  • server-sent responses and notifications to the client.

No other message direction exists. Because servers never send requests and clients never send responses, a transport only needs to carry traffic in this one shape. That is a large simplification compared with earlier revisions.

Messages are JSON-RPC, UTF-8 encoded. All protocol metadata lives in the message body (_meta). A transport MAY mirror some body fields into envelope metadata (HTTP does, as headers), but the body remains the source of truth.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
In the stdio transport, the client launches the server as a subprocess and they talk over the subprocess’s standard streams.

┌──────────── Host process ─────────────┐        ┌────── Server subprocess ──────┐
│                                       │ stdin  │                               │
│   Client ─────── requests, ──────────────────► │  reads one JSON message/line  │
│           notifications/cancelled     │        │                               │
│                                       │ stdout │                               │
│   Client ◄────── responses, ─────────────────── │  writes one JSON message/line │
│                  notifications        │        │                               │
│                                       │ stderr │                               │
│   (capture / forward / ignore) ◄──────────────── │  logs, anything else          │
└───────────────────────────────────────┘        └───────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: The framing rules
docs.text:
• The server reads JSON-RPC messages from stdin and writes them to stdout.
  • Each message is a single JSON-RPC request, notification or response.
  • Messages are delimited by newlines and MUST NOT contain embedded newlines.
  • The server MUST NOT write anything to stdout that is not a valid MCP message.
  • The client MUST NOT write anything to the server’s stdin that is not a valid MCP message.
  • The server MAY write UTF-8 to stderr for any logging: informational, debug or error.
  • The client MAY capture, forward or ignore stderr, and SHOULD NOT assume stderr output means an error.

The classic stdio bug

A server that calls print("Starting up...") writes a non-JSON line to stdout. The client tries to parse it as a JSON-RPC message and fails, often with a confusing error far from the cause. All logging in a stdio server goes to stderr. This is also the recommended replacement for the deprecated MCP Logging feature.

Pretty-printed JSON breaks it too: embedded newlines split one message across several lines.

docs.title: Direction on stdio
docs.text:
• The client writes requests and notifications to stdin, and MUST NOT write responses.
  • The server writes three kinds of message to stdout:
  • Responses, correlated by id
  • Request-scoped notifications such as notifications/progress
  • Subscription notifications for an active subscriptions/listen, which the client MUST correlate using io.modelcontextprotocol/subscriptionId in _meta, because everything shares one channel
  • The server MUST NOT write JSON-RPC requests to stdout.

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text: stdio has no header layer. Everything, including version and capabilities, is inline in each message’s _meta.

docs.title: Cancellation
docs.text: There are no per-request streams to close, so to cancel an in-flight request the client MUST send notifications/cancelled with the request’s id. The server SHOULD stop work as soon as practical and MUST NOT send further messages for that request.

docs.title: Shutdown
docs.text:
The client SHOULD shut down by:

  1. Closing the server’s stdin.
  2. Waiting for the server to exit.
  3. If it doesn’t exit in reasonable time, forcibly terminating it: on POSIX, escalating from SIGTERM to SIGKILL; on Windows, TerminateProcess or Job Objects.

Servers SHOULD exit promptly when stdin closes or reads return end-of-file. This is the primary, and only portable, graceful-shutdown signal. A server MAY initiate shutdown by closing its stdout and exiting.

docs.title: Unexpected termination
docs.text:
If the server process dies, the client SHOULD restart it. Because the protocol is stateless, in-flight requests are simply lost and can be retried against the new process. Active subscriptions/listen streams must be re-established; the server holds no subscription state across restarts.

A stdio process is not a session

Clients SHOULD NOT use an individual task, thread or conversation as the lifetime of the stdio process. One process can serve interleaved requests from many conversations, and the server must not treat process identity as conversation identity.

docs.title: Authorization on stdio
docs.text:
The authorization framework is for HTTP. Implementations using stdio SHOULD NOT follow it, and instead retrieve credentials from the environment: environment variables or configuration passed at launch.

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "github": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-github"],
      "env": { "GITHUB_TOKEN": "..." }
    }
  }
}

That configuration shape (used by Claude Desktop’s claude_desktop_config.json) is host-specific, not part of the specification.

docs.title: When to use stdio
docs.text:
• Local integrations: filesystem, local git, local databases, developer tools.
  • Single user, one client per process.
  • Lowest overhead: no network, no HTTP stack.
  • Natural access control: only the launching client can talk to the process. The security best practices recommend stdio for local servers precisely to “limit access to just the MCP client”.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
In Streamable HTTP, the server is an independent process that can handle many clients.

  • The server exposes one HTTP endpoint, the MCP endpoint, that accepts POST (for example https://example.com/mcp).
  • Every JSON-RPC message from the client is its own HTTP POST.
  • For each request the server replies with either a single JSON object or an SSE stream scoped to that request.
  • Server-to-client interactions (elicitation and friends) are embedded in results as MRTR input requests.
  • Long-lived change notifications arrive on the response stream of a subscriptions/listen request.

Streamable HTTP was introduced in 2025-03-26 to replace the two-endpoint HTTP+SSE transport, and was significantly reshaped in 2026-07-28: the GET stream endpoint and protocol-level sessions were removed.

docs.title: Sending messages
docs.text:
1. The client MUST use POST.
  2. The client MUST send an Accept header listing both application/json and text/event-stream.
  3. The client MUST include the request metadata headers (section 3.3).
  4. The body MUST be a single JSON-RPC request or notification. The client MUST NOT send responses.
  5. If the body is a notification:
    • accepted → 202 Accepted, no body;
    • not accepted → an HTTP error such as 400, optionally with a JSON-RPC error body that has no id.
  6. If the body is a request, the server MUST return either Content-Type: application/json or Content-Type: text/event-stream, and the client MUST support both.

No client notifications over HTTP in the core protocol

The only client-sent notification in the core, notifications/cancelled, is used only on stdio. On Streamable HTTP, closing the response stream is the cancellation.

docs.title: Receiving messages
docs.text:
When the server chooses an SSE response:

  • It MAY send notifications before the final response (for example notifications/progress). These MUST relate to the originating request.
  • It MUST NOT send independent JSON-RPC requests on the stream. That was allowed in 2025-03-26 through 2025-11-25 and is no longer part of the protocol.
  • The final JSON-RPC response SHOULD terminate the stream.

Streams are not resumable. Last-Event-ID is not supported. If a response stream breaks, the in-flight request is lost and the client MUST re-issue it as a new request with a new id.

Operational details worth knowing:

  • Servers SHOULD send X-Accel-Buffering: no on SSE responses, so reverse proxies such as nginx don’t buffer events and delay them.
  • For long-lived streams (especially subscriptions/listen), servers are encouraged to send periodic SSE comment lines (a line starting with :) as keep-alives, so idle connections aren’t closed by intermediaries. Clients must ignore them.
sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant Server
    Note over Client,Server: Simple response
    Client->>Server: POST tools/call
    Server-->>Client: 200 application/json, JSON-RPC response
    Note over Client,Server: Streaming response
    Client->>Server: POST tools/call
    Server-->>Client: 200 text/event-stream
    Server-->>Client: SSE: notifications/progress
    Server-->>Client: SSE: JSON-RPC response (stream closes)
    Note over Client,Server: Notification
    Client->>Server: POST (JSON-RPC notification)
    Server-->>Client: 202 Accepted

docs.title: 3.3 Request metadata headers 2026
docs.text:
Streamable HTTP mirrors selected body fields into HTTP headers, so load balancers, gateways, WAFs and observability tools can route and inspect traffic without parsing the JSON body.

Header Source field Required on MCP-Protocol-Version _meta["io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion"] Every POST Mcp-Method method All requests Mcp-Name params.name or params.uri tools/call, resources/read, prompts/get 
POST /mcp HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json, text/event-stream
MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28
Mcp-Method: tools/call
Mcp-Name: get_weather

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"get_weather", ...}}

Version handling:

  • MCP-Protocol-Version MUST match the body’s protocol version; otherwise 400 + HeaderMismatch (-32020).
  • Unsupported version → 400 + UnsupportedProtocolVersionError (-32022) listing supported versions.
  • Unknown method → 404 Not Found + JSON-RPC -32601 (Method not found). The JSON-RPC body is what distinguishes this from a 404 from a legacy server that doesn’t host the endpoint at all.
  • A server supporting clients older than 2025-06-18 (before the header existed) MAY treat a missing header as 2025-03-26; otherwise it MUST reject requests without it.

docs.title: Custom headers from tool parameters
docs.text:
A server MAY mark a tool parameter with x-mcp-header in its inputSchema. Clients MUST support this: when calling that tool over Streamable HTTP, they add a Mcp-Param-{Name} header carrying the argument value.

"region": { "type": "string", "x-mcp-header": "Region" }

Mcp-Param-Region: us-west1

This lets infrastructure route by region or tenant without reading the body.

Constraints on the annotation (a violating tool definition is invalid, and a client MUST exclude that tool from its tools/list result, SHOULD log a warning, and keep using the valid ones):

  • non-empty, valid HTTP token characters, no CR/LF
  • case-insensitively unique within the schema
  • only on primitive types: string, integer, boolean. Not number. Integers must be within the JavaScript safe range (±2⁵³−1)
  • only on properties statically reachable through a chain of properties keys: not through items, oneOf / anyOf / allOf / not, if/then/else, or $ref

Value encoding: strings as-is, integers as decimal, booleans as lowercase true/false. A value that isn’t safe plain ASCII (non-ASCII, control characters, leading/trailing whitespace) MUST be Base64-encoded with a sentinel:

Mcp-Param-Greeting: =?base64?SGVsbG8sIOS4lueVjA==?=

The same sentinel encoding applies to Mcp-Name for names or URIs outside the safe character set. A plain value that happens to look like the sentinel must itself be encoded, to avoid ambiguity.

A null or absent argument → the client omits the header. A present argument with the header missing → the server MUST reject the request.

Headers are visible to intermediaries

Server developers SHOULD NOT mark sensitive parameters (passwords, API keys, tokens, PII) with x-mcp-header. Proxies, load balancers and logs see headers.

docs.title: Server validation: why mismatches are rejected
docs.text:
Servers that process the body MUST reject any request where a mirrored header disagrees with the body, with 400 Bad Request and -32020 HeaderMismatch. Failure conditions include a missing required header, a value mismatch (after decoding Base64 values), and invalid characters.

The reason is a classic security bug: two components trusting two different sources of truth. Imagine a gateway that authorizes by Mcp-Name: read_report while the server executes params.name: "delete_all_reports" from the body. Forcing headers and body to match makes the check and the action refer to the same thing.

Intermediaries that enforce policy on mirrored headers SHOULD verify the protocol version requires header–body validation, and reject requests with older or missing versions rather than trusting unvalidated headers.

docs.title: Security and the endpoint
docs.text:
1. Servers MUST validate the Origin header on all incoming connections to prevent DNS rebinding. If Origin is present and invalid → 403 Forbidden.
  2. When running locally, servers SHOULD bind to 127.0.0.1, not 0.0.0.0.
  3. Servers SHOULD implement proper authentication for all connections.

DNS rebinding, explained: you visit evil.example in a browser. Its DNS record first points to the attacker’s server (which serves JavaScript), then is quickly changed to 127.0.0.1. The browser’s same-origin policy considers it the same origin (evil.example), so that JavaScript can now send requests to a service on your localhost, such as an unauthenticated local MCP server bound to a port. Checking Origin (which will say evil.example) and binding only to loopback defeat it.

docs.title: Cancellation on HTTP
docs.text: Closing the SSE response stream is cancellation. The server MUST treat a client disconnect as cancellation of that request, SHOULD stop work, and MUST NOT send further messages for it. No notifications/cancelled is needed or expected. Because every request has its own stream, the disconnect is unambiguous.

docs.title: Authorization on HTTP
docs.text: Implementations using HTTP SHOULD conform to the MCP OAuth 2.1 authorization framework. Access tokens go in Authorization: Bearer <token> on every request, and never in the query string. See Authorization with OAuth 2.1.

docs.title: Legacy HTTP traffic
docs.text:
A server that supports only 2026-07-28 and receives old-style traffic SHOULD:

Legacy traffic Response GET or DELETE to the MCP endpoint 405 Method Not Allowed Mcp-Session-Id header Ignore it; do not mint or echo session IDs Last-Event-ID header Ignore it; streams are not resumable

docs.title: 4. Choosing a transport
docs.text:
Consideration stdio Streamable HTTP Location Same machine Anywhere on the network Process model Client launches server Server runs independently Clients per server Typically one Many Framing Newline-delimited JSON One POST per message; JSON or SSE reply Metadata Inline _meta only _meta plus mirrored headers Cancellation notifications/cancelled Close the response stream Subscription correlation MUST use subscriptionId (shared channel) One stream per listen request (id still carried) Credentials Environment OAuth 2.1 bearer tokens Logging stderr Server’s own logging / OpenTelemetry Key security measures Sandboxing, consent before launch Origin validation, loopback bind locally, auth, token audience Scaling N/A (per user) Stateless: any instance serves any request

Exam reflex

Local, single-user, same machine → stdio. Remote, multi-user, networked → Streamable HTTP.

docs.title: 5. Custom transports
docs.text:
Clients and servers MAY implement custom transports. They MUST preserve:

  • the JSON-RPC message format,
  • the message patterns (request/response, MRTR, subscribe/notify), and
  • the per-request metadata model.

They SHOULD document connection establishment, framing and cancellation.

Custom transports over a reliable bidirectional byte stream (Unix domain sockets, TCP) SHOULD reuse the stdio framing, meaning newline-delimited JSON-RPC. Only the subprocess-specific parts (launch, stderr, shutdown by closing stdin, restart) need equivalents.

docs.title: 6. The deprecated HTTP+SSE transport
docs.text:
For recognition only. The 2024-11-05 HTTP+SSE transport used two endpoints: a GET endpoint that opened an SSE stream whose first event (endpoint) told the client where to POST, and a separate POST endpoint. It has been deprecated since 2025-03-26 and is formally Deprecated under the lifecycle policy, eligible for removal three months after SEP-2596 reaches Final. Migrate to Streamable HTTP.

A client supporting it falls back like this: POST to the URL; on 400/404/405 without a recognized modern JSON-RPC error body, issue a GET and wait for an endpoint event.

docs.title: 7. Recap
docs.text:
• A transport is a binding: framing, delivery, metadata placement, cancellation. Semantics are identical on every transport.
  • stdio: client launches server; newline-delimited JSON on stdin/stdout, no embedded newlines; nothing but MCP on stdout; logs to stderr; cancel with notifications/cancelled; shut down by closing stdin, then SIGTERM → SIGKILL; restart on crash; credentials from the environment.
  • Streamable HTTP: one MCP endpoint; every message is a POST; Accept lists JSON and SSE; reply is JSON or a request-scoped SSE stream; notifications get 202; no server requests on streams; not resumable; closing the stream cancels.
  • Required headers: MCP-Protocol-Version (all), Mcp-Method (all requests), Mcp-Name (tools/call, resources/read, prompts/get). Mismatch → 400 + -32020. Unknown method → 404 + -32601.
  • x-mcp-header → Mcp-Param-{Name}; primitives only (no number); Base64 sentinel =?base64?…?=; never for secrets.
  • Validate Origin (invalid → 403), bind to 127.0.0.1 locally, authenticate.
  • Legacy GET/DELETE → 405; ignore Mcp-Session-Id and Last-Event-ID.
  • HTTP+SSE is deprecated.

docs.title: Versioning & Discovery
docs.text:
Part of the exam focus on capabilities; supports the competency MCP Hosts, Clients and Servers.

Two programs written by strangers need to agree on which version of the protocol they speak and which features each supports. This chapter covers how that agreement works in 2026-07-28, and how modern implementations interoperate with the older, handshake-based protocol.

docs.title: 1. Version identifiers
docs.text:
MCP versions are strings in YYYY-MM-DD format, indicating the last date backward-incompatible changes were made.

The protocol version is not incremented for backward-compatible updates. The spec can gain clarifications, new optional fields and similar improvements while keeping the same version string, so interoperability is preserved.

docs.title: Revision states
docs.text:
State Meaning Draft In progress, not ready for consumption Current The current version, ready for use; may still receive backward-compatible changes Final Past, complete, frozen

At the time the exam was published, the current revision is 2026-07-28.

docs.title: Feature states
docs.text:
Individual features have their own lifecycle, under the feature lifecycle and deprecation policy:

State Meaning Active Normal Deprecated Still in the spec and working; new implementations SHOULD NOT adopt it; existing ones SHOULD migrate; stays at least 12 months (or 90 days under the expedited-removal exception) before becoming eligible for removal Removed Taken out in a later revision

“Eligible for removal” is a floor, not a schedule. The actual removal is a Core Maintainer decision taken during release preparation, and may happen later.

docs.title: 2. Terminology: protocol eras
docs.text:
2026-07-28 introduces three terms you should know precisely:

Term Meaning Modern Versions that convey version, identity and capabilities as per-request metadata (2026-07-28 and later) Legacy Versions that establish a session with an initialize handshake (2025-11-25 and earlier) Dual-era An implementation supporting both modern and legacy versions

docs.title: 3. Per-request version negotiation
docs.text:
There is no negotiation handshake. Every request declares its version, and the server accepts or rejects each request independently:

sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant Server
    Client->>Server: request (_meta protocolVersion: X)
    alt server supports X
        Server-->>Client: result
    else X unsupported
        Server-->>Client: UnsupportedProtocolVersionError (supported: [...])
        Note over Client,Server: Client retries with a mutually supported version
    end

Where the version lives:

  • In the body: _meta["io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion"] (always).
  • On Streamable HTTP, also in the MCP-Protocol-Version header, which must match.

If the server doesn’t implement the requested version, whether it is unknown or known but deliberately unsupported, it MUST return UnsupportedProtocolVersionError:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 1,
  "error": {
    "code": -32022,
    "message": "Unsupported protocol version",
    "data": { "supported": ["2026-07-28", "2025-11-25"], "requested": "1900-01-01" }
  }
}

On HTTP the status is 400 Bad Request. The client SHOULD pick a mutually supported version from supported and retry, or surface an error to the user if none exists.

Clients and servers MAY support multiple versions at once.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A request that returns the server’s supported protocol versions, capabilities and identity in one call. Servers MUST implement it. It carries no parameters beyond the standard _meta.

Request:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": "discover-1",
  "method": "server/discover",
  "params": {
    "_meta": {
      "io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion": "2026-07-28",
      "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo": { "name": "ExampleClient", "version": "1.0.0" },
      "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities": {}
    }
  }
}

Response:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": "discover-1",
  "result": {
    "resultType": "complete",
    "supportedVersions": ["2026-07-28"],
    "capabilities": { "tools": {}, "resources": {} },
    "_meta": {
      "io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo": { "name": "ExampleServer", "version": "1.0.0" }
    },
    "instructions": "This server provides weather and resource utilities.",
    "ttlMs": 3600000,
    "cacheScope": "public"
  }
}

docs.title: DiscoverResult fields
docs.text:
Field Meaning supportedVersions Versions the server supports; the client should choose one of these capabilities Server capabilities: tools, resources, prompts, completions, logging, extensions _meta["io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo"] Name and version of the server software (SHOULD be included; unverified) instructions Optional natural-language guidance for LLMs on how to use this server well ttlMs, cacheScope Caching hints (required on this result)

The instructions field deserves a moment. It is text the server writes for the model, for example “Always call search_tickets before create_ticket to avoid duplicates.” A host may add it to the model’s context. Like tool descriptions, it is server-authored text entering the model’s context, and should be treated with the same trust as the server itself.

docs.title: When to call it
docs.text:
Calling server/discover is optional for clients. A client may send any RPC directly and handle UnsupportedProtocolVersionError. The spec gives two situations where calling it is useful:

  1. Presenting server information. One request returns identity, capabilities and versions, instead of probing with tools/list, prompts/list and resources/list separately.
  2. stdio backward-compatibility probe. On stdio there are no HTTP status codes to drive fallback, so a dual-era client SHOULD send server/discover first (section 6).

Because the result carries caching hints, a client normally does not repeat discovery on every request. It caches the result for ttlMs.

server/discover vs. initialize, precisely

initialize (legacy) server/discover (modern) Server must implement? Yes Yes Client must call? Yes, first No, optional Establishes a session? Yes No Client capabilities sent Once, here On every request Result cacheable? No Yes (ttlMs, cacheScope)

docs.title: Server capabilities (from server/discover)
docs.text:
Capability Sub-options Enables tools listChanged tools/list, tools/call; listChanged → tool list-change notifications resources subscribe, listChanged resources/list, resources/read, templates; subscribe → per-URI update notifications prompts listChanged prompts/list, prompts/get completions — completion/complete logging — Log notifications (deprecated) extensions per-extension settings Optional extensions, e.g. io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks

Implemented features MUST be advertised. Invoking tools requires the server to declare tools; receiving resource-update notifications requires the server to support subscribe and the client to open a subscriptions/listen stream naming those URIs.

docs.title: Client capabilities (in every request’s _meta)
docs.text:
Capability Sub-options Lets the server… elicitation form, url Include elicitation/create in inputRequests (only the declared modes) sampling tools, context (deprecated) Include sampling/createMessage roots — Include roots/list (deprecated) extensions per-extension settings Use negotiated extensions

Two detailed rules:

  • An empty elicitation: {} object means form mode only, for backward compatibility. A client supporting URL mode must declare url explicitly.
  • A server MUST NOT include in inputRequests any request type the client hasn’t declared, and MUST NOT rely on undeclared capabilities at all. If it needs one, it returns MissingRequiredClientCapabilityError (-32021) with data.requiredCapabilities.

docs.title: Capabilities are per request
docs.text: Because client capabilities travel on each request, they can legitimately differ from one request to the next. A host might declare elicitation for requests made during an interactive chat, and omit it for a background job where no user is present to answer. The server must evaluate each request against that request’s declared capabilities.

docs.title: 6. Extension negotiation
docs.text:
Extensions are advertised in the extensions field of capabilities: a map from extension identifier to a settings object.

"capabilities": {
  "tools": {},
  "extensions": {
    "io.modelcontextprotocol/ui": { "mimeTypes": ["text/html;profile=mcp-app"] },
    "io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks": {}
  }
}
  • Identifiers follow the _meta key naming rules, with a mandatory prefix ({vendor-prefix}/{name}). Official extensions use io.modelcontextprotocol/.
  • Each extension defines its settings schema. An empty object means “supported, no settings”.
  • Extensions are always opt-in, and disabled by default.

If only one side supports an extension, the supporting side MUST either fall back to core protocol behavior or reject the request with an appropriate error (if the extension is mandatory for it). Extensions SHOULD document their fallback. For example, a server offering MCP Apps UI should still return meaningful text to clients without the UI extension.

Full coverage: Extensions.

docs.title: The compatibility matrix
docs.text:
Client Server Outcome Modern Modern Works. Discovery optional; version mismatches → retry Modern Legacy Fails. The server may reject, stay silent, or even process an ambiguous method under legacy rules. On stdio the client SHOULD probe first so it fails deterministically with an actionable error Dual-era Modern Works. Probe succeeds or returns a modern error; client stays modern Dual-era Legacy Works. Probe fails in a non-modern way; client falls back to initialize (and possibly to HTTP+SSE) Legacy Modern Fails. stdio: initialize is unknown and lacks _meta, so it is rejected. HTTP: missing headers → 400 Legacy Dual-era Works. Server answers initialize and serves legacy semantics Legacy Legacy Works per the legacy revision

The asymmetry to remember: dual-era clients can reach everyone; legacy clients can’t reach modern-only servers, because legacy clients have no fall-forward mechanism.

For that reason a modern-only server SHOULD name its supported versions in whatever error it returns to an initialize request, on any transport. It may be the only diagnostic a legacy user ever sees.

docs.title: Detecting the era on stdio
docs.text:
A dual-era client SHOULD send server/discover first, with its preferred modern version:

Probe outcome Conclusion Action DiscoverResult Modern server Choose a version from supportedVersions; continue Recognized modern error (e.g. UnsupportedProtocolVersionError) Modern server, different version Use a version from supported; do not fall back to initialize Any other error, or timeout Legacy server Fall back to the initialize handshake

The fallback MUST NOT be keyed to one specific error code. Legacy servers answer unknown pre-initialize requests with implementation-defined errors (commonly -32601 or -32602), or not at all.

Probing is RECOMMENDED even for modern-only clients. Some legacy servers don’t check that initialize came first, and would process an era-ambiguous method like tools/call under legacy semantics, producing confusing partial success. A probe gives a clean, deterministic failure.

docs.title: Detecting the era on Streamable HTTP
docs.text:
A dual-era client MAY send a modern request first. On 400 Bad Request it SHOULD inspect the body before falling back, because modern servers also use 400 for version, capability and header errors:

400 body Conclusion Action Recognized modern JSON-RPC error Modern server Retry with a supported version, or fix the request Empty, or not a recognized modern error Legacy server Fall back to initialize, and possibly to HTTP+SSE

docs.title: Caching the result
docs.text: The era is a property of the server, not of a request. Clients SHOULD cache the determination for the lifetime of the server process (stdio) or origin (HTTP), and MAY persist it across restarts of the same configuration, re-probing if the cached assumption later fails.

docs.title: Dual-era servers
docs.text:
A dual-era server picks its behavior from how the client opens:

  • A request with modern per-request _meta → served statelessly under 2026-07-28.
  • An initialize request → legacy semantics, scoped to the stdio process or the HTTP session.

It MAY serve both eras concurrently on the same endpoint or process.

docs.title: 8. Recap
docs.text:
• Versions are YYYY-MM-DD = last backward-incompatible change. Revisions: Draft, Current, Final. Features: Active, Deprecated (≥12 months, or 90 days expedited), Removed.
  • Modern = per-request metadata (2026-07-28+); legacy = initialize handshake; dual-era = both.
  • No handshake: every request declares its version; unsupported → -32022 with supported, and the client retries.
  • server/discover: servers MUST implement, clients MAY call. Returns supportedVersions, capabilities, serverInfo, optional instructions, and cache hints.
  • Server capabilities come from discovery; client capabilities ride on every request and may differ per request. Empty elicitation = form only.
  • Needing an undeclared client capability → -32021.
  • Extensions: extensions map, prefixed identifiers, opt-in; if unsupported by the peer, fall back or reject.
  • stdio era detection: probe with server/discover; non-modern error or timeout → legacy. Never key fallback on one code.
  • HTTP era detection: modern request first; on 400, inspect the body.
  • Legacy clients can’t reach modern-only servers; such servers should name their versions in the initialize error. Cache era per process or origin.

docs.title: Domain 3 — Interactions & Execution 26%
docs.text:
The heaviest domain, and the most mechanical. It covers how clients and servers actually do things together: calling tools, reading resources, getting prompts, pausing for user input, streaming progress, cancelling, handling failure, caching and paginating.

Most of what changed in 2026-07-28 lives here. If you study one domain twice, study this one.

docs.title: Competencies
docs.text: Competency Chapters Interaction Patterns & Response Handling MRTR & Elicitation, Subscriptions, Progress & Cancellation Error Handling Error Handling Tool Invocation Lifecycle Tools & the Invocation Lifecycle Protocol Primitives Resources & Prompts, Caching, Pagination & Completion, Deprecated Features

docs.title: The three message patterns
docs.text:
Every interaction in this domain is built from exactly three patterns. The specification says all core features are built from them, and every transport carries all three.

Pattern Shape Used for Request and response Client request → (optional request-scoped notifications) → result or error Almost everything Multi Round-Trip Requests Request → InputRequiredResult → client retries with input → result Elicitation, and deprecated sampling and roots Subscribe and notify subscriptions/listen → acknowledgment → stream of notifications List changes, resource updates
  • Tools & the Invocation Lifecycle: discovery, selection, confirmation, execution, results, stateful handles.
  • Resources & Prompts: URIs, templates, reading, subscriptions, prompt templates.
  • MRTR & Elicitation: InputRequiredResult, requestState, form and URL elicitation.
  • Subscriptions, Progress & Cancellation: subscriptions/listen, progress tokens, cancellation and timeouts.
  • Error Handling: protocol vs. tool errors, every code, HTTP statuses.
  • Caching, Pagination & Completion: ttlMs, cacheScope, cursors, argument completion.
  • Deprecated: Sampling, Roots & Logging: how they work, why they are deprecated, what to use instead.
  • Quiz: 20 questions.

docs.title: Deprecated: Sampling, Roots & Logging
docs.text:
Competency: Protocol Primitives.

2026-07-28 deprecated three long-standing features. Deprecated is not removed: they remain in the specification, still work, and still appear in exam questions. You need to know how they work, why they were deprecated, and what replaces them.

docs.title: 1. What “deprecated” means precisely
docs.text:
Under the feature lifecycle and deprecation policy adopted in this revision (SEP-2596):

  • A Deprecated feature remains part of the specification and remains fully functional.
  • New implementations SHOULD NOT adopt it.
  • Existing implementations SHOULD migrate before its earliest removal.
  • It stays for at least twelve months before becoming eligible for removal (or ninety days under the expedited-removal exception).
  • Eligible is a floor, not a date. Actual removal is a Core Maintainer decision made during release preparation, and may be later.
  • Every deprecated feature is listed in the public deprecated features registry with its SEP, migration path and earliest removal.
Feature Deprecated in Migration path Earliest removal Sampling 2026-07-28 (SEP-2577) Integrate directly with LLM provider APIs First revision on or after 2027-07-28 Roots 2026-07-28 (SEP-2577) Pass directories/files via tool parameters, resource URIs or server configuration First revision on or after 2027-07-28 Logging 2026-07-28 (SEP-2577) Log to stderr (stdio); use OpenTelemetry First revision on or after 2027-07-28 includeContext: "thisServer" / "allServers" 2025-11-25, reclassified by SEP-2596 Omit it or use "none" No later than Sampling Dynamic Client Registration 2026-07-28 (PR #2858) Client ID Metadata Documents First revision on or after 2027-07-28 HTTP+SSE transport 2025-03-26, reclassified by SEP-2596 Streamable HTTP Three months after SEP-2596 reaches Final

Exam trap

  • “Sampling has been removed from MCP” → wrong.
  • “Servers can no longer request sampling” → wrong. They can, via MRTR.
  • “New implementations should not adopt sampling” → right.

docs.title: 2. What sampling does
docs.text:
The Model Context Protocol provides a standardized way for servers to request LLM sampling (“completions” or “generations”) from language models via clients. This flow allows clients to maintain control over model access, selection, and permissions while enabling servers to leverage AI capabilities — with no server API keys necessary.

The appeal was clear. A server wanting AI help (summarizing, classifying, picking the best of 47 flights) could borrow the client’s model instead of bringing its own API key, and the client kept control of which model, cost and permissions.

docs.title: 3. How it works in 2026-07-28
docs.text:
Like all server-to-client requests, sampling now goes through MRTR. The server returns an InputRequiredResult containing a sampling/createMessage request; the client runs it through its LLM (with human review) and retries the original request with the CreateMessageResult in inputResponses.

Capability (in each request’s client capabilities):

{ "sampling": {} }                    // basic
{ "sampling": { "tools": {} } }       // tool use inside sampling
{ "sampling": { "context": {} } }     // context inclusion (itself deprecated)

Input request:

{
  "method": "sampling/createMessage",
  "params": {
    "messages": [ { "role": "user", "content": { "type": "text", "text": "What is the capital of France?" } } ],
    "modelPreferences": {
      "hints": [ { "name": "claude-3-sonnet" } ],
      "costPriority": 0.3,
      "intelligencePriority": 0.8,
      "speedPriority": 0.5
    },
    "temperature": 0.1,
    "systemPrompt": "You are a helpful assistant.",
    "maxTokens": 100
  }
}

Client result (inside inputResponses):

{
  "role": "assistant",
  "content": { "type": "text", "text": "The capital of France is Paris." },
  "model": "claude-3-sonnet-20240307",
  "stopReason": "endTurn"
}

docs.title: 4. Model selection: preferences, not names
docs.text:
A server cannot simply demand a model by name. The client may not have it, or may prefer an equivalent from another provider. So MCP uses abstract priorities plus hints:

Priorities (each 0–1):

Priority Higher value prefers costPriority Cheaper models speedPriority Faster (lower-latency) models intelligencePriority More capable models

Hints: an ordered list of { name } treated as substrings that match model names flexibly ("claude-3-sonnet", then fallback "claude"). Clients MAY map hints to equivalent models from other providers. A client with only Gemini might map a Sonnet hint to a comparable Gemini model. Hints are advisory; the client makes the final choice.

docs.title: 5. Parameters and their obligations
docs.text:
Parameter Client obligation maxTokens Required. The client MUST respect it temperature, stopSequences, metadata Client MAY modify or ignore (the model may not support them) systemPrompt Client MAY modify or ignore without telling the server includeContext "none" (default), "thisServer", "allServers"; client MAY modify or ignore. The last two are deprecated

includeContext is instructive. "allServers" asked the client to include context from every connected server in a completion requested by one server, which runs directly against the design principle that servers must not “see into” other servers. Its deprecation predates sampling’s.

docs.title: 6. Result fields
docs.text:
• role ("assistant")
  • content: a single block, or an array (e.g. multiple tool uses)
  • model: the model actually used
  • stopReason: "endTurn", "stopSequence", "maxTokens", "toolUse", or an implementation-defined value

docs.title: 7. Tools in sampling
docs.text:
Since 2025-11-25, a server can let the client’s LLM use tools during sampling, by sending tools and optional toolChoice. The tool definitions are scoped to that request; they don’t need to be tools the server exposes.

  • Clients MUST declare sampling.tools to receive tool-enabled sampling requests; servers MUST NOT send them otherwise.
  • toolChoice.mode: auto (model decides; default), required (must use at least one tool), none (must not use tools).

The multi-turn tool loop:

  1. Server sends messages + tools; the LLM answers with tool_use blocks (stopReason: "toolUse").
  2. Server executes the tools itself.
  3. Server sends a new sampling request with the history plus tool_result blocks.
  4. Repeat until a final answer. Servers might cap iterations, and can pass toolChoice: {mode: "none"} on the last one to force an answer.

Two message constraints (for compatibility with provider APIs that use dedicated tool roles):

  • A user message containing tool_result MUST contain only tool results, no mixed text.
  • Every assistant message with tool_use MUST be followed by a user message of tool_results, one per tool_use id (toolUseId matches id), before any other message.

Servers MUST honor that pairing; both sides SHOULD implement iteration limits.

docs.title: 8. Human in the loop
docs.text:
For trust & safety and security, there SHOULD always be a human in the loop with the ability to deny sampling requests.

Applications SHOULD make requests easy to review, let users view and edit prompts before sending, and present generated responses for review before delivery back to the server. That gives two checkpoints: one on the way to the LLM, one on the way back.

Security considerations: approval controls, content validation on both sides, respecting model hints, rate limiting, and handling sensitive data appropriately. If an error occurs or the user declines, the client does not need to reply (MRTR: the server isn’t waiting).

docs.title: 9. Why sampling was deprecated
docs.text:
SEP-2577 states the reasons:

  • Complex to implement. Correct sampling needs human-in-the-loop approval, model selection logic, security considerations and, since SEP-1577, tool-loop support. That complexity contributed to low client adoption.
  • Low adoption. Few clients support it, despite it being available since the November 2024 specification.
  • Direct alternatives. Servers that need LLM capabilities can integrate directly with LLM provider APIs, gaining full control over model selection, parameters and streaming.

Migration: integrate directly with LLM provider APIs.

docs.title: 10. What roots do
docs.text:
Roots inform servers about the directories and files the client considers relevant, so that servers can focus their operations accordingly. They are informational guidance rather than an access-control mechanism. The protocol does not enforce that servers stay within roots.

Typically a host exposes the folders the user has open. A filesystem or git server then knows where to work.

docs.title: 11. How it works in 2026-07-28
docs.text:
Capability: {"roots": {}} in each request’s client capabilities.

Input request (inside inputRequests):

{ "method": "roots/list" }

Client result (inside inputResponses):

{ "roots": [ { "uri": "file:///home/user/projects/myproject", "name": "My Project" } ] }

A root has:

  • uri: MUST be a file:// URI in the current spec
  • name: optional display name

Changes: notifications/roots/list_changed was removed. Servers see updated roots the next time they request them.

docs.title: 12. Roots are not a security boundary
docs.text:
This is the examinable point. The client-concepts guide:

Roots serve as a coordination mechanism between clients and servers, not a security boundary. The specification requires that servers “SHOULD respect root boundaries,” and not that they “MUST enforce” them, because servers run code the client cannot control.

Real restriction must come from the operating system: file permissions, sandboxing, containers. Roots prevent accidents by well-behaved servers; they don’t stop malicious ones.

Security requirements still apply. Clients MUST only expose roots with appropriate permissions, validate root URIs to prevent path traversal, implement access controls, and monitor accessibility. Servers SHOULD handle unavailable roots, respect boundaries, and validate paths against them. Clients SHOULD prompt for consent before exposing roots.

docs.title: 13. Why roots were deprecated
docs.text:
From SEP-2577:

  • Low adoption. Few clients implement roots, and few servers rely on them.
  • Vague semantics. Roots are informational; servers aren’t required to respect them, which reduces their usefulness.
  • Overlapping alternatives. Working-directory context can be given through tool parameters, resource URIs, server configuration or environment variables, all of which are more explicit.

Migration: pass directories or files via tool parameters, resource URIs, or server configuration.

docs.title: 14. What logging does
docs.text:
Servers send structured log messages to clients, with syslog severity levels (RFC 5424):

Level Use debug Detailed debugging (function entry/exit) info General progress notice Normal but significant (config changes) warning Warning conditions (deprecated feature use) error Operation failures critical System component failures alert Immediate action needed (data corruption) emergency System unusable

docs.title: 15. How it works in 2026-07-28
docs.text:
Capability (server): {"logging": {}}.

Per-request level. logging/setLevel was removed. A client wanting logs for a request includes io.modelcontextprotocol/logLevel in that request’s _meta:

{ "_meta": { "io.modelcontextprotocol/logLevel": "warning" } }
  • The server MUST NOT emit notifications/message for a request that did not include this field.
  • When present, the server MAY send messages at or above that level, on that request’s response stream, before the final response.
  • Log notifications are request-scoped: MUST NOT be delivered on a subscriptions/listen stream or any other stream.
  • An unrecognized level → -32602.
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "method": "notifications/message",
  "params": { "level": "error", "logger": "database", "data": { "error": "Connection failed", "details": { "host": "localhost", "port": 5432 } } }
}

docs.title: 16. Security
docs.text:
Log messages MUST NOT contain:

  • credentials or secrets,
  • personal identifying information,
  • internal system details that could aid attacks.

Servers SHOULD rate limit, include relevant context, use consistent logger names, and remove sensitive information. Clients MAY display, filter or persist logs.

docs.title: 17. Why logging was deprecated
docs.text:
From SEP-2577:

  • Overlapping infrastructure. Standard mechanisms (stderr for stdio, OpenTelemetry for structured observability) are mature, widely adopted, and better suited to logging than an application-protocol channel. MCP now reserves traceparent, tracestate and baggage in _meta for exactly this.
  • Low value relative to complexity. Log message types, severity levels and logging/setLevel added implementation surface for every client and server.

Migration: log to stderr for stdio transports; use OpenTelemetry for observability. See Auditability & Observability.

docs.title: 4. The common thread
docs.text:
SEP-2577 frames all three deprecations with one principle: “The MCP specification aims to remain minimal and focused. Features that see low adoption, overlap with existing alternatives, or impose disproportionate implementation burden relative to their value are candidates for removal.”

A useful way to see the pattern (this framing is the course’s, not the SEP’s): all three were ways for a server to reach back into the client.

Feature Server reaches into the client’s… Replacement Sampling model The server’s own provider integration Roots workspace Explicit arguments, URIs, configuration Logging log view stderr, OpenTelemetry

The SEP also notes that during the deprecation period wire-level behavior is unchanged: no types are removed, capability negotiation is unchanged, and no existing implementation breaks. The deprecation is a signal to stop building on these features.

Elicitation is not deprecated. Asking the user for input or consent has no substitute outside the host, which is the only party with a UI.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Deprecated ≠ removed. Still in the spec and functional; new implementations SHOULD NOT adopt; ≥ 12 months before removal eligibility; earliest removal for all three: first revision on or after 2027-07-28.
