  • Sampling: sampling/createMessage via MRTR; modelPreferences (cost/speed/intelligence priorities + substring hints; client decides); maxTokens required and must be respected; tools via sampling.tools with auto/required/none and strict tool_use / tool_result pairing; two human review checkpoints. Migrate to direct provider APIs. includeContext thisServer/allServers deprecated.
  • Roots: roots/list via MRTR; file:// only; advisory, not a security boundary; roots/list_changed removed. Migrate to tool parameters, resource URIs, server configuration.
  • Logging: syslog levels; per-request io.modelcontextprotocol/logLevel (logging/setLevel removed); no messages without it; request-scoped only; no secrets or PII. Migrate to stderr and OpenTelemetry.
  • Elicitation remains active.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Competency: Error Handling.

Things go wrong in several distinct ways in MCP, and each has a specific, required reporting mechanism. Getting the mechanism right matters for more than tidiness: it decides whether a language model can recover. This chapter builds the full decision tree and every code you need.

docs.title: 1. Two families of failure
docs.text:
The tools specification defines the split that the rest of MCP follows:

Tools use two error reporting mechanisms:

  1. Protocol Errors indicate issues with the request structure itself that models are less likely to be able to fix.
  2. Tool Execution Errors contain actionable feedback that language models can use to self-correct and retry with adjusted parameters.
Protocol error Tool execution error Meaning The request couldn’t be processed as a request The request was valid; the operation failed Wire form JSON-RPC error response (error: {code, message, data?}) A normal result with isError: true resultType None (it’s not a result) "complete" Examples Unknown tool; malformed request; missing required _meta; unsupported version; internal server failure Upstream API failure; invalid date; value out of range; business rule violated; expired handle Who it’s for The client/host The model Client SHOULD give it to the model? MAY (unlikely to help) SHOULD (so it can self-correct)

docs.title: Why the distinction exists
docs.text:
Picture a model calling a flight booking tool with departure: "2025-08-01" when today is 2026-09-15.

As a protocol error:

{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 4, "error": { "code": -32602, "message": "Invalid params" } }

Many hosts surface JSON-RPC errors as generic failures, and even if the model sees this, “Invalid params” tells it nothing actionable. The conversation stalls.

As a tool execution error:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 4,
  "result": {
    "resultType": "complete",
    "content": [ { "type": "text", "text": "Invalid departure date: must be in the future. Current date is 2026-09-15." } ],
    "isError": true
  }
}

The model reads that, understands exactly what went wrong, and retries with a valid date. The error message is part of the tool’s interface to the model.

Input validation errors are tool execution errors

Since 2025-11-25 the spec has made this explicit: input validation errors (date in the wrong format, value out of range) should be returned as tool execution errors, not protocol errors, to enable model self-correction.

A schema-level failure of the request envelope, where the request doesn’t satisfy CallToolRequest at all, is a protocol error. A semantic problem with argument values the model chose is a tool execution error.

docs.title: 2. The decision tree
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Request arrives] --> B{Parseable JSON?}
    B -- no --> E1["-32700 Parse error<br/>(id may be absent)"]
    B -- yes --> C{Valid JSON-RPC request?}
    C -- no --> E2["-32600 Invalid Request"]
    C -- yes --> D{"Required _meta present?<br/>(protocolVersion, clientCapabilities)"}
    D -- no --> E3["-32602 Invalid params<br/>HTTP 400"]
    D -- yes --> F{Version supported?}
    F -- no --> E4["-32022 UnsupportedProtocolVersion<br/>data.supported, HTTP 400"]
    F -- yes --> G{"HTTP: headers match body?"}
    G -- no --> E5["-32020 HeaderMismatch<br/>HTTP 400"]
    G -- yes --> H{Method exists?}
    H -- no --> E6["-32601 Method not found<br/>HTTP 404"]
    H -- yes --> I{"Needs an undeclared<br/>client capability?"}
    I -- yes --> E7["-32021 MissingRequiredClientCapability<br/>data.requiredCapabilities, HTTP 400"]
    I -- no --> J{"Target exists?<br/>(tool / prompt / resource / cursor)"}
    J -- no --> E8["-32602 Invalid params<br/>(unknown tool, prompt, resource, cursor)"]
    J -- yes --> K{Needs more input?}
    K -- yes --> R1["result: resultType input_required"]
    K -- no --> L{Operation succeeds?}
    L -- "no (bad values, API failure, business rule)" --> R2["result: complete, isError: true"]
    L -- "no (server bug / crash)" --> E9["-32603 Internal error"]
    L -- yes --> R3["result: complete"]

The order in real implementations varies slightly, but the mapping of condition to mechanism is what the spec defines.

docs.title: Standard JSON-RPC codes
docs.text:
Code Name MCP use -32700 Parse error Invalid JSON -32600 Invalid Request Not a valid JSON-RPC request object -32601 Method not found Unknown method (HTTP 404); also “capability not supported” for completions -32602 Invalid params Missing required _meta; unknown tool; invalid prompt name; missing required prompt arguments; resource not found; invalid cursor; invalid log level; unknown skill (Skills extension) -32603 Internal error Server-side failures

-32602 is overloaded, so learn its list. When in doubt about a “doesn’t exist / wrong parameter” condition in MCP, the answer is usually -32602.

docs.title: MCP-defined codes 2026
Retired codes
docs.text:
Code Was Status -32002 Resource not found (2025-11-25 and earlier) Replaced by -32602. Implementations of this version MUST NOT emit it; clients SHOULD still accept it from older servers -32042 URL elicitation required (2025-11-25 only) MUST NOT emit. Replaced by MRTR

Codes from earlier versions remain reserved and will not be reused for something else.

docs.title: The range policy 2026
docs.text:
JSON-RPC reserves -32000 to -32099 for implementation-defined server errors. MCP partitions it:

 -32099 ┐
        │  -32020 … -32099   RESERVED FOR THE MCP SPECIFICATION
 -32020 ┘                    Only spec-defined codes, only with their defined meanings.
 -32019 ┐
        │  -32000 … -32019   LEGACY, implementation-defined
 -32000 ┘                    No new allocations. Receivers assume no meaning (except -32002).

 -32768 … -32000             Whole JSON-RPC reserved range: don't invent new codes here.
 everything else             Available for application-defined errors.

Rules:

  • New codes MUST NOT be allocated in -32000…-32019, and new implementations SHOULD NOT use them.
  • Implementations MUST NOT emit any code in -32020…-32099 that the spec doesn’t define, and MUST use defined codes only with their specified meanings.
  • New error codes for other purposes SHOULD be allocated outside -32768…-32000 entirely.
  • Errors purely local to an implementation (an SDK-side timeout, for example) have no assigned codes, and implementations should make sure they can’t be mistaken for errors received from the peer.

docs.title: 4. Errors by feature
docs.text: Feature Condition Mechanism Tools Unknown tool -32602 Request fails CallToolRequest schema Protocol error API failure, invalid values, business logic, expired handle isError: true Resources Not found -32602 (accept legacy -32002); never empty contents Internal -32603 Prompts Invalid name / missing required arguments -32602 Internal -32603 Completion Capability not supported -32601 Invalid prompt name / missing arguments -32602 Pagination Invalid cursor -32602 Logging (deprecated) Unrecognized logLevel in _meta -32602 Base protocol Missing required _meta -32602 + HTTP 400 Undeclared capability needed -32021 + HTTP 400 Unsupported version -32022 + HTTP 400 Streamable HTTP Header/body mismatch -32020 + HTTP 400 Unknown method -32601 + HTTP 404 Invalid Origin HTTP 403 (body may be an id-less JSON-RPC error) Notification not accepted HTTP 4xx (e.g. 400) Legacy GET / DELETE HTTP 405 MRTR Malformed inputResponses JSON-RPC error Missing needed input on retry New InputRequiredResult, not an error requestState fails verification Reject Elicitation User declines or cancels Not an error: action: decline / cancel; server must handle Cancellation Unknown / completed / malformed Ignore

docs.title: 5. HTTP status codes
docs.text:
On Streamable HTTP, errors have an HTTP status and usually a JSON-RPC body. Both matter: the body is how a dual-era client tells a modern server’s 400 from a legacy server’s.

Status Used for 200 Request answered (JSON or SSE), including results with isError: true and input_required 202 Notification accepted (no body) 400 Malformed request, missing _meta, header mismatch (-32020), missing capability (-32021), unsupported version (-32022) 401 Authorization required, or token invalid or expired, with WWW-Authenticate 403 Invalid Origin; insufficient scope (error="insufficient_scope"); insufficient permissions 404 Unknown method (with -32601 body) 405 GET or DELETE on a modern-only endpoint

A tool execution error is HTTP 200

isError: true lives inside a successful JSON-RPC result, so over HTTP it is a 200. An option claiming a failed tool returns a 4xx or 5xx status is describing a protocol error, not a tool execution error.

docs.title: 6. Handling errors on the client side
docs.text:
Protocol errors

  • -32022 → pick a version from data.supported and retry.
  • -32021 → the server needs a capability you didn’t declare. If you can support it (for instance, a user is present to answer elicitations), declare it and retry; otherwise surface the error.
  • -32020 → for Mcp-Param-* problems, the client SHOULD call tools/list to check for an updated inputSchema, then retry with the right headers.
  • -32601 on a supported-looking method → the server may be legacy, or lacks the capability.
  • -32602 “unknown tool” after a cached tools/list → the list may be stale. Clients MAY re-fetch before the TTL expires when they have reason to believe data changed, such as this.

Tool execution errors

  • Pass the content to the model (SHOULD) so it can adjust and retry.
  • In code-mode sandboxes, wrappers should convert isError: true into a thrown exception so model-written code can use try/catch.

Local errors

  • An SDK timeout or connection failure is local. Don’t present it as if the server returned it.

docs.title: Writing good tool error messages (server side)
docs.text:
The error text is instructions for a model. It should say:

  1. What was wrong (“departure date is in the past”),
  2. What valid looks like (“must be after 2026-09-15”, “one of: staging, production”),
  3. What to do next (“create a new basket with create_basket”).

And it must not leak secrets or internals: stack traces, connection strings, internal hostnames.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Protocol errors = JSON-RPC error responses about the request. Tool execution errors = results with isError: true about the operation, meant for the model to self-correct.
  • Input validation errors are tool execution errors.
  • Standard: -32700 parse, -32600 invalid request, -32601 method not found (HTTP 404), -32602 invalid params, -32603 internal.
  • -32602 covers: missing _meta, unknown tool, invalid prompt / missing arguments, resource not found, invalid cursor, invalid log level.
  • MCP codes: -32020 HeaderMismatch, -32021 MissingRequiredClientCapability, -32022 UnsupportedProtocolVersion, all HTTP 400.
  • -32002 retired (accept, don’t emit); -32042 retired. -32000…-32019 legacy; -32020…-32099 reserved for the spec.
  • Resource not found must never be an empty contents array.
  • Missing input on MRTR retry → new InputRequiredResult. Elicitation decline/cancel are not errors. Bad cancellations are ignored.
  • HTTP: 202 notifications, 401 auth, 403 Origin or scope, 404 unknown method, 405 legacy GET/DELETE; isError: true is still 200.

docs.title: Multi Round-Trip Requests & Elicitation
docs.text:
Competencies: Interaction Patterns & Response Handling, Protocol Primitives.

This is the most important chapter in the course for 2026-07-28. Multi Round-Trip Requests (MRTR) replaced the way servers used to ask clients for things, and elicitation is the main thing they ask for. The two are covered together because in the current protocol you cannot understand one without the other.

docs.title: Servers sometimes need something mid-request
docs.text:
A server is processing a request and discovers it can’t finish without more information:

  • A booking tool needs the user to confirm a $3,000 charge.
  • A GitHub tool needs the user’s username before it can look anything up.
  • A deploy tool wants explicit approval before touching production.
  • A server wants the user to connect a third-party account first.

Failing the request would be a poor experience. The server wants to pause, ask, and continue.

docs.title: How it used to work, and why that broke
docs.text:
Through 2025-11-25, the server sent its own JSON-RPC request to the client in the middle of handling the client’s request:

sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant Server as Server instance A
    Client->>Server: tools/call (id: 1)
    Note over Server: suspend call 1, keep its state in memory
    Server->>Client: elicitation/create (id: 99)
    Note over Client: user takes 45 seconds to answer
    Client-->>Server: result for id 99
    Note over Server: resume call 1 from memory
    Server-->>Client: result for id 1

Look at what that requires:

  1. Suspended state in memory on instance A for as long as the user takes: seconds, or hours.
  2. The answer must come back to the same instance A, or the state is lost: sticky routing, or a shared store that every instance can consult.
  3. A channel for server-initiated requests to reach the client, which on HTTP meant long-lived SSE streams or a separate GET endpoint.

For a local stdio server, fine. For a remote server running twenty instances behind a load balancer, autoscaling up and down, this is exactly the kind of state that makes horizontal scaling painful.

SEP-2322, which introduced MRTR, is blunt about the consequence: adoption of server-initiated request features like elicitation, sampling and roots was “very low or blocked for many Remote MCP servers” because of the operational complexity of SSE streams and server-side state. It also observes that most tools are ephemeral (they accumulate no server-side state and can simply start over once they have the missing information), so the protocol should be optimized for that case.

docs.title: The MRTR idea
docs.text:
Invert it. Instead of the server asking and waiting, the server answers (“I can’t finish yet; here is what I need”) and forgets. The client gathers the information and asks again, attaching the answers.

The MRTR page’s own description:

The multi round-trip requests pattern provides a standardized way to handle these server-requests without requiring a shared storage layer across server instances or requiring stateful load balancing.

The four steps:

  1. The client sends the initial request with its parameters.
  2. The server determines it needs more information and responds requesting it.
  3. The client gathers it (from the user or elsewhere) and retries the original request including that information.
  4. The server has enough and responds with the final result.
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server
    C->>S: request (id: 1, params)
    Note over S: needs more info
    S-->>C: InputRequiredResult (id: 1)
    Note over C: gather input, retry
    C->>S: request (id: 2, params + inputResponses)
    Note over S: has enough
    S-->>C: Result (id: 2)

The sentence that defines MRTR

“The requests in each step are completely independent: the server processing the retry does not need any information beyond what is directly present in the retry request.”

Request 1 ends when the server returns InputRequiredResult. Request 2 is a brand-new request that could land on a different server instance. That is the whole point.

docs.title: InputRequests
docs.text:
A map of server-to-client requests. Keys are identifiers the server chooses; values are request objects of exactly three kinds:

Request Asks for Status elicitation/create (ElicitRequest) Information or confirmation from the user Active sampling/createMessage (CreateMessageRequest) An LLM completion from the client’s model Deprecated roots/list (ListRootsRequest) The client’s filesystem roots Deprecated 
{
  "github_login": {
    "method": "elicitation/create",
    "params": {
      "mode": "form",
      "message": "Please provide your GitHub username",
      "requestedSchema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": { "name": { "type": "string" } },
        "required": ["name"]
      }
    }
  },
  "capital_of_france": {
    "method": "sampling/createMessage",
    "params": {
      "messages": [ { "role": "user", "content": { "type": "text", "text": "What is the capital of France?" } } ],
      "systemPrompt": "You are a helpful assistant.",
      "maxTokens": 100
    }
  }
}

A map rather than a single request means the server can ask for several things at once, and the client can fulfil them all before one retry.

docs.title: InputResponses
docs.text:
A map with the same keys, holding the client’s result for each request:

{
  "github_login": { "action": "accept", "content": { "name": "octocat" } },
  "capital_of_france": {
    "role": "assistant",
    "content": { "type": "text", "text": "The capital of France is Paris." },
    "model": "claude-3-sonnet-20240307",
    "stopReason": "endTurn"
  }
}

docs.title: InputRequiredResult
docs.text:
A result (not an error, and not a request) with resultType: "input_required" and:

Field Meaning inputRequests (optional) The InputRequests map the client must fulfil requestState (optional) An opaque string meaningful only to the server, which the client must echo back

At least one of the two MUST be present.

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 1,
  "result": {
    "resultType": "input_required",
    "inputRequests": {
      "github_login": {
        "method": "elicitation/create",
        "params": {
          "mode": "form",
          "message": "Please provide your GitHub username",
          "requestedSchema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "name": { "type": "string" } }, "required": ["name"] }
        }
      }
    },
    "requestState": "AEAD-protected blob"
  }
}

docs.title: Which requests can return it
docs.text:
Client request May return InputRequiredResult tools/call Yes resources/read Yes prompts/get Yes Anything else MUST NOT

So tools/list, server/discover, completion/complete and subscriptions/listen can never be interrupted for input.

docs.title: A complete tool call with elicitation
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server
    C->>S: tools/call (id: 1)
    Note over S: needs info via elicitation
    S-->>C: InputRequiredResult (id: 1, ElicitRequest, requestState)
    Note over C,S: initial request terminated
    C->>U: prompt for input
    U-->>C: responses
    C->>S: tools/call (id: 2, inputResponses, requestState)
    Note over S: reconstitute state, complete
    S-->>C: Result (id: 2, CallToolResult)

On the wire:

// 1. C→S
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/call",
 "params":{"name":"get_weather","arguments":{"location":"New York"},
           "_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion":"2026-07-28",
                    "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities":{"elicitation":{"form":{}}}}}}

// 2. S→C  request 1 is now over
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"result":{"resultType":"input_required",
  "inputRequests":{"github_login":{"method":"elicitation/create","params":{"mode":"form",
     "message":"Please provide your GitHub username",
     "requestedSchema":{"type":"object","properties":{"name":{"type":"string"}},"required":["name"]}}}},
  "requestState":"v1.Rk9PQkFSX1NUQVRF.hmac-8f3a1c"}}

// 3. C→S  NEW id, SAME name/arguments, + inputResponses, + EXACT requestState
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/call",
 "params":{"name":"get_weather","arguments":{"location":"New York"},
           "inputResponses":{"github_login":{"action":"accept","content":{"name":"octocat"}}},
           "requestState":"v1.Rk9PQkFSX1NUQVRF.hmac-8f3a1c",
           "_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion":"2026-07-28",
                    "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities":{"elicitation":{"form":{}}}}}}

// 4. S→C
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"result":{"resultType":"complete",
  "content":[{"type":"text","text":"Weather for octocat's saved location, New York: 72°F"}]}}

docs.title: Server requirements
docs.text: # Requirement 1 MAY respond to a supported request with InputRequiredResult 2 MAY include inputRequests. Keys MUST be unique within the request. Values MUST be ElicitRequest, CreateMessageRequest or ListRootsRequest 3 MAY include requestState, in any encoding (base64 JSON, encrypted JWT, binary…) 4 MUST treat incoming requestState as attacker-controlled. If it influences authorization, resource access or business logic, MUST protect its integrity (HMAC or AEAD) and MUST reject state that fails verification. Integrity protection may be omitted only when tampering can cause nothing worse than request failure 5 To prevent replay, SHOULD include inside the protected payload and verify: the authenticated principal; a short expiry (TTL); an identifier for the originating request (method name plus a digest of salient parameters) 6 MUST include at least one of inputRequests or requestState 7 MUST NOT send inputRequests the client hasn’t declared capability for (no elicitation/create without elicitation) 8 MUST NOT assume the client will fulfil the requests or retry. MAY return InputRequiredResult again on the retry, to keep prompting until it has what it needs

docs.title: Client requirements
docs.text: # Requirement 1 If inputRequests is present, MUST construct the requested inputs before retrying. If absent, MAY retry immediately 2 If requestState is present, MUST echo back its exact value; MUST NOT inspect, parse, modify or assume anything about it. If absent, MUST NOT include one in the retry 3 The retry’s JSON-RPC id MUST differ from the original’s 4 inputRequests and requestState affect only the retry of that request; MUST NOT be used for any other request the client is sending in parallel

docs.title: Why requestState exists
docs.text:
Statelessness means the retry must carry everything. But the server may have done work before it hit the need for input: validated arguments, fetched a quote, chosen a price, allocated a reservation. requestState lets the server hand that context to the client to carry, instead of storing it.

An InputRequiredResult with only requestState and no inputRequests is legal and useful: it means “I need you to come back; here’s my progress.” The client retries immediately, and the server continues from the state. Servers can use this to break long work into steps without holding anything between them.

docs.title: Why requestState must be protected
docs.text:
requestState travels through the client. A malicious or compromised client can modify it. Consider a naive server that puts plain JSON in it:

{"step": "confirm_purchase", "userId": "u_123", "amount": 3000, "approved": false}

An attacker base64-decodes it, sets "amount": 1 and "approved": true, re-encodes it and retries. If the server trusts requestState, the attacker just bought a $3,000 item for $1.

Hence the MUSTs: integrity protection (HMAC or AEAD, so tampering is detected), and rejection on failure.

Then replay. Even untampered, a valid state blob could be reused:

Replay Mitigation inside the protected payload Another user presents Alice’s captured state Authenticated principal; reject a different principal Alice presents an old state days later Short TTL; reject after expiry State from buy_ticket(concert) presented on refund_ticket(other) Request identifier: method + digest of salient params; reject on mismatch

These bound replay; they don’t guarantee single use

Principal, TTL and request binding stop cross-user, stale and cross-request reuse. They do not stop the same user replaying the same state twice within its TTL. For operations that must happen at most once (a one-time redemption, a payment), the server MUST enforce single use server-side, for example by recording a nonce as consumed.

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
• Servers SHOULD validate that the retry carries a valid InputResponses object that parses correctly.
  • Malformed JSON, invalid schema or internal errors → a normal JSON-RPC error.
  • Extra, unexpected entries in inputResponses → the server SHOULD ignore what it doesn’t recognize.
  • Missing required information → the server SHOULD return a new InputRequiredResult asking again, rather than an error.
  • If the user declines or the client can’t fulfil the requests, the client does not need to send anything. The server isn’t waiting, because request 1 already ended. (Compare the legacy pattern, where the server was blocked on a reply.)

docs.title: MRTR and caching
docs.text: Results from a retry carrying inputResponses or requestState MUST NOT be cached, since they depend on inputs outside the cache key. InputRequiredResults themselves are not cacheable and carry no cache hints.

docs.title: 1. What elicitation is
docs.text:
The Model Context Protocol provides a standardized way for servers to request additional information from users through the client during interactions. This flow allows clients to maintain control over user interactions and data sharing while enabling servers to gather necessary information dynamically.

Two modes:

Mode What happens Data exposed to the client? For Form The client renders a form from a schema and returns the user’s answers Yes Structured, non-sensitive input: preferences, confirmations, names URL The client sends the user to a URL; the interaction happens out of band No (only the URL itself) Sensitive interactions: credentials, payments, third-party OAuth

docs.title: 2. The non-negotiable safety rules
docs.text:
Sensitive data must use URL mode

  • Servers MUST NOT use form mode to request sensitive information such as passwords, API keys, access tokens or payment credentials.
  • Servers MUST use URL mode for interactions involving such information.

“Sensitive” here means secrets and credentials that grant access or authorize transactions. General contact or profile information (name, email, username) is not categorically prohibited in form mode; whether to ask for it is at the server’s discretion, subject to the user’s ability to review and decline.

Why? Form data passes through the MCP client: its memory, its logs, possibly its LLM context, possibly intermediate proxies. A password typed into a form-mode elicitation is exposed to all of them. URL mode keeps the secret between the user’s browser and a page the server controls.

And clients MUST:

  • make it clear which server is requesting information,
  • respect privacy and provide clear decline and cancel options,
  • in form mode, let users review and modify responses before sending,
  • in URL mode, clearly display the target domain/host and gather consent before navigating.

docs.title: 3. Capability
docs.text:
{
  "_meta": {
    "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities": {
      "elicitation": { "form": {}, "url": {} }
    }
  }
}
  • A client declaring elicitation MUST support at least one mode.
  • An empty elicitation: {} equals { "form": {} }, form only, for backward compatibility.
  • Servers MUST NOT send an elicitation with a mode the client didn’t declare.

docs.title: 4. Common parameters
docs.text:
Every elicitation request MUST include:

Parameter Notes mode "form" or "url". May be omitted for form mode; clients MUST treat a missing mode as form message Human-readable explanation of why the interaction is needed

docs.title: 5. Form mode
docs.text:
Adds requestedSchema: a restricted JSON Schema, a flat object with primitive properties only.

Type Supported keywords string title, description, minLength, maxLength, format (email, uri, date, date-time), default number / integer title, description, minimum, maximum, default boolean title, description, default single-select enum enum, or oneOf of {const, title} for labelled options; default multi-select enum type: "array", items.enum or items.anyOf of {const, title}, minItems, maxItems, default

Not supported: nested objects, arrays of objects beyond enums, other advanced JSON Schema. Clients that support defaults SHOULD pre-fill fields with them.

A realistic booking confirmation:

{
  "method": "elicitation/create",
  "params": {
    "mode": "form",
    "message": "Please confirm your Barcelona vacation booking details:",
    "requestedSchema": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "confirmBooking": { "type": "boolean", "description": "Confirm the booking (Flights + Hotel = $3,000)" },
        "seatPreference": { "type": "string", "enum": ["window", "aisle", "no preference"] },
        "roomType": { "type": "string", "enum": ["sea view", "city view", "garden view"] },
        "travelInsurance": { "type": "boolean", "default": false, "description": "Add travel insurance ($150)" }
      },
      "required": ["confirmBooking"]
    }
  }
}

Clients SHOULD validate responses against the schema; servers SHOULD validate what they receive.

docs.title: 6. URL mode
docs.text:
Adds url, which MUST be a valid URL:

{
  "method": "elicitation/create",
  "params": {
    "mode": "url",
    "url": "https://mcp.example.com/ui/set_api_key",
    "message": "Please provide your API key to continue."
  }
}

The client’s response is just:

{ "action": "accept" }

Read that carefully. accept means the user consented to open the URL. It does not mean the interaction is complete. The interaction happens out of band, and the client is not told its outcome. When the client retries the original request, the server works out (from requestState or its own stored state) whether the out-of-band step finished, and either returns the final result or another InputRequiredResult. Clients SHOULD give users manual controls to retry or cancel the original request.

sequenceDiagram
    participant UA as User agent (browser)
    participant User
    participant Client
    participant Server
    Client->>Server: tools/call (id: 1)
    Note over Server: needs out-of-band input<br/>creates requestState
    Server-->>Client: InputRequiredResult (elicitation mode: url, requestState)
    Client->>User: show full URL + domain, ask consent
    User-->>Client: consent
    Client->>UA: open URL (secure, not inspectable by client/LLM)
    Client->>Server: tools/call (id: 2, action: accept, requestState)
    Note over User,UA: user completes interaction
    UA-->>Server: interaction complete
    Server-->>Client: Result (id: 2) or another InputRequiredResult

URL mode is not MCP authorization

URL mode is not for authorizing the MCP client’s access to the MCP server. That is MCP authorization. URL mode is for when the server needs sensitive information or third-party authorization on the user’s behalf. The client’s bearer token is unchanged.

docs.title: 7. The three response actions
docs.text:
Both modes use the same three actions:

Action Meaning content Server should accept User explicitly approved and submitted Form: the data. URL: omitted Process the data decline User explicitly refused (“No”, “Reject”) Typically omitted Handle the refusal, e.g. offer alternatives cancel User dismissed without choosing (closed dialog, Escape, clicked outside, browser failed to load) Typically omitted Handle dismissal, e.g. ask again later

The decline/cancel distinction is examinable. Decline is a decision. Cancel is the absence of one.

Servers SHOULD NOT assume elicitations succeed, and MUST handle decline, cancel and client failure.

docs.title: 8. Safe URL handling
docs.text:
URL mode sends users to server-chosen URLs, a classic phishing surface. The rules on both sides:

Servers requesting URL elicitation:

  1. MUST NOT put sensitive end-user information (credentials, PII) in the URL.
  2. MUST NOT provide a pre-authenticated URL to a protected resource, since a malicious client could use it to impersonate the user.
  3. SHOULD NOT put clickable URLs in any field of a form-mode elicitation.
  4. SHOULD use HTTPS outside development.

Clients handling URL elicitation:

  1. MUST NOT pre-fetch the URL or any of its metadata.
  2. MUST NOT open it without explicit user consent.
  3. MUST show the full URL for examination before consent.
  4. MUST open it securely, in a way that does not let the client or the LLM inspect the page or the user’s input. On iOS, SFSafariViewController is acceptable; WKWebView is not.
  5. SHOULD highlight the domain, to counter subdomain spoofing.
  6. SHOULD warn about ambiguous or suspicious URIs, such as those containing Punycode.
  7. SHOULD NOT render URLs as clickable anywhere except the url field of a URL elicitation.

docs.title: 9. URL mode for third-party OAuth
docs.text:
A key pattern: an MCP server integrates with third-party APIs (say, a Google Drive or Salesforce account) and needs the user’s authorization for those APIs.

MCP authorization Third-party authorization Between MCP client ↔ MCP server MCP server ↔ third-party API Mechanism Core authorization spec URL-mode elicitation MCP server’s role OAuth resource server OAuth client (and resource server to the MCP client)

The critical requirements:

  1. Third-party credentials MUST NOT transit through the MCP client.
  2. The MCP server MUST NOT use the client’s credentials for the third-party service. That would be token passthrough, which is forbidden.
  3. The user MUST authorize the MCP server directly, outside the MCP protocol.
  4. The MCP server is responsible for the tokens: it stores and manages them, bound to the user’s identity. The server must be stateful for this.
  5. The server MUST NOT transmit credentials obtained via URL elicitation to the MCP client.
  6. MCP servers MUST NOT rely on URL elicitation to authorize users for themselves.

docs.title: 10. The phishing attack, and the fix
docs.text:
The spec describes a concrete account-takeover attack against a naive implementation:

  1. Alice (malicious), connected to a benign server, triggers an elicitation.
  2. The server generates a third-party authorization URL and returns it to Alice’s client.
  3. Instead of clicking it, Alice sends the link to Bob, another user of the same server.
  4. Bob clicks it and completes authorization, believing he’s connecting his own account.
  5. The third-party service redirects back to the server, which binds the tokens to Alice’s request.
  6. Alice now has access to Bob’s third-party account.

The fix is a MUST: the server must verify that the user who completes the flow is the same user who started the elicitation.

The spec’s example design: instead of eliciting the third-party authorization URL directly, elicit a “connect” URL on the MCP server itself (https://mcp.example.com/connect?...). That page checks the browser’s session cookie, comparing the authenticated subject (sub claim from the MCP server’s authorization server) with the user who generated the elicitation, and only then redirects to the third party. If Bob opens Alice’s link, the subjects don’t match and the flow stops.

In all implementations, the identity check MUST be resilient to an attacker modifying the elicitation URL.

docs.title: 11. Identifying the user
docs.text:
Servers MUST NOT rely on client-provided identification without verification, because it can be forged:

  • Incorrect: treating user input like “I am joe@example.com” as authoritative.
  • Correct: relying on authorization to identify the user.

And if a server does keep state about elicitations (MRTR doesn’t require it, but URL-mode OAuth does):

  • state storage MUST be protected against unauthorized access, and
  • for remote servers, user identity MUST come from credentials acquired via MCP authorization when possible (for example the sub claim).

docs.title: 12. Security summary
docs.text:
1. Servers MUST bind elicitation requests to the client and user identity.
  2. Clients MUST clearly indicate which server is asking.
  3. Clients SHOULD implement user approval controls, and SHOULD allow users to decline at any time.
  4. Clients SHOULD make clear what is requested and why.
  5. Form mode: servers MUST NOT request sensitive data; clients SHOULD validate against the schema; servers SHOULD validate received data.

docs.title: Part 5: What changed from 2025-11-25
docs.text: Legacy 2026-07-28 Server sends elicitation/create as a JSON-RPC request Server returns it inside InputRequiredResult.inputRequests Server blocks, holding the original request Original request ends; client retries with a new id Server-side suspended state requestState carried by the client, integrity-protected URL elicitations carried an elicitationId Removed; servers correlate via requestState notifications/elicitation/complete told the client an out-of-band step finished Removed; the client learns the outcome by retrying Error -32042 “URL elicitation required” Removed; implementations of this version MUST NOT emit it

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• MRTR replaces server-initiated requests. Server returns resultType: "input_required"; client gathers input and retries. Each request is independent, so any instance can serve the retry.
  • InputRequiredResult has inputRequests (map of elicitation / sampling / roots requests) and/or requestState (opaque string). At least one is required.
  • Only tools/call, resources/read, prompts/get may return it.
  • Client MUST: construct requested inputs, echo requestState exactly without inspecting it, use a new id, and not reuse inputs or state for other requests.
  • Server MUST: treat requestState as attacker-controlled, HMAC/AEAD it when it matters, reject on failure; SHOULD bind to principal, TTL, originating request; enforce single use server-side where needed; never request undeclared capabilities; never assume the client will retry.
  • Missing input on a retry → another InputRequiredResult, not an error. Retry results are not cacheable.
  • Elicitation: form mode (flat primitive schema, no secrets) or URL mode (sensitive interactions, out of band). Empty elicitation: {} = form only.
  • URL accept = consent to open, not completion; the server decides on retry.
  • Actions: accept, decline (explicit no), cancel (dismissed).
  • Clients: show which server asks, never pre-fetch or auto-open URLs, show the full URL and domain, open it where the client and LLM can’t inspect it.
  • Third-party OAuth via URL mode: credentials never through the client, no token passthrough, server stores tokens, and verify the completing user is the initiating user to prevent phishing account takeover.

docs.title: Domain 3 Quiz — Interactions & Execution
docs.text:
20 exam-style questions. This is the heaviest domain. Target: 17/20.

1. A server processing tools/call needs the user to confirm a purchase. In 2026-07-28, what does the server do?

  • A. Sends an elicitation/create JSON-RPC request to the client and waits
  • B. Returns a result with resultType: "input_required" containing an elicitation in inputRequests
  • C. Returns JSON-RPC error -32042
  • D. Sends notifications/elicitation/complete
Answer

B. Servers MUST NOT initiate requests. They return an InputRequiredResult, and the client retries. A is legacy; -32042 and the completion notification were removed.

2. When retrying a request after an InputRequiredResult, which is REQUIRED of the client?

  • A. Reuse the original JSON-RPC id so the server can correlate
  • B. Use a new id, include inputResponses, and echo requestState exactly if one was provided
  • C. Decode requestState and update the fields that changed
  • D. Send the retry to a different endpoint
Answer

B. The retry MUST use a different id, and the client MUST echo requestState byte-for-byte without inspecting or modifying it.

3. Which client requests may a server answer with InputRequiredResult?

  • A. Any request
  • B. tools/call, resources/read and prompts/get only
  • C. tools/list and server/discover only
  • D. subscriptions/listen only
Answer

B. Servers MUST NOT send InputRequiredResult on any other request.

4. A server stores {"amount": 3000, "approved": false} as plain base64 JSON in requestState, and uses it to decide whether to charge. What is the flaw?

  • A. requestState must be JSON
  • B. requestState is attacker-controlled; because it influences business logic, its integrity MUST be protected (HMAC/AEAD) and failed verification rejected
  • C. requestState may only contain the tool name
  • D. There is no flaw because the client must echo it exactly
Answer

B. The spec requires servers to treat requestState as attacker-controlled. A malicious client can edit it. The client-side “echo exactly” rule does not protect the server.

5. Which set of measures does the spec say servers SHOULD bind into requestState to limit replay?

  • A. The client IP, User-Agent and TLS version
  • B. The authenticated principal, a short expiry, and an identifier of the originating request
  • C. The model name and temperature
  • D. The subscription id
Answer

B. These stop cross-user, stale and cross-request reuse. For operations that must be single-use, the server must additionally enforce that server-side.

6. A server needs a user’s third-party API key to call an external service. Which elicitation mode must it use?

  • A. Form mode with a password field
  • B. URL mode, so the secret never passes through the MCP client
  • C. Either mode, at the server’s discretion
  • D. Sampling
Answer

B. Servers MUST NOT use form mode for passwords, API keys, tokens or payment credentials, and MUST use URL mode for them.

7. A client declares "elicitation": {} in its capabilities. What does this mean?

  • A. The client supports both form and URL modes
  • B. The client supports form mode only
  • C. The client supports no elicitation
  • D. The declaration is invalid
Answer

B. For backward compatibility, an empty object is equivalent to { "form": {} }.

8. A user opens a URL-mode elicitation and the client returns {"action": "accept"}. What does accept indicate?

  • A. The out-of-band interaction has completed successfully
  • B. The user consented to open the URL; the server determines completion when the request is retried
  • C. The user entered their credentials into the client
  • D. The server must now send a completion notification
Answer

B. The client isn’t told the outcome of the out-of-band interaction. The server works it out on retry from requestState or its own state.

9. A user closes an elicitation dialog by pressing Escape without choosing. Which action should the client return?

  • A. decline
  • B. cancel
  • C. accept with empty content
  • D. A JSON-RPC error
Answer

B. cancel means dismissed without an explicit choice. decline is an explicit refusal.

10. Which is a MUST for clients handling URL-mode elicitation?

  • A. Pre-fetch the URL to show a preview
  • B. Show the full URL and obtain explicit consent before opening it, and never auto-open or pre-fetch it
  • C. Open the URL in an embedded web view the LLM can read
  • D. Render the URL as a clickable link in the chat
Answer

B. Clients MUST NOT pre-fetch, MUST NOT open without consent, MUST show the full URL, and MUST open it in a way the client and LLM can’t inspect.

11. A tool is called with departure_date: "2020-01-01" and the date must be in the future. How should the server report this?

  • A. JSON-RPC error -32602
  • B. JSON-RPC error -32603
  • C. A result with isError: true and an actionable message
  • D. HTTP 422
Answer

C. Input validation errors are tool execution errors, so the model can self-correct. Protocol errors are for unknown tools or malformed requests.

12. In 2026-07-28, what does a server return for resources/read on a URI that doesn’t exist?

  • A. A result with an empty contents array
  • B. JSON-RPC error -32002
  • C. JSON-RPC error -32602
  • D. JSON-RPC error -32601
Answer

C. Not-found changed from -32002 to -32602. Servers MUST NOT return empty contents for a missing resource. Clients SHOULD still accept -32002 from older servers.

13. Which error code does a server return when a request needs a client capability the client did not declare?

  • A. -32020
  • B. -32021
  • C. -32022
  • D. -32600
Answer

B. MissingRequiredClientCapability (-32021), with data.requiredCapabilities. -32020 is HeaderMismatch; -32022 is UnsupportedProtocolVersion.

14. A client opens subscriptions/listen with JSON-RPC id 7. What value appears in io.modelcontextprotocol/subscriptionId on notifications from that stream?

  • A. A random UUID chosen by the server
  • B. 7
  • C. The session id
  • D. The tool name
Answer

B. The subscription id is the JSON-RPC id of the subscriptions/listen request.

15. Which notification is NOT delivered on a subscriptions/listen stream?

  • A. notifications/tools/list_changed
  • B. notifications/resources/updated
  • C. notifications/progress
  • D. notifications/subscriptions/acknowledged
Answer

C. Progress (and log) notifications are request-scoped and travel on the response stream of the request they relate to.

16. How does a client cancel an in-flight request over stdio?

  • A. Close stdin
  • B. Send notifications/cancelled with the request id
  • C. Send HTTP DELETE
  • D. Stop reading stdout
Answer

B. On stdio the client MUST send notifications/cancelled. Closing stdin is how a client shuts the server down.

17. A server returns tools/list with ttlMs: 300000 and cacheScope: "private". Which is correct?

  • A. Any gateway may serve this list to any user for 5 minutes
  • B. The client may reuse it for 5 minutes within the same authorization context only; a different token needs a different cache
  • C. The client must poll every 5 minutes
  • D. The list must not be cached
Answer

B. private restricts reuse to the same authorization context. TTL is a freshness hint, not a polling interval.

18. A paginated list response contains "nextCursor": "". What should the client do?

  • A. Treat it as the end of results
  • B. Request the next page, passing the empty string as the cursor
  • C. Treat it as an error
  • D. Decode the cursor
Answer

B. Clients may make no determination from a cursor’s value other than whether one was provided. An empty string is a valid cursor. Only an absent nextCursor means the end.

19. Which statement about Sampling in 2026-07-28 is correct?

  • A. It has been removed from the specification
  • B. It is deprecated: still functional, delivered via MRTR, but new implementations should not adopt it and should call LLM provider APIs directly
  • C. It moved to the Tasks extension
  • D. It replaced elicitation
Answer

B. Sampling, Roots and Logging are deprecated, not removed. Elicitation remains active.

20. A server wants to keep a shopping cart across multiple tool calls. Which approach fits 2026-07-28?

  • A. Store the cart against the connection or Mcp-Session-Id
  • B. Return an explicit handle from a creation tool, accept it as an argument on later calls, and validate the caller’s authorization against it every call
  • C. Keep the cart in requestState on every tool call
  • D. Use ping to keep the cart alive
Answer

B. MCP has no protocol-level session. State uses explicit handles, which for authenticated servers are names, not capabilities, so authorization is checked on each call.

Score Verdict 18–20 Ready for Domain 4. 14–17 Re-read MRTR & Elicitation and Error Handling. < 14 Rework the domain; it is a quarter of the exam.

docs.title: Resources & Prompts
docs.text:
Competency: Protocol Primitives.

Tools let the model act. Resources and prompts supply context and workflows, and they are controlled differently: resources by the application, prompts by the user. This chapter covers both in full.

docs.title: 1. What a resource is
docs.text:
Resources allow servers to share data that provides context to language models, such as files, database schemas, or application-specific information. Each resource is uniquely identified by a URI.

The essential property is the URI. A resource is an addressable piece of data: file:///project/src/main.rs, calendar://events/2024, postgres://db/schema/users. Clients discover what exists, read what they need, and optionally watch for changes.

docs.title: 2. Application-driven
docs.text:
Resources are application-driven: the host decides how context gets incorporated. The spec lists examples:

  • UI elements for explicit selection, such as a tree or list view,
  • search and filter over available resources,
  • automatic context inclusion based on heuristics or the model’s selection.

This is the key contrast with tools. A model does not “call” a resource. The application reads resources and decides what reaches the model: passing everything, selecting a portion, or searching with embeddings.

docs.title: 3. Capability
docs.text:
{ "capabilities": { "resources": { "listChanged": true, "subscribe": true } } }
Sub-capability Meaning listChanged Server emits notifications/resources/list_changed when the set of resources changes subscribe Server supports per-resource update notifications requested via subscriptions/listen

Either, both or neither may be declared. A server supporting neither can declare "resources": {}.

As with tools, resources/list returns what is available to the requesting client. It MUST NOT vary per connection, and MAY vary by the authorization on the request.

docs.title: 4. Listing: resources/list
docs.text:
{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "resources/list", "params": { "cursor": "optional-cursor-value" } }

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 1,
  "result": {
    "resultType": "complete",
    "resources": [
      {
        "uri": "file:///project/src/main.rs",
        "name": "main.rs",
        "title": "Rust Software Application Main File",
        "description": "Primary application entry point",
        "mimeType": "text/x-rust"
      }
    ],
    "nextCursor": "next-page-cursor",
    "ttlMs": 300000,
    "cacheScope": "public"
  }
}

A resource has uri and name, and optionally title, description, icons, mimeType and size (in bytes). The list is paginated and cacheable.

docs.title: 5. Reading: resources/read
docs.text:
{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 2, "method": "resources/read", "params": { "uri": "file:///project/src/main.rs" } }

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 2,
  "result": {
    "resultType": "complete",
    "contents": [
      { "uri": "file:///project/src/main.rs", "mimeType": "text/x-rust", "text": "fn main() {\n    println!(\"Hello world!\");\n}" }
    ],
    "ttlMs": 60000,
    "cacheScope": "private"
  }
}

Contents are text:

{ "uri": "file:///example.txt", "mimeType": "text/plain", "text": "Resource content" }

or binary, base64-encoded in blob:

{ "uri": "file:///example.png", "mimeType": "image/png", "blob": "iVBORw0KGgo..." }

Details worth knowing:

  • A server MAY return multiple contents for one read. Reading a directory resource might return several files.
  • resources/read supports MRTR: a server may return an InputRequiredResult (for example, asking the user to confirm access to a sensitive document) and the client retries with inputResponses and requestState.
  • resources/read is cacheable. Note cacheScope: "private" in the example: file contents that depend on who is asking must not be shared across users.
  • If the URI scheme is https://, the client may fetch the resource directly from the web rather than through the server.

docs.title: 6. Resource templates: resources/templates/list
docs.text:
Many data sources are too large or dynamic to enumerate. Resource templates expose parameterized URIs using RFC 6570 URI templates:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 3,
  "result": {
    "resultType": "complete",
    "resourceTemplates": [
      {
        "uriTemplate": "file:///{path}",
        "name": "Project Files",
        "title": "📁 Project Files",
        "description": "Access files in the project directory",
        "mimeType": "application/octet-stream"
      }
    ],
    "ttlMs": 300000,
    "cacheScope": "public"
  }
}

The documentation’s travel examples show the idea:

Kind Example Meaning Direct resource calendar://events/2024 A fixed URI Template travel://activities/{city}/{category} A family of URIs Expanded template travel://activities/barcelona/museums One concrete member, read with resources/read

Template arguments can be autocompleted: as a user types “Par” for {city}, the host calls completion/complete with ref/resource and the server suggests “Paris” or “Park City”. See Utilities.

Templates are paginated and cacheable.

docs.title: 7. Watching for changes
docs.text:
Two kinds of change, two notifications, both delivered on a subscriptions/listen stream:

Change Notification Client opts in with Server must declare The set of resources changed notifications/resources/list_changed resourcesListChanged: true listChanged A specific resource’s content changed notifications/resources/updated (with uri) resourceSubscriptions: ["uri", …] subscribe 
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "method": "notifications/resources/updated",
  "params": { "_meta": { "io.modelcontextprotocol/subscriptionId": 4 }, "uri": "file:///project/src/main.rs" }
}

The notification carries only the URI, not the new content. The client decides whether to re-read.

Legacy vs. modern

resources/subscribe and resources/unsubscribe no longer exist in 2026-07-28. Per-resource subscriptions are the resourceSubscriptions filter of subscriptions/listen.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant Server
    Client->>Server: resources/list
    Server-->>Client: resources
    Client->>Server: resources/templates/list
    Server-->>Client: templates
    Client->>Server: resources/read
    Server-->>Client: contents
    Client->>Server: subscriptions/listen (resourceSubscriptions)
    Server--)Client: notifications/subscriptions/acknowledged
    Server--)Client: notifications/resources/updated
    Client->>Server: resources/read
    Server-->>Client: updated contents

docs.title: 8. Annotations
docs.text:
Resources, templates and content blocks accept annotations:

  • audience: ["user"], ["assistant"] or both, for whom the resource is intended;
  • priority: 0.0–1.0, where 1 means effectively required and 0 entirely optional;
  • lastModified: ISO 8601 timestamp.

Hosts use them to filter by audience, prioritize what to include in limited context, and show or sort by recency.

docs.title: 9. URI schemes
docs.text:
Scheme Use Guidance https:// A resource on the web Servers SHOULD use it only when the client can fetch it directly without going through the server. Otherwise use another scheme, even if the server itself downloads the content from the internet file:// Filesystem-like resources Need not map to a real filesystem. MAY use XDG MIME types like inode/directory for non-regular files git:// Git version control Custom (calendar://, postgres://…) Anything else MUST comply with RFC 3986

The https:// rule is subtle and worth understanding. An https:// URI tells the client “you can fetch this yourself”. If the content actually requires the server’s credentials or processing, a client fetching directly would get the wrong thing or nothing, so use a scheme that routes through resources/read.

docs.title: 10. Errors
docs.text:
• Resource not found → JSON-RPC -32602 (Invalid params). 2026
  • Internal errors → -32603.
  • Clients SHOULD also accept -32002 as not-found, from servers implementing earlier versions.
  • A server MUST NOT return an empty contents array for a non-existent resource. An empty array is ambiguous: it could mean the resource exists but is empty.
{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 5, "error": { "code": -32602, "message": "Resource not found", "data": { "uri": "file:///nonexistent.txt" } } }

docs.title: 11. Security
docs.text:
1. Servers MUST validate all resource URIs.
  2. Access controls SHOULD be implemented for sensitive resources.
  3. Binary data MUST be properly encoded.
  4. Resource permissions SHOULD be checked before operations.
  5. Servers MUST sanitize file paths to prevent directory traversal when serving file:// resources.

Directory traversal concretely: a template file:///{path} rooted at /srv/project, read with path = "../../etc/passwd", resolves outside the project unless the server normalizes the path and verifies it is still inside the allowed root.

docs.title: 12. What a prompt is
docs.text:
Prompts allow servers to provide structured messages and instructions for interacting with language models. Clients can discover available prompts, retrieve their contents, and provide arguments to customize them.

A prompt is a server-authored template for a conversation: “review this code”, “summarize my meetings”, “plan a vacation”. It packages domain expertise, telling the model how to use this server’s tools and resources well.

docs.title: 13. User-controlled
docs.text:
Prompts are user-controlled: exposed so that the user explicitly selects them. Typically they appear as slash commands, command-palette entries, buttons or context-menu suggestions.

The spec adds a precise clarification that is easy to miss:

This refers to who decides when the prompt is used, not who authors its content. Prompt content is defined by the server.

So: user chooses when, server writes the content, host places it in the conversation.

docs.title: 14. Capability
docs.text:
{ "capabilities": { "prompts": { "listChanged": true } } }

Declared in the DiscoverResult. prompts/list returns prompts available to the requesting client, not varying per connection and possibly varying by authorization.

docs.title: 15. Listing: prompts/list
docs.text:
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 1,
  "result": {
    "resultType": "complete",
    "prompts": [
      {
        "name": "code_review",
        "title": "Request Code Review",
        "description": "Asks the LLM to analyze code quality and suggest improvements",
        "arguments": [ { "name": "code", "description": "The code to review", "required": true } ]
      }
    ],
    "nextCursor": "next-page-cursor",
    "ttlMs": 600000,
    "cacheScope": "public"
  }
}

A prompt has name, optional title, description, icons and arguments. Each argument is { name, description?, required? }. This is not JSON Schema; prompt arguments are a simple list.

docs.title: 16. Getting: prompts/get
docs.text:
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 2,
  "method": "prompts/get",
  "params": { "name": "code_review", "arguments": { "code": "def hello():\n    print('world')" } }
}

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 2,
  "result": {
    "resultType": "complete",
    "description": "Code review prompt",
    "messages": [
      { "role": "user", "content": { "type": "text", "text": "Please review this Python code:\ndef hello():\n    print('world')" } }
    ]
  }
}

The server returns messages, not a single string. Each has a role ("user" or "assistant") and a content block: text, image, audio, resource_link or embedded resource, all accepting annotations.

Why a message list? Because a good prompt is often a multi-turn scaffold: a user message with context, an assistant message demonstrating the expected format, then the real question. Prompts can also embed resources, pulling server-managed documentation or code samples straight into the conversation:

{ "role": "user", "content": { "type": "resource", "resource": { "uri": "resource://style-guide", "mimeType": "text/markdown", "text": "# Style guide…" } } }

Embedded resources in prompts MUST include a valid URI, the appropriate MIME type, and either text or base64 blob.

prompts/get supports MRTR: a server can return InputRequiredResult to ask for something before resolving the prompt. Arguments can be autocompleted with completion/complete and ref/prompt.

Note prompts/get results are not in the list of operations that must carry cache hints; prompts/list is.

docs.title: 17. List changes
docs.text: A server declaring listChanged SHOULD send notifications/prompts/list_changed to clients subscribed with promptsListChanged: true.

docs.title: 18. Errors and security
docs.text:
Case Code Invalid prompt name -32602 (Invalid params) Missing required arguments -32602 (Invalid params) Internal error -32603

Servers SHOULD validate prompt arguments. Clients SHOULD handle pagination. Implementations MUST carefully validate all prompt inputs and outputs to prevent injection attacks or unauthorized access to resources.

Prompt injection risk here runs in an interesting direction: the server authors the messages that enter the conversation, with the user’s apparent endorsement (they selected the prompt). A malicious server’s prompt can instruct the model to misuse other servers’ tools. Hosts should show users what a prompt will insert.

docs.title: Part 3: Choosing the right primitive
docs.text:
Question Primitive Should the model decide when to use it, and does it do something? Tool Is it data the application should be able to attach as context? Resource Is it a workflow the user starts on purpose? Prompt

Worked example: a database MCP server.

Capability Primitive Why Run a SQL query Tool run_query The model decides when a query is needed; it executes something The schema of every table Resource postgres://db/schema Context the app can attach so the model writes correct SQL One table’s schema Resource template postgres://db/schema/{table} A family of data, too many to list “Analyze slow queries” Prompt analyze_slow_queries A workflow the user triggers, bundling instructions and few-shot examples

A server author sometimes has a genuine choice. “Get the README” could be a resource (the app attaches it) or a tool (the model fetches it when needed). Prefer the resource when the data is stable context the user or app should see and choose. Prefer the tool when the model needs to decide dynamically, especially if the call has parameters or side effects.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
Resources

  • Data identified by a URI; application-controlled.
  • Capability resources with optional listChanged (set changes) and subscribe (content updates).
  • resources/list (paginated, cacheable), resources/templates/list (RFC 6570), resources/read (text or base64 blob, possibly multiple contents, MRTR-capable, cacheable).
  • Changes via subscriptions/listen: resourcesListChanged → list_changed; resourceSubscriptions → updated (URI only). No more resources/subscribe.
  • Not found → -32602 (accept legacy -32002); never an empty contents for a missing resource.
  • https:// only when the client can fetch directly. Validate URIs; prevent directory traversal.

Prompts

  • Server-authored message templates; user-controlled (user decides when, server authors content).
  • prompts/list (arguments are a simple list, not JSON Schema), prompts/get returns messages with roles and content blocks (can embed resources), MRTR-capable.
  • Invalid name or missing arguments → -32602. Validate inputs and outputs against injection.

docs.title: Subscriptions, Progress & Cancellation
docs.text:
Competency: Interaction Patterns & Response Handling.

Three mechanisms for interactions that aren’t a quick request and response: learning about changes the client didn’t ask about, watching progress on slow work, and abandoning work that is no longer wanted. Each is short in the spec, and each has transport-specific details that show up in questions.

docs.title: 1. The problem
docs.text:
A server’s tool list changes when a plugin loads. A file the user is working with gets edited. The client has no reason to ask right now, but wants to know. Something has to flow from server to client without a fresh request.

In a stateless protocol where servers never initiate requests, the only option is: the client opens a long-lived request, and the server uses its response stream to deliver notifications as they happen.

docs.title: 2. subscriptions/listen
docs.text:
subscriptions/listen opens a long-lived notification stream from the server to the client. Unlike one-off requests, the stream stays open and delivers notifications until the client cancels it. It replaces the former resources/subscribe RPC and the HTTP GET endpoint.

The client names what it wants in a notifications filter:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 1,
  "method": "subscriptions/listen",
  "params": {
    "_meta": {
      "io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion": "2026-07-28",
      "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo": { "name": "ExampleClient", "version": "1.0.0" },
      "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities": {}
    },
    "notifications": {
      "toolsListChanged": true,
      "resourceSubscriptions": ["file:///project/config.json"]
    }
  }
}

docs.title: 3. The filter
docs.text:
Field Type Delivers toolsListChanged boolean notifications/tools/list_changed promptsListChanged boolean notifications/prompts/list_changed resourcesListChanged boolean notifications/resources/list_changed resourceSubscriptions string[] notifications/resources/updated for these URIs

All fields are optional; omitting one means not subscribing to it. The server MUST NOT send notification types the client didn’t explicitly request. Extensions can add their own types (the Tasks extension uses this to push task status).

Requesting something requires the server to support it: toolsListChanged is meaningful only if the server’s tools capability has listChanged: true; resourceSubscriptions requires resources.subscribe: true.

docs.title: 4. Acknowledgment
docs.text:
The server MUST send notifications/subscriptions/acknowledged first, and MUST NOT send any notification on the subscription before it:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "method": "notifications/subscriptions/acknowledged",
  "params": {
    "_meta": { "io.modelcontextprotocol/subscriptionId": 1 },
    "notifications": { "toolsListChanged": true, "resourceSubscriptions": ["file:///project/config.json"] }
  }
}

The acknowledgment’s notifications field is the subset the server agreed to honor. Unsupported types are omitted. The client SHOULD compare it with what it asked for and handle the gaps gracefully.

On stdio, where every subscription shares one channel, the ordering rule applies per subscription id, not per channel. Messages for other subscriptions may be interleaved before a new subscription’s acknowledgment.

docs.title: 5. The subscription id
docs.text:
Every message on the stream carries io.modelcontextprotocol/subscriptionId in _meta, and its value is the JSON-RPC id of the subscriptions/listen request that opened it. The request above used "id": 1, so the acknowledgment and every later notification carry subscriptionId: 1:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "method": "notifications/resources/updated",
  "params": { "_meta": { "io.modelcontextprotocol/subscriptionId": 1 }, "uri": "file:///project/config.json" }
}

A client MAY hold several subscriptions at once (one for tool changes, another for resource updates), and uses subscriptionId to tell them apart. On stdio, where everything shares stdout, clients MUST use it to correlate.

docs.title: 6. What is not delivered on a listen stream
docs.text:
Request-scoped notifications stay with their request:

Notification Travels on notifications/progress The response stream of the request it relates to notifications/message (deprecated logging) The response stream of the request that set logLevel List-changed and resource-updated notifications The subscriptions/listen stream

docs.title: 7. How a subscription ends
docs.text:
Who ends it How Client on Streamable HTTP Closes the SSE stream Client on stdio Sends notifications/cancelled referencing the listen request’s id Server (e.g. shutdown) SHOULD send a successful response to the listen request, then close Transport HTTP timeout, TCP disconnect, stdio process exit

Graceful closure. When the server ends a subscription itself, it SHOULD respond to the original subscriptions/listen request with a completion result, still tagged with the subscription id:

{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "result": { "resultType": "complete", "_meta": { "io.modelcontextprotocol/subscriptionId": 1 } } }

This lets the client distinguish “ended cleanly” (a response arrived) from “connection dropped” (no response), which the client MAY treat as a reason to reconnect. The cancellation page adds that a server MUST send notifications/cancelled referencing the listen request id when it tears down a subscription stream, and that this is the only purpose for which servers send notifications/cancelled.

On stdio, if the connection is terminated and re-established, the client MUST re-send subscriptions/listen. The server holds no subscription state across reconnections.

Notifications are best effort

Notifications can be missed, especially across reconnects. That is why list results carry ttlMs: clients combine push (notifications invalidate caches immediately) with freshness (TTL expiry triggers a re-fetch).

docs.title: 8. Keeping listen streams alive
docs.text:
On Streamable HTTP, a subscription stream may sit idle for long periods. Servers are encouraged to send periodic SSE comment lines (starting with :) as keep-alives so intermediaries don’t close the connection, and SHOULD send X-Accel-Buffering: no so proxies don’t buffer events. Clients must ignore comment lines.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant Server
    Client->>Server: POST subscriptions/listen (id 1, filter)
    Server-->>Client: SSE: notifications/subscriptions/acknowledged (subscriptionId 1)
    Note over Client,Server: stream stays open
    Server-->>Client: SSE: ":" (keep-alive comment)
    Server-->>Client: SSE: notifications/tools/list_changed (subscriptionId 1)
    Client->>Server: POST tools/list (separate request)
    Server-->>Client: updated tools
    Server-->>Client: SSE: notifications/resources/updated (subscriptionId 1)

docs.title: 9. Opting in
docs.text:
Progress is optional, and the client opts in per request by including a progressToken in _meta:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 1,
  "method": "tools/call",
  "params": { "name": "build_index", "arguments": {}, "_meta": { "progressToken": "abc123" } }
}
  • The token MUST be a string or integer.
  • The client chooses it by any means, but it MUST be unique across all active requests.

docs.title: 10. Notifications
docs.text:
The server MAY send:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "method": "notifications/progress",
  "params": { "progressToken": "abc123", "progress": 50, "total": 100, "message": "Reticulating splines..." }
}
Field Rules progressToken The original token progress MUST increase with each notification, even if total is unknown; may be floating point total Optional; may be floating point; omit if unknown message Optional; SHOULD be human-readable progress information

docs.title: 11. Behavior requirements
docs.text:
• Notifications MUST only reference tokens from an active request with an in-progress operation.
  • A server receiving a token MAY send no notifications at all, MAY choose any frequency, and MAY omit total.
  • Both sides SHOULD track active tokens and SHOULD rate limit to prevent flooding.
  • Progress notifications MUST stop after completion.

Progress is request-scoped: on Streamable HTTP it travels on that request’s SSE response stream, so a server that wants to report progress answers with text/event-stream rather than a single JSON object.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant Server
    Client->>Server: request with progressToken
    Server-->>Client: progress 0.2 / 1.0
    Server-->>Client: progress 0.6 / 1.0
    Server-->>Client: progress 1.0 / 1.0
    Server->>Client: response

Why progress must increase even without a total

An indeterminate operation (scanning an unknown number of files) can’t report “40%”. A monotonically increasing count (files scanned so far) still proves work is happening, which is what a client needs to decide whether to keep waiting (see timeouts below).

docs.title: 12. Cancelling a request
docs.text:
A client SHOULD signal when a request it issued should be terminated. How depends on the transport:

Transport Cancellation signal Streamable HTTP Close the SSE response stream. The server MUST treat the disconnect as cancellation. No notifications/cancelled is required or expected stdio MUST send notifications/cancelled referencing the request id (there’s no per-request stream to close)

The stdio notification:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "method": "notifications/cancelled",
  "params": { "requestId": "123", "reason": "User requested cancellation" }
}

reason is optional and can be logged or displayed.

docs.title: 13. Behavior requirements
docs.text:
1. Cancellation notifications MUST only reference requests that the client previously issued and that are believed to still be in progress.
  2. Server-sent notifications/cancelled MUST reference a subscriptions/listen request, to end that stream. Servers MUST NOT send it for any other purpose.
  3. Servers receiving a cancellation SHOULD: stop processing, free resources, and not send a response for the cancelled request.
  4. Servers MAY ignore a cancellation if the request is unknown, already completed, or cannot be cancelled.
  5. The client SHOULD ignore any response to the cancelled request that arrives afterward.

Both transports’ binding pages add: after cancellation, the server MUST NOT send any further messages for that request.

docs.title: 14. The race condition
docs.text:
Networks have latency. The cancellation may arrive after the server finished, and even after it sent the response.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant Server
    Client->>Server: request (id 123)
    Note over Server: processing starts
    Client--)Server: notifications/cancelled (123)
    alt already completed
        Note over Server: response may already be on its way
    else still running
        Note over Server: stop processing
    end

Both sides MUST handle these races gracefully. That is why:

  • servers may ignore cancellations for completed or unknown requests,
  • clients ignore late responses,
  • invalid cancellations SHOULD be ignored: unknown ids, completed requests, malformed notifications. This preserves the “fire and forget” nature of notifications.

Implementations SHOULD log cancellation reasons, and application UIs SHOULD indicate that cancellation was requested.

Cancellation doesn’t undo side effects

If a tool had already charged a card or sent an email when the cancellation arrived, stopping processing doesn’t reverse it. Cancellation is cooperative and best effort. Servers with irreversible steps should make that clear, and hosts should confirm before starting them, not rely on cancelling them.

docs.title: 15. Timeouts
docs.text:
Implementations SHOULD set timeouts for all sent requests, to prevent hung connections and resource exhaustion. When a timeout expires, the sender SHOULD cancel the request and stop waiting, which on Streamable HTTP means closing the stream and on stdio means sending notifications/cancelled.

  • SDKs and middleware SHOULD allow timeouts to be configured per request.
  • Implementations MAY reset the timeout clock when a progress notification arrives for the request, since it shows work is happening.
  • They SHOULD always enforce a maximum timeout regardless of progress, to limit the damage from a misbehaving peer that sends progress forever.

Combining the two gives a sensible policy: “Give up after 30 seconds of silence, or 10 minutes total, whichever comes first.”

docs.title: 16. When a response stream breaks
docs.text:
Streams are not resumable in 2026-07-28 (no Last-Event-ID). If a Streamable HTTP response stream breaks, the in-flight request is lost, and the client MUST re-issue it as a new request with a new id.

Re-issuing means executing again. That makes the retry safe only if the operation is safe to repeat. For tools with side effects, idempotency matters: servers should design operations (or accept idempotency keys as arguments) so a retried call doesn’t double-charge or double-send. The idempotentHint annotation lets a trusted server signal this.

For operations that must survive disconnects, the Tasks extension gives a durable handle the client can poll after reconnecting.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
Subscriptions

  • subscriptions/listen replaces resources/subscribe and the HTTP GET stream.
  • Filter: toolsListChanged, promptsListChanged, resourcesListChanged, resourceSubscriptions (URIs). Server MUST NOT send unrequested types.
  • Acknowledgment first (the honored subset); every message carries subscriptionId = the listen request’s JSON-RPC id; stdio clients MUST correlate by it.
  • progress and message notifications stay on their own request’s stream.
  • Ends by: client closing the stream (HTTP) or sending notifications/cancelled (stdio); server sending a completion response (graceful); transport loss. stdio reconnect → re-send listen. Notifications are best effort.

Progress

  • Client opts in with progressToken (string or int, unique among active requests) in _meta.
  • notifications/progress with increasing progress, optional total and message; stops after completion; rate-limited.

Cancellation

  • HTTP: close the response stream. stdio: notifications/cancelled with requestId.
  • Servers SHOULD stop, free resources, not respond; MAY ignore unknown or completed requests. Clients ignore late responses. Server-sent notifications/cancelled only ends a listen stream.
  • Timeouts on all requests; progress may reset the clock, but always enforce a maximum.
  • Broken stream → request lost → re-issue with a new id. Mind idempotency.

docs.title: Tools & the Invocation Lifecycle
docs.text:
Competencies: Tool Invocation Lifecycle, Protocol Primitives.

Tools are the primitive that gives AI applications agency: querying databases, calling APIs, writing files, sending messages. They are also the primitive with the most risk. This chapter follows a tool from the moment a server advertises it to the moment its result reaches the model.

docs.title: 1. What a tool is
docs.text: The Model Context Protocol allows servers to expose tools that can be invoked by language models. Tools enable models to interact with external systems, such as querying databases, calling APIs, or performing computations. Each tool is uniquely identified by a name and includes metadata describing its schema.

docs.title: Model-controlled, human-supervised
docs.text:
Tools are model-controlled: the language model discovers and invokes them based on context and the user’s request. The protocol doesn’t mandate a UI, but for trust and safety the specification is firm:

There SHOULD always be a human in the loop with the ability to deny tool invocations.

Applications SHOULD:

  • make clear in the UI which tools are exposed to the model,
  • show clear visual indicators when tools are invoked,
  • present confirmation prompts so a human is in the loop.

The combination is the essence of the tool lifecycle: the model proposes, the host disposes.

docs.title: 2. The lifecycle at a glance
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["1. Advertise<br/>server declares tools capability"] --> B["2. Discover<br/>tools/list (paginated, cached)"]
    B --> C["3. Expose<br/>host gives definitions to the model"]
