  • namespace management through verification,
  • a REST API for clients and aggregators to discover servers,
  • standardized installation and configuration information.

docs.title: 7. What it stores: server.json
docs.text:
Metadata, not code:

{
  "$schema": "https://static.modelcontextprotocol.io/schemas/2025-12-11/server.schema.json",
  "name": "io.github.username/email-integration-mcp",
  "title": "Email Integration",
  "description": "Send emails and manage email accounts",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "packages": [
    {
      "registryType": "npm",
      "identifier": "@username/email-integration-mcp",
      "version": "1.0.0",
      "transport": { "type": "stdio" }
    }
  ]
}

It contains the server’s unique name, where to find it (a package or a remote URL), how to run it (arguments, environment variables), and discovery data (description, capabilities).

docs.title: 8. Relationship to package registries
docs.text: npm, PyPI, NuGet, Docker Hub and others host packages with code. The MCP Registry hosts metadata pointing to them. Supported registryType values are npm (registry.npmjs.org only), pypi (pypi.org only), nuget, oci (Docker/OCI images), cargo (crates.io) and mcpb (prebuilt MCP bundles from GitHub or GitLab releases). Remote servers can be listed by URL.

docs.title: 9. Namespaces and verification
docs.text:
Server names use reverse-DNS namespaces that tie a server to a verified owner:

Namespace Proof required io.github.domdomegg/my-cool-mcp Logged in to GitHub as domdomegg, or a GitHub Action on that user’s repos me.adamjones/my-cool-mcp Ownership of adamjones.me via DNS or HTTP challenge

Package ownership is verified too:

  • npm: package.json mcpName must equal the server name.
  • PyPI: the README (package description) must contain mcp-name: <server name>, which may be hidden in an HTML comment.

Verified publisher ≠ safe server

Namespace verification proves who published the metadata. It says nothing about whether the code is safe. The registry delegates security scanning to the underlying package registries and to downstream aggregators, and focuses on namespace authentication and metadata hosting.

docs.title: 10. Consumers: aggregators, subregistries, hosts
docs.text:
• The registry is designed to be consumed primarily by downstream aggregators, such as marketplaces, which scrape its unauthenticated read-only REST API (for example GET /v0.1/servers, cursor-paginated, filterable by updated_since) on a regular but infrequent basis (about hourly) and store data themselves. There are no uptime or durability guarantees.
  • Its metadata is deliberately unopinionated; aggregators add curation, ratings and security scanning.
  • A subregistry is an aggregator that also implements the registry’s OpenAPI spec, so hosts can consume it through a standard interface. Subregistries may add custom data under a namespaced _meta key (ratings, download counts, scan results).
  • Host applications are not meant to consume the official registry directly. They consume subregistries or marketplaces implementing the OpenAPI spec.
  • Private servers (internal networks, private package registries) are not supported. Organizations should run their own private registry implementing the OpenAPI spec. The official registry codebase isn’t designed for self-hosting.

docs.title: 11. Lifecycle, moderation, spam
docs.text:
• Version metadata is immutable once published; update by publishing a new version.
  • The status field can change to deprecated or deleted. Deleted servers are hidden from default listings but never permanently removed, and aggregators should keep statuses current. deleted typically indicates a moderation-policy violation (spam, malware).
  • Spam prevention: namespace verification, character limits and validation, manual takedown.
  • Publishers may include custom metadata under _meta["io.modelcontextprotocol.registry/publisher-provided"], up to 4 KB.
  • Abuse: report to the package registry and open a registry issue titled Abuse report: ….

docs.title: Part 4: Host support
docs.text:
MCP is supported across AI assistants (Claude, ChatGPT), development tools (VS Code, Cursor, JetBrains, MCPJam), agent frameworks (Goose) and more. Support for optional features varies by host:

  • Some hosts support tools only; others add resources, prompts and elicitation.
  • Extension support is tracked in the extension support matrix; MCP Apps is broadly supported, authorization extensions and Skills less so.
  • Protocol version adoption also varies during the 2026-07-28 transition.

Design implication for server authors: depend only on what the client declares. Check capabilities per request, provide text fallbacks, and don’t assume elicitation, subscriptions or any extension.

docs.title: 12. What is portable, and what isn’t
docs.text:
Portable (defined by the spec) Not portable (host-specific) JSON-RPC messages and their semantics Configuration files (claude_desktop_config.json, VS Code settings…) Primitives: tools, resources, prompts UI for prompts, resources, approvals Capability negotiation Which optional features and extensions a host supports Transports: stdio, Streamable HTTP Tool selection and context management strategy Authorization flow Approval policies and auto-approval rules Error codes and result types The model and how it behaves with your tools Caching and pagination semantics Tool name disambiguation scheme

server.json narrows the configuration gap by standardizing installation metadata that hosts and marketplaces can translate into their own config.

docs.title: 13. Transport portability
docs.text:
The same data-layer messages run over stdio and Streamable HTTP, so one server implementation can offer both, typically by choosing the transport at startup. What changes between them:

  • metadata: HTTP adds mirrored headers;
  • cancellation: stream close vs. notifications/cancelled;
  • credentials: environment vs. OAuth;
  • security controls: Origin validation and loopback binding for HTTP.

Custom transports over byte streams SHOULD reuse stdio framing, which keeps them portable too.

docs.title: 14. Portability across protocol eras
docs.text:
The biggest portability challenge right now is the legacy → modern transition.

Situation Outcome What to do Modern client, modern server Works — Dual-era client, legacy server Works via fallback stdio: probe server/discover, fall back to initialize. HTTP: inspect the 400 body Modern-only client, legacy server Fails Probe first (on stdio) to fail cleanly; upgrade the server or add dual-era support Legacy client, modern-only server Fails (no fall-forward) Server should name its supported versions in the initialize error; support dual-era during migration Legacy client, dual-era server Works Server answers initialize with legacy semantics

Cache the detected era per server process (stdio) or origin (HTTP). Details: Versioning & Discovery.

docs.title: 15. Portability over time: deprecations
docs.text: Deprecated features (sampling, roots, logging, DCR, HTTP+SSE) still work, but a server that depends on them will become less portable as hosts drop support and as the features become eligible for removal (on or after 2027-07-28 for most). Portable designs avoid building new functionality on deprecated features.

docs.title: 16. A portability checklist for server authors
docs.text:
• Target 2026-07-28; add dual-era support only if legacy clients matter
  • Implement server/discover with accurate capabilities and useful instructions
  • Offer stdio and Streamable HTTP if the server makes sense both locally and remotely
  • Check client capabilities per request; never assume elicitation or extensions
  • Provide text fallbacks for structured content and MCP Apps
  • Use clear, collision-resistant tool names within the spec’s character rules
  • Provide outputSchema so hosts can type results (and use code mode)
  • Avoid deprecated features for new work
  • Publish server.json to the MCP Registry under a verified namespace
  • Test with the Inspector (web for exploration, CLI in CI), and against more than one host

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• SDKs: Tier 1 = TypeScript, Python, C#, Go, Rust; Tier 2 = Java, Ruby; Tier 3 = Swift, PHP, Kotlin. Tier 1 = 100% conformance, new features before spec release, triage in 2 business days, critical fixes in 7 days. Extensions aren’t required for any tier.
  • Conformance tests make “implements MCP” verifiable, and gate Final SEPs.
  • Inspector: one package, web / CLI / TUI, shared transports, OAuth state and era negotiation; CLI for CI.
  • MCP Registry (preview): metadata only (server.json); reverse-DNS namespaces verified via GitHub, DNS or HTTP; package ownership via mcpName (npm) and mcp-name: (PyPI); verification ≠ safety (scanning delegated to package registries and aggregators); consumed by aggregators and subregistries (OpenAPI), not directly by hosts; no private servers; immutable versions; deleted status.
  • Portable: messages, primitives, capabilities, transports, auth flow, errors. Not portable: host config, UI, optional feature support, tool selection, approval policy, model behavior.
  • Era portability: dual-era clients reach everyone; legacy clients can’t reach modern-only servers. Avoid deprecated features for durability.

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text:
Competency: Ecosystem & Portability.

The core protocol is deliberately minimal. Extensions add capabilities that are modular, specialized or experimental, without making every client and server implement them. In 2026-07-28, several significant capabilities live here: Tasks (moved out of the core), MCP Apps, Skills, and two authorization extensions.

docs.title: 1. What an extension is
docs.text:
MCP extensions are optional additions to the specification that define capabilities beyond the core protocol. Extensions enable functionality that may be modular (e.g., distinct features like authentication), specialized (e.g., industry-specific logic), or experimental (e.g., features being incubated for potential core inclusion).

The specification’s overview adds that extensions are always opt-in and require explicit support from both client and server, negotiated through capabilities. SDKs keep them disabled by default; developers must opt in explicitly.

docs.title: 2. Identifiers
docs.text:
Format: {vendor-prefix}/{extension-name}, following the _meta key naming rules with a mandatory prefix.

Identifier Extension io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks Tasks io.modelcontextprotocol/ui MCP Apps io.modelcontextprotocol/skills Skills over MCP io.modelcontextprotocol/oauth-client-credentials OAuth Client Credentials io.modelcontextprotocol/enterprise-managed-authorization Enterprise-Managed Authorization
  • Official extensions use io.modelcontextprotocol/.
  • Third-party extensions use a reversed domain the author owns: a company owning example.com uses com.example/my-extension.

docs.title: 3. Negotiation
docs.text:
Clients declare extensions in _meta["io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities"].extensions on each request:

"_meta": {
  "io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion": "2026-07-28",
  "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities": {
    "extensions": {
      "io.modelcontextprotocol/ui": { "mimeTypes": ["text/html;profile=mcp-app"] }
    }
  }
}

Servers declare them in the server/discover response:

"capabilities": {
  "tools": {},
  "extensions": { "io.modelcontextprotocol/ui": {} }
}

Each extension defines the schema of its settings object; an empty object means supported with no settings.

docs.title: 4. Graceful degradation
docs.text:
If only one side supports an extension, the supporting side MUST either:

  • fall back to core protocol behavior, or
  • reject the request with an appropriate error, if the extension is mandatory for it.

Extensions SHOULD document their fallback. Examples from the docs: a server offering UI-enhanced tools should still return meaningful text content to clients without the UI extension; a server requiring a specific authentication extension can reject clients that don’t support it.

docs.title: 5. Where extensions live and how they’re created
docs.text:
• Official extensions live in repositories prefixed ext- in the MCP GitHub organization (ext-auth, ext-apps, ext-skills, ext-tasks).
  • Experimental extensions live in experimental-ext- repositories, must belong to a Working Group or Interest Group, must clearly state their experimental status, and remain under Core Maintainer oversight.

Lifecycle for official extensions (SEP-2133):

  1. Propose: a SEP of type Extensions Track.
  2. Implement: at least one reference implementation in an official SDK, required before review.
  3. Review: Core Maintainers have final authority.
  4. Publish: PR into the extension repository.
  5. Adopt: other clients, servers and SDKs implement it.

Requirements: RFC 2119 language, and an associated working or interest group. An experimental extension graduates by going through the same Extensions Track SEP process.

docs.title: 6. Evolution and breaking changes
docs.text:
Extensions evolve independently of the core, managed by their repository maintainers without core review for routine updates.

Backward compatibility still matters: prefer capability flags or versioning inside the settings object. If a breaking change is unavoidable, use a new identifier, such as io.modelcontextprotocol/my-extension-v2.

A breaking change includes: removing or renaming fields, changing field types, altering existing semantics, or adding new required fields.

docs.title: 7. SDK support
docs.text: SDKs may implement extensions; it’s not required for protocol conformance, and SDK tier requirements exclude experimental features and extensions such as Tasks and MCP Apps. SDKs that support extensions should document which.

docs.title: 8. Why Tasks exist
docs.text:
Some operations take seconds, minutes or longer: CI pipelines, batch processing, human approvals. Blocking a request until they finish fails for several reasons:

Problem with blocking What Tasks provide Long-lived connections; clients and intermediaries time out No long-lived connection: return a handle immediately Disconnect loses the request (streams aren’t resumable) Crash resilience: a durable taskId survives disconnects and restarts No visibility into what’s happening Status metadata: working, input_required, completed, failed, cancelled Mid-operation input needs extra channels Mid-flight interaction via tasks/update Per-tool setup Server-directed: the server decides per request whether to create a task

Tasks were experimental in the core in 2025-11-25 and moved into this extension in 2026-07-28 (SEP-2663), redesigned in the process.

docs.title: 9. How Tasks work
docs.text:
1. Negotiate. The client includes io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks in its per-request capabilities; the server advertises it in server/discover.
  2. Create. For a supported request (e.g. tools/call) the server returns a CreateTaskResult with resultType: "task", containing a taskId, initial status, ttlMs and a suggested pollIntervalMs. The task is durably created before the response is sent.
  3. Poll. The client calls tasks/get with the taskId, respecting pollIntervalMs.
  4. Mid-flight input. If status becomes input_required, the tasks/get response includes an inputRequests map; the client answers with tasks/update carrying inputResponses.
  5. Complete. On completed, result holds what the original request would have returned synchronously. On failed, error holds the JSON-RPC error.
  6. Cancel. tasks/cancel at any time. Cancellation is cooperative: acknowledged, but the task may still reach a non-cancelled terminal state.
sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant Server
    Client->>Server: tools/call (tasks capability declared)
    Server-->>Client: CreateTaskResult (resultType "task", taskId, status working)
    loop poll
        Client->>Server: tasks/get (taskId)
        Server-->>Client: status: working
    end
    Client->>Server: tasks/get
    Server-->>Client: status: input_required, inputRequests
    Client->>Server: tasks/update (taskId, inputResponses)
    Server-->>Client: ack
    Client->>Server: tasks/get
    Server-->>Client: status: completed, result

docs.title: 10. Lifecycle states
docs.text:
Status Meaning Terminal? working In progress No input_required Needs client input (see inputRequests) No completed Done; result has the output Yes failed JSON-RPC error; error has details Yes cancelled Cancelled (not always honored) Yes

Terminal states never change.

docs.title: 11. Notifications instead of polling
docs.text: Servers can push notifications/tasks carrying the full task state, which clients opt into through subscriptions/listen. Polling is the default; clients may rely on notifications when the server supports them.

docs.title: 12. Obligations
docs.text:
Clients: declare support; handle polymorphic results (a normal result or resultType: "task"); poll until terminal; handle input_required via tasks/update; persist task IDs durably so polling resumes after a crash.

Servers: advertise support; check the client declared the extension on that request and never return a task otherwise; create tasks durably before responding; serve tasks/get (with result or error on terminal states); accept tasks/update and ignore responses for unknown or already-satisfied keys; acknowledge tasks/cancel.

docs.title: 13. Differences from the legacy core tasks
docs.text:
2025-11-25 experimental core 2026-07-28 extension Blocking tasks/result Polling with tasks/get No client-to-server input method tasks/update for mid-flight input tasks/list Removed Per-request opt-in required Servers may return task handles unsolicited once the client has the capability

Good fits: long-running jobs, human approval gates, wrapping external job systems that already have job IDs, unreliable (e.g. mobile) connections, batch processing where partial progress matters.

docs.title: 14. What they are
docs.text:
MCP Apps (io.modelcontextprotocol/ui) let servers return interactive HTML interfaces (charts, forms, dashboards, viewers) that render inside the conversation.

Why not a separate web app?

  • Context preservation: the UI lives beside the conversation that produced it.
  • Bidirectional data flow: the app can call the server’s tools, and the host can push fresh results, with no separate API or auth.
  • Host capability integration: the app can ask the host to do things through the user’s already-connected capabilities, with consent.
  • Security guarantees: a sandboxed iframe controlled by the host.

docs.title: 15. How they work
docs.text:
1. UI preloading. A tool’s description includes _meta.ui.resourceUri pointing to a ui:// resource. The host can preload it before the tool is called.
  2. Resource fetch. The host reads the resource: an HTML page, usually bundling its JS and CSS. External origins must be declared in _meta.ui.csp.
  3. Sandboxed rendering. The HTML runs in a sandboxed iframe. _meta.ui can request permissions (camera, microphone) and set csp.
  4. Communication. App and host talk over postMessage using a JSON-RPC dialect of MCP: some messages shared with core (tools/call), some similar (ui/initialize), most new with a ui/ prefix. The app can request tool calls, send messages, update the model’s context and receive data.

The sandbox prevents the app from touching the parent DOM, reading host cookies or storage, navigating the parent page, or running scripts in the parent context. The host decides which capabilities the app gets, such as restricting which tools it can call or disabling link opening.

Client MIME type for app content: text/html;profile=mcp-app.

Good fits: exploring complex data, many-option configuration, rich media viewing, real-time monitoring, multi-step review workflows.

Fallback: servers should still return meaningful text for hosts without the extension.

Support includes Claude, Claude Desktop, VS Code GitHub Copilot, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Goose, Postman, MCPJam, ChatGPT and Cursor, per the extension support matrix. The @modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps package provides an optional App class; hosts can use @mcp-ui/client or the SDK’s App Bridge.

docs.title: 16. What they are
docs.text: Skills over MCP (io.modelcontextprotocol/skills) lets servers expose Agent Skills: directories containing a SKILL.md (YAML frontmatter with name and description, then instructions) and optional supporting files, following the Agent Skills specification. Skills package reusable workflows that combine tools with instructions and references (code review checklists, document processing procedures) and keep them with the service they describe.

docs.title: 17. Protocol
docs.text:
Capabilities: servers MUST declare both resources and the extension. Optional setting directoryRead (default false).

Method Purpose skills/list Catalog: each entry has uri (of SKILL.md), full frontmatter, and a resources manifest (each file’s URI, SHA-256 digest, size), or "dynamic" skills/get One entry by URI; servers MUST answer for every skill they serve, listed or not resources/read Read SKILL.md and supporting files resources/directory/read List direct children of a directory, only if directoryRead: true

Servers SHOULD use the skill:// scheme; hosts MUST NOT identify skills by scheme alone. Skill identity = originating server + URI (names aren’t unique). Servers SHOULD NOT exceed 512 files or 16 MiB per skill.

Reading SKILL.md does not activate a skill. Loading goes through the host’s skill-loading path, which verifies content and applies approval.

docs.title: 18. Integrity and security
docs.text:
Hosts MUST:

  • restrict file reads to URIs in the retained manifest;
  • verify each file’s size and SHA-256 digest before use, and compare SKILL.md frontmatter field by field;
  • not use content failing verification (refresh the entry with skills/get);
  • bind persisted approval to the full set of URIs and digests, so any changed, added or removed file revokes approval;
  • not retrieve files ahead of need;
  • prevent same-name skills from silently replacing each other;
  • tag content with its originating server; cross-server reads need explicit per-call approval naming both servers;
  • treat skill content as untrusted: host-side code execution and permission grants (such as allowed-tools) require explicit per-skill approval;
  • obtain fresh consent before activating a nested skill.

Digests establish consistency with the manifest, not trust in the content. For "dynamic" skills, hosts MAY decline, and approval never covers arbitrary future content.

docs.title: Part 5: Authorization extensions
docs.text:
Covered fully in Authorization. In brief:

Extension For Mechanism OAuth Client Credentials Machine-to-machine: services, CI/CD, daemons client_credentials grant; JWT bearer assertions (RFC 7523) recommended over client secrets Enterprise-Managed Authorization Employees under corporate policy Enterprise IdP issues an ID-JAG after evaluating policy; exchanged for an MCP access token; central revocation and audit

Both are opt-in and require explicit client support.

docs.title: Part 6: Support matrix
docs.text: Extension support varies by host and is tracked in the community-maintained extension support matrix. At the time of writing, MCP Apps has the broadest support; the authorization extensions and Skills have narrower, sometimes partial, support. Always design for fallback.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Extensions are optional, opt-in, disabled by default, and need both sides. Identifiers: vendor-prefix/name; official = io.modelcontextprotocol/; third-party = reverse domain.
  • Negotiated via extensions in client capabilities (per request) and server capabilities (server/discover); empty object = supported, no settings.
  • Unsupported by the peer → fall back to core or reject; document the fallback.
  • Official repos ext-*, experimental experimental-ext-*; created via Extensions Track SEP with an SDK reference implementation; breaking change → new identifier. Not required for SDK conformance.
  • Tasks (moved from core): resultType: "task", taskId, ttlMs, pollIntervalMs; tasks/get polling; tasks/update for input; tasks/cancel (cooperative); states working, input_required, completed, failed, cancelled; optional notifications/tasks via listen; never return a task to a client without the capability.
  • MCP Apps (io.modelcontextprotocol/ui): ui:// resource via _meta.ui.resourceUri; sandboxed iframe; postMessage JSON-RPC dialect (ui/…); csp, permissions; text fallback.
  • Skills (io.modelcontextprotocol/skills): skills/list, skills/get, resources/read; manifests with SHA-256 digests; approvals bound to digests; content untrusted; reading ≠ activating.
  • Auth extensions: Client Credentials (M2M) and Enterprise-Managed (IdP, ID-JAG).

docs.title: Operational Use Cases
docs.text:
Competency: Operational Use Cases.

Where MCP is used, how each use case maps onto primitives, transports and authorization, and the operational patterns that make large deployments work. The patterns here come from the official Client Best Practices and the tools and extensions documentation.

docs.title: 1. Developer tools and coding agents
docs.text:
Hosts: Claude Code, VS Code (GitHub Copilot), Cursor, JetBrains IDEs, Goose.

Servers: filesystem, git, GitHub, issue trackers, error monitoring (Sentry), CI systems, databases, cloud consoles, design tools (Figma).

The documentation’s headline example: “Claude Code can generate an entire web app using a Figma design.”

Need Primitive Typical deployment Read and edit project files Tools (and resources) on a filesystem server Local, stdio Inspect repo history Tools / resources on a git server Local, stdio Open PRs, read issues Tools on a GitHub server Remote (Streamable HTTP + OAuth) or local with a token in env Investigate production errors Tools on Sentry’s hosted server Remote, OAuth Standard workflows (“/review”, “/fix-issue”) Prompts Any Project context (open file, README) Resources Any

Risks to manage: code-execution tools; prompt injection through issue and PR text written by outsiders; secrets in the workspace; one-click installation of local servers.

docs.title: 2. Knowledge and data access
docs.text:
Example: “Enterprise chatbots can connect to multiple databases across an organization, empowering users to analyze data using chat.”

A database server typically exposes:

  • resources for schemas (postgres://db/schema/{table} via templates),
  • tools for queries (run_query, ideally read-only),
  • prompts with few-shot examples of good queries.

Operational concerns: read-only credentials behind the tool; per-user row-level authorization from the validated token; cacheScope: "private" for user-specific reads; pagination for large lists; completion on template parameters (with access control, to avoid disclosure); audit logging of queries.

docs.title: 3. Enterprise systems of record
docs.text:
CRM, ticketing, HR, finance, document management. Characteristics:

  • Remote servers, often operated by the platform team or the SaaS vendor.
  • Corporate identity: Enterprise-Managed Authorization, or core OAuth backed by the corporate IdP.
  • Strong need for consent on writes, least-privilege scopes, auditability.
  • Elicitation for confirmations (“Approve refund of $1,200?”) and URL-mode elicitation for connecting third-party accounts.
  • Sometimes an MCP gateway in front of many internal servers, centralizing authentication, policy, rate limits and logging. The Streamable HTTP header mirroring (Mcp-Method, Mcp-Name, Mcp-Param-*) exists precisely so such intermediaries can route and enforce policy without parsing bodies.

docs.title: 4. Personal productivity
docs.text:
Example: “Agents can access your Google Calendar and Notion, acting as a more personalized AI assistant.”

Calendar, email, notes, task managers. Mostly remote servers with per-user OAuth. The travel-planning scenario from the docs composes several such servers: a prompt starts the workflow, calendar resources give context, tools search flights, book hotels, create events and send email, with elicitation for booking confirmation.

Risks: these hosts combine private data (email, calendar) with untrusted content (incoming email bodies) and outbound actions (send email). That is the high-risk combination from Trust Boundaries, so confirmation with visible arguments matters most here.

docs.title: 5. Creative and physical-world automation
docs.text:
Example: “AI models can create 3D designs on Blender and print them out using a 3D printer.”

Tools that drive desktop applications or devices, usually local. MCP Apps fit well when the user needs to see and manipulate rich output (a 3D preview, a chart, a PDF) in the conversation.

docs.title: 6. Automation and machine-to-machine
docs.text:
CI/CD pipelines, scheduled reports, back-office agents: no human in the loop at call time.

  • Authorization via the OAuth Client Credentials extension (JWT bearer assertions recommended).
  • Clients don’t declare elicitation when no user is present, so servers must not depend on it. A server that truly needs a human returns MissingRequiredClientCapabilityError, or is simply not used in that context.
  • Tasks extension for long jobs, with durable handles that survive restarts.
  • Human oversight moves earlier (policy, scoped credentials, approval of the automation itself) and later (audit review).

docs.title: Part 2: Deployment patterns
docs.text:
Pattern Shape Good for Watch out for Local stdio server Host launches server subprocess Files, local tools, single user Runs with user privileges; consent to command; sandbox Local HTTP server Server on 127.0.0.1 Sharing one local server among several local apps Origin validation, loopback binding, token auth Remote server Public or internal HTTPS endpoint Shared services, many users OAuth, audience validation, rate limits, SSRF-safe clients Horizontally scaled remote Many stateless instances behind a load balancer High traffic Explicit handles and requestState carry state; no sticky sessions needed Gateway / proxy One endpoint fronting many servers Central policy, auth, logging Confused deputy if using static upstream client IDs; header–body validation Embedded / in-process Custom transport inside one application Tight integration Must preserve JSON-RPC, patterns and per-request metadata

Why statelessness matters operationally

Because 2026-07-28 requests are self-contained, a remote MCP server scales like any stateless web service: round-robin load balancing, autoscaling, rolling deploys, instance failure without lost sessions. MRTR retries and explicit handles carry the little state that must survive between requests. SEP-2575’s motivation was exactly this operational pain.

docs.title: Part 3: Patterns for hosts at scale
7. The problem
docs.text:
As hosts connect more servers they accumulate hundreds or thousands of tools. Two costs appear:

  1. Definition cost. Every tool definition in the model’s context costs tokens every turn. With dozens of servers, definitions can consume most of the context window before the model reads the user’s message. Too many options also degrade tool selection. The documentation’s illustration: roughly 150,000 tokens of definitions loaded up front, versus about 2,000 with progressive discovery.
  2. Intermediate-result cost. In a multi-step task (read a document, transform it, write it elsewhere), every intermediate result passes through the model’s context, costing tokens and latency even when the model doesn’t need to read it.

Two patterns address them: progressive discovery controls when definitions enter context; programmatic tool calling controls how tools are invoked. Neither changes the protocol. Both are host design.

docs.title: 8. Progressive tool discovery
docs.text:
Idea: fetch tool definitions with tools/list as normal, but don’t inject them all into the model’s context. Give the model a lightweight search_tools meta-tool, and load full definitions only when needed.

When to switch: implement a threshold, for example when definitions exceed 1–5% of the context window. Below it, loading everything is fine.

Search strategies:

Strategy How Trade-off Keyword BM25, regex over names and descriptions Simple and effective with descriptive names Embedding Vector similarity over descriptions Handles synonyms and semantics better Subagent A small fast model picks tools for the task Usually very good; costs more Hybrid Combine rankings, or pick a strategy per query Best of several

Some model providers offer built-in tool search, which may be preferable unless you need custom ranking or access-control filtering.

The three-layer approach:

  1. Catalog. The model calls search_tools({ query: "update salesforce record" }) and gets names and one-line descriptions only.
  2. Inspect. The model calls get_tool_details({ name: "salesforce_updateRecord" }) and gets the full schema for that tool alone.
  3. Execute. The model calls the tool with full knowledge of its interface.

Dynamic server management extends this to whole servers: keep a registry of available servers with descriptions, connect a server only when the model needs it (then server/discover and tools/list), and disconnect servers no longer relevant, freeing context. Skills can declare which servers they need, so the host connects them only when the skill is invoked.

Implementation guidelines:

Guideline Why Offer multiple detail levels (name only, name+description, full schema) Let the model pay only for what it needs Cache definitions host-side Re-injecting later needs no new tools/list Refresh on list_changed Keep the search catalog correct Group tools by server Helps the model reason about related capabilities and provenance Follow ttlMs / cacheScope; treat a list as stale on list_changed even before TTL expiry Correct freshness

Prompt caching interaction. Providers cache the prompt prefix, including the tools array. Adding or removing tools mid-conversation invalidates it, and the cache miss can cost more than the definitions saved. To preserve caching: append new definitions after the cache breakpoint instead of re-sorting, or route every call through a single stable call_tool({name, args}) meta-tool so the array never changes; treat server disconnection as a conversation-boundary operation. This is also why servers SHOULD return tools in deterministic order.

docs.title: 9. Programmatic tool calling (“code mode”)
docs.text:
Idea: instead of calling tools one at a time with every result flowing through the model, the model writes code that calls tools. The code runs in a sandbox, and only the final output returns to the model.

How it works:

  1. Generate a typed API from MCP schemas. The host turns each tool’s inputSchema and outputSchema into typed functions.

    function logging_getLogs(input: { level: "error" | "warn" | "info"; since: number }):
  Promise<{ entries: LogEntry[] }> { return mcp.callTool("logging_getLogs", input); }

function ticketing_createIssue(input: { title: string; body?: string; priority: "low" | "medium" | "high" }):
  Promise<{ issueId: string }> { return mcp.callTool("ticketing_createIssue", input); }

  2. The model writes a script. “File a ticket for each unique error in the last hour”:

    const logs = await logging_getLogs({ level: "error", since: Date.now() - 3600000 });
const unique = new Map<string, LogEntry>();
for (const log of logs.entries) if (!unique.has(log.message)) unique.set(log.message, log);
for (const [message, log] of unique) {
  await ticketing_createIssue({ title: `Error: ${message}`, body: `First seen: ${log.timestamp}`, priority: "high" });
}
console.log(`Filed ${unique.size} tickets from ${logs.entries.length} error logs`);

  3. The sandbox executes it. Function calls are intercepted and routed through the host broker as tools/call requests. Thousands of log entries flow between servers without entering the model’s context. The model sees one summary line.

Why outputSchema matters here: with it, the host generates precise return types. Without it, use a generic type, or extract a typed result with a small model through a host-brokered helper (validating the result, since extraction can hallucinate or drop fields). The real fix is for server authors to provide outputSchema.

Architecture:

  • Sandbox: runs model code with no direct network access; its only interface is the generated stubs.
  • Host broker: maps calls to servers, executes them, returns results; holds credentials, which are never exposed to generated code.
  • Model: sees only console.log output or a return value.

Example runtimes: Deno or isolated-vm (JavaScript), Monty (Python, experimental), pctx (TypeScript, early), Wasmtime (any language via Wasm).

Security considerations (from the docs):

  • Per-call authorization. The broker is still the MCP host for spec purposes. Apply the same human-in-the-loop policy to sandbox-originated calls. Approving a script isn’t blanket approval for every call it makes; categorical grants are allowed but each call is still checked against them.
  • Cross-server data flow. Results from one server are untrusted input to another; review brokered calls like direct ones. Output truncation alone doesn’t prevent exfiltration.
  • Network isolation of the sandbox; no credential exposure; resource limits (timeouts, memory); filter and truncate output before it reaches the model.

Error handling: a tool failure arrives as isError: true, not a transport error. Generated wrappers should throw on it so model code can try/catch; an uncaught error is surfaced as the script’s result so the model can self-correct, and the model must report partial side effects already committed.

Combining both patterns: discover the few tools needed, load their schemas, then write one script calling them. This minimizes both definition tokens and result tokens.

docs.title: 10. Stateful workflows
docs.text: MCP has no session. For multi-step stateful work (carts, browser sessions, transactions), servers return explicit handles from creation tools; the model passes them back; servers validate ownership on every call, state the retention in the tool description, and return a tool execution error for expired handles so the model can start over.

docs.title: 11. Human approval workflows
docs.text:
• Inline confirmation: host dialog before a tool call.
  • Server-driven confirmation: the server returns InputRequiredResult with a form elicitation (“Confirm deploy to production?”) and completes on retry with accept. The server enforces the approval itself, so it can’t be bypassed by a misconfigured host policy.
  • Long approval gates: the Tasks extension, where a task moves to input_required and the client supplies input via tasks/update.

docs.title: 12. Long-running operations
docs.text: Duration Mechanism Seconds Normal request; progress notifications; timeouts Tens of seconds to minutes Progress with timeout reset, plus a maximum timeout; cancellation Minutes to hours, or unreliable connections Tasks extension: durable taskId, tasks/get polling, tasks/cancel

docs.title: 13. Rich interactive output
docs.text: When text isn’t enough (exploring data, many-option configuration, rich media, live monitoring, multi-step review), MCP Apps render a sandboxed HTML UI inside the conversation that can call the server’s tools. Servers should still return meaningful text for hosts without the extension.

docs.title: 14. Reusable expertise
docs.text: Skills over MCP lets a server publish workflow instructions (SKILL.md plus supporting files) that hosts discover and load on demand, keeping instructions next to the service they describe. Prompts are the core-protocol analogue for user-triggered templates.

docs.title: Part 5: Anti-patterns
docs.text: Anti-pattern Why it’s a problem Better Exposing every tool of every server to the model every turn Token cost; poor tool selection Progressive discovery above a threshold One mega-tool execute(action, params) Model can’t see capabilities; weak validation; coarse permissions Focused tools with precise schemas Vague tool descriptions Wrong calls Say what it does, when to use it, argument formats Returning huge results to the model Context bloat Pagination, resource_link, audience annotations, code mode Relying on connection state Breaks under load balancing; forbidden Explicit handles, requestState Auto-approving based on untrusted annotations Trivially bypassed Trust by server provenance; confirm risky calls Asking for secrets in form elicitation Secrets pass through the client URL mode Passing user tokens to upstream APIs Forbidden token passthrough Separate upstream credentials Shuffling tools/list order Breaks client and prompt caches Deterministic order Protocol errors for bad argument values Model can’t self-correct isError: true with actionable text Building new features on sampling, roots or logging Deprecated Provider APIs; arguments/config; stderr/OpenTelemetry

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Use cases: developer tools (local filesystem/git, remote GitHub/Sentry), data access (schema resources, read-only query tools), enterprise systems (remote, corporate identity, gateways), personal productivity (per-user OAuth; high injection risk), creative/physical (local tools, MCP Apps), M2M (client credentials, no elicitation, Tasks).
  • Deployment: local stdio, local HTTP (Origin + loopback + auth), remote, stateless horizontally scaled, gateways (watch confused deputy), in-process custom transports.
  • Progressive discovery: threshold klzzwxh:0163 of context; kword / embedding / subagent / hybrid search; catalog → inspect → exute**; dynamic server connection; cache and refresh on list_changed; protect prompt caching (append, stable call_tool, deterministic order).
  • Code mode: typed API from schemas (outputSchema matters), model-written script in a network-isolated sandbox, host broker holds credentials, same per-call approval policy, cross-server results untrusted, isError → exception.
  • Workflows: explicit handles; elicitation-based approvals; Tasks for long jobs; MCP Apps for rich UI; Skills for reusable instructions.

docs.title: Domain 5 Quiz — Use Cases & Ecosystem
docs.text:
18 exam-style questions. Target: 15/18.

1. Under which organization is MCP governed today?

  • A. The Cloud Native Computing Foundation
  • B. The Agentic AI Foundation, a directed fund under the Linux Foundation
  • C. The W3C
  • D. Anthropic alone
Answer

B. The AAIF was announced on 9 December 2025 with MCP, goose and AGENTS.md as founding projects.

2. Who holds final decision authority in MCP’s technical governance?

  • A. The largest corporate member
  • B. The Lead Maintainers (BDFL role)
  • C. A public vote of contributors
  • D. The Linux Foundation board
Answer

B. Lead Maintainers can veto any decision and appoint Core Maintainers. Membership is for individuals, not companies.

3. What is the difference between an Interest Group and a Working Group?

  • A. They are the same
  • B. Interest Groups identify and discuss problems (non-binding); Working Groups build concrete solutions such as SEPs and implementations (binding decisions)
  • C. Working Groups are for companies; Interest Groups for individuals
  • D. Interest Groups write the specification
Answer

B. Typical flow: discuss in an IG, then form or join a WG to build a solution and submit a SEP.

4. A SEP found no sponsor within six months. What is its status?

  • A. rejected
  • B. dormant, which can be revived if a sponsor is found
  • C. withdrawn
  • D. final
Answer

B. Dormant is explicitly not the same as rejected.

5. Which is REQUIRED before a Standards Track SEP with observable protocol behavior can reach final?

  • A. Implementations in every Tier 1 SDK
  • B. A reference implementation and a merged conformance test scenario
  • C. Approval by the Linux Foundation board
  • D. A blog post
Answer

B. SDK implementations are not required for Final.

6. Which SEP type is used to propose a new MCP extension?

  • A. Informational
  • B. Process
  • C. Extensions Track
  • D. Standards Track only
Answer

C. Extensions Track follows the same review as Standards Track, and requires a reference implementation in an official SDK before review.

7. A host connects to 40 servers exposing 900 tools, and tool definitions consume most of the context window. Which pattern does the Client Best Practices guide recommend?

  • A. Remove servers until fewer than 20 tools remain
  • B. Progressive tool discovery: give the model a search meta-tool and load full definitions only when needed
  • C. Ask servers to shorten their descriptions
  • D. Use sampling to summarize tool lists
Answer

B. Switch past a threshold (for example 1–5% of the context window), using keyword, embedding, subagent or hybrid search.

8. In programmatic tool calling (“code mode”), which statement about security is correct?

  • A. Approving the script grants blanket approval for every tool call it makes
  • B. The sandbox should have direct network access to call servers
  • C. The broker should apply the same per-call authorization policy to sandbox-originated calls, and credentials stay in the host
  • D. Tool results from one server can be trusted as input to another
Answer

C. The sandbox is network-isolated, the host broker holds credentials, and cross-server results remain untrusted.

9. Why does a host implementing progressive discovery sometimes route calls through a single stable call_tool({name, args}) meta-tool?

  • A. To bypass authorization
  • B. To avoid changing the tools array mid-conversation, which would invalidate the provider’s prompt cache
  • C. Because MCP requires it
  • D. To reduce the number of servers
Answer

B. Adding or removing definitions mid-conversation breaks prompt caching; appending after the breakpoint or a stable meta-tool avoids that.

10. Which MCP extension moved from the core protocol into an extension in 2026-07-28?

  • A. Elicitation
  • B. Tasks
  • C. Resources
  • D. Completion
Answer

B. Tasks is now io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks, with tasks/get polling and tasks/update for input.

11. A client that did not declare the Tasks extension calls a long-running tool. What must the server do?

  • A. Return a CreateTaskResult anyway
  • B. Never return a task to that client; fall back to core behavior or reject
  • C. Switch the client to Streamable HTTP
  • D. Return resultType: "input_required"
Answer

B. Servers must check the client declared the extension on the request. If one side lacks an extension, the other falls back or rejects.

12. How are MCP Apps rendered by web hosts?

  • A. Directly in the host page’s DOM
  • B. In a sandboxed iframe, communicating with the host over postMessage using a JSON-RPC dialect of MCP
  • C. As images generated by the server
  • D. In a separate browser window with full cookie access
Answer

B. The UI comes from a ui:// resource referenced by _meta.ui.resourceUri, rendered in a sandboxed iframe.

13. Under Skills over MCP, what must a host do before using a supporting file from a skill?

  • A. Nothing; skills from connected servers are trusted
  • B. Verify the file’s size and SHA-256 digest against the retained manifest
  • C. Execute it to check it works
  • D. Fetch all files at connection time
Answer

B. Hosts must restrict reads to the manifest, verify digests and sizes, and must not retrieve files ahead of need.

14. Which SDKs are Tier 1?

  • A. TypeScript, Python, Java, Kotlin, Swift
  • B. TypeScript, Python, C#, Go, Rust
  • C. Python and TypeScript only
  • D. Go, Rust, Ruby, PHP
Answer

B. Java and Ruby are Tier 2; Swift, PHP and Kotlin are Tier 3.

15. What does Tier 1 require for conformance tests?

  • A. 50% pass rate
  • B. 80% pass rate
  • C. 100% pass rate
  • D. No requirement
Answer

C. Tier 2 requires 80%; Tier 3 has no minimum.

16. What does the official MCP Registry store?

  • A. Server source code and binaries
  • B. Metadata (server.json) pointing to packages on registries like npm and PyPI, or to remote server URLs
  • C. Only servers built by Anthropic
  • D. Private enterprise servers
Answer

B. Package registries host code; the MCP Registry hosts metadata. Private servers aren’t supported.

17. A server is published as io.github.alice/weather-mcp in the MCP Registry. What does that guarantee?

  • A. The server’s code has been security-audited
  • B. The publisher authenticated as the GitHub user alice (namespace ownership), not that the code is safe
  • C. The server supports every MCP feature
  • D. Anthropic endorses it
Answer

B. The registry verifies namespace ownership and delegates security scanning to package registries and aggregators.

18. Which is NOT portable across MCP hosts by virtue of the specification?

  • A. The JSON-RPC message format
  • B. Capability negotiation
  • C. The configuration file format used to register servers
  • D. Error codes
Answer

C. Host configuration (for example claude_desktop_config.json) is host-specific. server.json in the registry standardizes installation metadata, not host config.

Score Verdict 16–18 Ready for the mock exams. 12–15 Re-read Operational Use Cases and Extensions. < 12 Rework the domain.

docs.title: Roles, Responsibilities & Adoption
docs.text:
Competency: Roles, Responsibilities & Adoption.

MCP distributes responsibilities across many parties, most of whom never coordinate. This chapter maps who owns what, explains how the protocol itself is governed, and covers how organizations adopt MCP sensibly.

docs.title: 1. The roles
docs.text: Role Who they are Builds or operates Server author Developer exposing a system via MCP An MCP server (local package or remote service) Host / client developer Team building an AI application The host: UI, agent loop, clients, consent Server operator Team running a remote server in production Hosting, scaling, authorization, monitoring Authorization server operator Identity team or IdP vendor Token issuance, client registration, policy Security / governance team AppSec, IT, compliance Policies: which servers, which tools, which data, audit End user The person using the AI application Consent decisions, server configuration Enterprise IdP administrator Corporate IT Enterprise-Managed Authorization policy Registry publisher / aggregator Server maintainers; marketplaces Publishing server.json; curating catalogs SDK maintainer Language SDK teams Protocol implementations, conformance Spec contributor / maintainer MCP community SEPs, working groups, the specification

docs.title: 2. Who owns which responsibility
docs.text:
The specification assigns obligations to specific parties. Knowing the owner is how you answer “who must…” questions.

Server authors and operators

  • Implement server/discover (MUST) and advertise every implemented capability.
  • Never initiate requests; use InputRequiredResult for client input.
  • Validate all tool inputs, implement access controls, rate limit, sanitize outputs (MUST).
  • Validate resource URIs and prevent directory traversal (MUST).
  • Write clear, accurate tool descriptions and schemas; provide outputSchema where useful; keep tools/list deterministic.
  • Set correct ttlMs and cacheScope; never rely on cache scope for access control.
  • Protect requestState (HMAC/AEAD, principal, TTL, request binding).
  • Bind state handles to the authenticated user.
  • For remote servers: implement Protected Resource Metadata, validate token audience, never pass tokens through, validate Origin, and reject header/body mismatches.
  • For local servers: prefer stdio, log to stderr, bind HTTP to 127.0.0.1.
  • Never use form elicitation for secrets; verify the user in URL-mode flows.

Host and client developers

  • Enforce consent: explicit consent before invoking tools and before exposing user data to servers.
  • Keep a human in the loop, show tool inputs before calling, confirm sensitive operations.
  • Treat server metadata as untrusted (annotations, descriptions) unless the server is trusted.
  • Validate tool results before they reach the model; set timeouts; log tool usage.
  • Put required _meta on every request; handle resultType correctly (absent → complete; unknown → invalid).
  • Perform MRTR retries correctly (new id, exact requestState).
  • Disambiguate tool names across servers.
  • Implement OAuth correctly: PKCE S256, resource parameter, iss validation, issuer-keyed credentials, SSRF protections, safe URL opening.
  • For one-click local installs, show the exact command and sandbox.
  • Handle elicitation safely: identify the requesting server, never pre-fetch or auto-open URLs.

Security and governance teams

  • Decide which servers may be used (allowlists, registry namespaces, internal registries).
  • Define approval policy by risk tier.
  • Enforce least privilege scopes and central identity (Enterprise-Managed Authorization).
  • Require audit logging and trace propagation; review usage.
  • Track deprecations (sampling, roots, logging, DCR, HTTP+SSE) and protocol migrations.

End users

  • Grant or deny consent knowingly; review tool arguments; install servers only from trusted sources.

The division in one sentence

Servers protect themselves and their data; hosts protect the user; authorization servers protect identity; governance teams decide what is allowed at all.

docs.title: Part 2: How MCP itself is governed
3. From Anthropic to a neutral foundation
docs.text:
• November 2024: Anthropic open-sources MCP.
  • 9 December 2025: the Linux Foundation announces the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF), a directed fund under the Linux Foundation, with three founding project contributions:
    • Model Context Protocol (Anthropic)
    • goose (Block), an open-source, local-first AI agent framework built on MCP integration
    • AGENTS.md (OpenAI), a standard file giving AI coding agents project-specific guidance
  • AAIF platinum members at formation include Amazon Web Services, Anthropic, Block, Bloomberg, Cloudflare, Google, Microsoft and OpenAI.

Why it matters: a protocol intended to be vendor-neutral infrastructure is more credible, and more widely adopted, when no single vendor controls it. Competitors can build on it without depending on a rival’s goodwill.

MCP is legally established as Model Context Protocol a Series of LF Projects, LLC, and follows LF Projects policies (including trademark usage).

docs.title: 4. Licensing
docs.text:
Material License Code and specifications Apache License 2.0 Documentation (excluding specifications) Creative Commons Attribution 4.0

Contributors retain copyright in their contributions; no copyright assignment is required. Core Maintainers may approve alternative open licenses by exception.

docs.title: 5. Technical governance structure
docs.text:
A hierarchy like Python’s or PyTorch’s:

Role Scope Lead Maintainers (BDFL) Final decision authority; can veto any decision; appoint and remove Core Maintainers Core Maintainers Overall project direction and the specification; can veto Maintainer decisions by majority vote; appoint and remove Maintainers Maintainers Specific areas: SDKs, documentation, Working Groups Contributors Issues, pull requests, discussions

Maintainers, Core Maintainers and Lead Maintainers together form the MCP Steering Group.

Principles worth knowing:

  • Membership is for individuals, not companies. No seats are reserved for any employer.
  • Maintainers at every level use the same pull-request process as outside contributors.
  • Core Maintainers meet every two weeks to discuss and vote on proposals; decisions and discussions are recorded transparently.
  • The current Lead Maintainers are David Soria Parra and Den Delimarsky; Justin Spahr-Summers, MCP’s co-inventor, is Lead Maintainer Emeritus.

docs.title: 6. Interest Groups and Working Groups
docs.text:
Interest Group (IG) Working Group (WG) Purpose Identify and discuss problems Build concrete solutions Output Problem statements, use cases, recommendations SEPs, implementations, code Duration Ongoing while relevant Until deliverables complete Leadership Facilitators Leads Decisions Rough consensus, non-binding Binding (lazy consensus → vote → escalation) Example “Security in MCP” “Server Identity”

Typical flow: discuss a problem in an IG → validate it’s worth solving → form or join a WG → submit a SEP → implement.

docs.title: 7. Specification Enhancement Proposals (SEPs)
docs.text:
What a SEP is: a design document proposing a feature or process change, with rationale. SEPs are the primary mechanism for major features and the historical record of design decisions. They live as Markdown files in the seps/ directory of the specification repository, numbered by their pull request (PR #1850 becomes SEP-1850).

When a SEP is needed: new features or protocol changes, breaking changes, governance or process changes, complex or controversial topics. Not for bug fixes, typos, documentation clarifications, added examples or minor schema fixes.

SEP types:

Type For Standards Track A new protocol feature or interoperability standard Informational Design guidance without proposing a feature Process Changes to MCP processes Extensions Track A protocol extension; same review as Standards Track

Workflow and statuses:

flowchart TD
    Idea -->|PR with SEP file| AS{"Awaiting sponsor<br/>(up to 6 months)"}
    AS --> Draft
    AS --> Dormant["Dormant (no sponsor)"]
    AS --> Withdrawn
    Draft -->|sponsor review| InReview[In-Review]
    InReview --> Decision{Core Maintainers}
    Decision --> Accepted
    Decision --> Rejected
    Accepted -->|reference implementation<br/>+ conformance test| Final
Status Meaning draft Has a sponsor; informal review in-review Formal Core Maintainer review accepted Approved; awaiting implementation and conformance rejected Declined withdrawn Author withdrew final Complete with implementation and conformance superseded Replaced by a newer SEP dormant No sponsor within 6 months; can be revived. Not the same as rejected

Key rules:

  • A sponsor (a Core Maintainer or Maintainer) champions the SEP and updates its status. Authors don’t change status themselves.
  • Acceptance requires a prototype implementation (pseudocode or a design doc is not enough), clear ecosystem benefit, and community consensus.
  • Final requires a reference implementation and, for Standards Track SEPs with observable protocol behavior, a conformance test merged in the conformance repository. SDK implementations are not required for Final.
  • Final SEPs are historical records; the current specification is authoritative if they differ.

The 2026-07-28 redesign came through this process: SEP-2575 (stateless MCP), SEP-2322 (MRTR), SEP-2567 (sessionless handles), SEP-2577 (deprecations), SEP-2596 (feature lifecycle), SEP-2663 (Tasks as an extension).

docs.title: 8. The feature lifecycle
docs.text: Adopted in 2026-07-28 (SEP-2596): features are Active, Deprecated (at least 12 months before removal eligibility, or 90 days expedited) or Removed, tracked in a public deprecated features registry. It gives adopters a predictable migration window.

docs.title: 9. Why organizations adopt MCP
docs.text:
• Reuse: one server per system of record, usable by every AI application.
  • Vendor neutrality: an open, foundation-governed protocol supported by most major AI platforms.
  • Central control point: authorization, logging and rate limiting for AI access to a system, in one place.
  • Ecosystem leverage: existing public servers for common tools (GitHub, Sentry, Slack, databases).
  • Faster delivery: SDKs make simple servers a few dozen lines.

docs.title: 10. A phased adoption path
docs.text: Phase Scope Controls to establish 1. Explore Individual developers, local stdio servers, read-only tools Approved server list; sandboxing; no production credentials 2. Pilot A team; a few internal remote servers OAuth via the corporate IdP; audit logging; tool confirmation policy 3. Scale Many teams and servers Internal registry or subregistry; Enterprise-Managed Authorization; OpenTelemetry tracing; scope minimization 4. Operate Business-critical workflows Conformance testing; version pinning; deprecation tracking; incident response for AI actions

docs.title: 11. Decisions every adopter faces
docs.text:
Build or reuse a server? Reuse vetted public servers for standard tools; build internal servers for proprietary systems.

Local or remote?

Choose local (stdio) when Choose remote (Streamable HTTP) when Data lives on the user’s machine (files, local git) Data lives in a shared service Single user Many users Credentials can come from the environment Per-user authorization and audit are needed Low latency, no network Central updates without redistributing binaries

Which authorization model?

Scenario Model Local stdio server Environment credentials Interactive users of a remote server Core OAuth 2.1 Background jobs, CI/CD OAuth Client Credentials extension Employees under corporate policy Enterprise-Managed Authorization extension

Which primitives? Tools for actions the model decides on; resources for context the application attaches; prompts for workflows users start.

Which protocol version? New implementations target 2026-07-28. Organizations with legacy clients or servers plan dual-era support during migration.

docs.title: 12. Migrating to 2026-07-28
docs.text:
A checklist for teams with existing MCP implementations:

Servers

  • Implement server/discover
  • Read version and capabilities from per-request _meta; reject missing fields with -32602
  • Add resultType to every result
  • Replace server-initiated elicitation/create (and sampling, roots) with InputRequiredResult; protect requestState
  • Remove reliance on sessions; move cross-call state to explicit handles bound to users
  • Replace resources/subscribe and the GET stream with subscriptions/listen
  • Add ttlMs / cacheScope to cacheable results
  • Return tools in deterministic order
  • Switch resource not-found to -32602
  • Validate MCP-Protocol-Version / Mcp-Method / Mcp-Name headers; answer legacy GET/DELETE with 405
  • Plan migration off sampling, roots, logging (provider APIs, arguments/config, stderr/OpenTelemetry)
  • Move experimental tasks to the Tasks extension

Clients

  • Send required _meta on every request, plus HTTP headers
  • Handle input_required and retry correctly
  • Handle UnsupportedProtocolVersionError and MissingRequiredClientCapabilityError
  • Use subscriptions/listen; correlate by subscriptionId
  • Honor cache hints
  • Implement era detection if legacy servers must still work
  • Prefer CIMD over DCR; validate iss; set application_type if still using DCR

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Servers protect themselves (validation, access control, audience checks, requestState integrity); hosts protect users (consent, human in the loop, untrusted metadata, safe URLs); ASes protect identity; governance teams decide what is allowed.
  • MCP joined the Agentic AI Foundation, a directed fund under the Linux Foundation, on 9 December 2025, alongside goose and AGENTS.md.
  • Licenses: Apache 2.0 for code and specs; CC-BY 4.0 for docs; no copyright assignment.
  • Governance: Lead Maintainers (BDFL) → Core Maintainers → Maintainers → Contributors; individuals, not companies.
  • Interest Groups discuss problems (non-binding); Working Groups build solutions (binding).
  • SEPs: Standards Track, Informational, Process, Extensions Track; numbered by PR; need a sponsor and a prototype; Final needs reference implementation and conformance tests; dormant ≠ rejected.
  • Feature lifecycle: Active → Deprecated (≥ 12 months) → Removed.
  • Adopt in phases; choose local vs. remote, authorization model and primitives deliberately; migrate to 2026-07-28 with a checklist.

docs.title: Exam Guide
docs.text:
Everything about the exam itself: what it covers, how the protocol changed, how to prepare, and what to do on the day.

  • Official Blueprint. The five domains and every competency, mapped to the chapters that cover them.
  • What Changed in 2026-07-28. The redesign the exam is built on, and the legacy knowledge it invalidates.
  • Study Plan. A 4-week plan and a 10-day sprint.
  • Official Resources. The specification, docs and community material the exam draws on.
  • Exam-Day Strategy. Proctoring, time budget and how to handle the question types.
  • Glossary. Every term and method name you should recognize on sight.

docs.title: Logistics
docs.text:
• Purchase and scheduling go through the Linux Foundation Training portal. You have 12 months from purchase to take the exam, and one retake is included.
  • Delivery is online and proctored. You must comply with the Linux Foundation Global Certification & Confidentiality Agreement, and should read the Candidate Handbook and Important Instructions before exam day.
  • Duration is 90 minutes of multiple-choice questions.
  • Number of questions and passing score are not published. Linux Foundation associate-level multiple-choice exams have typically been around 60 questions in 90 minutes with a passing score around 75%. Treat those as planning assumptions, not facts: budget about 90 seconds per question and aim for 85%+ on the mock exams.
  • Validity is two years.

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text:
The Linux Foundation positions MCPA for people moving into AI engineering and platform roles and AI governance and security roles, and for teams building AI assistants and enterprise AI solutions.

That split explains the domain weights. Engineering questions (architecture, interactions) and governance questions (security, consent, auditability) together make up most of the exam. Domain 4 alone is almost a quarter of it.

docs.title: Recommended background
docs.text:
There are no formal prerequisites. The Linux Foundation recommends:

Recommended experience Where this course covers it JSON-RPC or message-based protocols JSON-RPC Messages Calling LLM APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Ollama) Model Interaction Flow Agentic concepts: ReAct, tool use, chain-of-thought Core Concepts, Tools Security basics: API keys, OAuth 2.1, tokens Authorization with OAuth 2.1 Reading server manifests and capability definitions Schemas, Versioning & Discovery

docs.title: Official Blueprint
docs.text:
The five domains and their competencies, as published on the Linux Foundation MCPA page, mapped to the chapters that cover them.

How to read this page

The Linux Foundation publishes only competency names for each domain, not detailed task statements. The descriptions under each competency below are this course’s interpretation, grounded in the 2026-07-28 specification and in the exam focus statement: “architecture, message flow, client-server interactions, capabilities, tools, resources, prompts, transports, and security considerations.”

docs.title: Domain 1 — MCP Fundamentals · 16%
docs.text: Competency What it means in practice Covered in MCP Purpose & Scope The integration problem MCP solves; what the protocol covers and what it deliberately leaves out Why MCP Exists Core MCP Concepts Hosts, clients, servers; the three server primitives and their control model; JSON-RPC; capabilities; statelessness Core Concepts Interoperability & Value Why a shared protocol matters to developers, AI applications and end users; composability; build once, integrate everywhere Interoperability & Value

docs.title: Domain 2 — Architecture & Components · 14%
docs.text:
Competency What it means in practice Covered in Schemas & Structured Data JSON Schema 2020-12, inputSchema / outputSchema, structuredContent, content types, annotations, $ref rules Schemas & Structured Data MCP Hosts, Clients and Servers The role of each participant, the 1:1 client–server rule, isolation between servers, design principles Hosts, Clients & Servers Model Interaction Flow End to end: user → host → LLM → client → server → result → LLM. Where the model actually sits Model Interaction Flow

Also architectural, and part of the exam focus statement: JSON-RPC Messages & _meta, Transports and Versioning & Discovery.

docs.title: Domain 3 — Interactions & Execution · 26%
docs.text:
The heaviest domain.

Competency What it means in practice Covered in Interaction Patterns & Response Handling Request/response, Multi Round-Trip Requests, subscribe/notify; resultType; streaming vs. JSON responses MRTR & Elicitation, Subscriptions, Progress & Cancellation Error Handling Protocol errors vs. tool execution errors; the error code table; HTTP status mapping Error Handling Tool Invocation Lifecycle Discover → select → confirm → call → (input required → retry) → result → back to the model Tools & the Invocation Lifecycle Protocol Primitives Tools, resources, prompts, elicitation; utilities (caching, pagination, completion); deprecated sampling, roots, logging Resources & Prompts, Utilities, Deprecated Features

docs.title: Domain 4 — Security & Governance · 24%
docs.text: Competency What it means in practice Covered in Trust Boundaries Where trust changes: user, host, model, client, server, upstream API. What each may see and do Trust Boundaries Permissions & Consent Human in the loop, tool confirmation, elicitation rules, URL mode for sensitive data, OAuth scopes and least privilege Permissions & Consent, Authorization Risk & Safety Controls Confused deputy, token passthrough, SSRF, state handle hijacking, local server compromise, prompt injection, tool poisoning Attacks & Mitigations Auditability & Observability Logging tool use, OpenTelemetry trace context in _meta, stderr, audit trails, identity for accountability Auditability & Observability

docs.title: Domain 5 — Use Cases & Ecosystem · 20%
docs.text: Competency What it means in practice Covered in Roles, Responsibilities & Adoption Server authors, host developers, platform and security teams; governance (AAIF, Linux Foundation, SEPs, maintainers) Roles, Responsibilities & Adoption Operational Use Cases Local vs. remote servers, developer tools, enterprise data access, agents at scale, progressive discovery, code mode Operational Use Cases Ecosystem & Portability SDKs and tiers, the MCP Registry, Inspector, extensions, backward compatibility across protocol eras Ecosystem & Portability, Extensions

docs.title: The recommended experience, restated as study targets
docs.text:
The Linux Foundation lists five areas of recommended experience. Each maps to something you should be able to do by the end of this course.

  1. JSON-RPC or message-based protocols. Read a raw MCP message and say whether it is a request, result, error or notification, and what it is doing.
  2. LLM API interaction. Explain how a host turns MCP tool definitions into an LLM API call, and how a tool result flows back into the model’s context.
  3. Agentic concepts. Explain why tools are model-controlled, and where a human must stay in the loop.
  4. Security literacy. Walk through the MCP OAuth 2.1 flow and explain why audience validation and PKCE are required.
  5. Reading manifests and capabilities. Read a server/discover response or a tool definition and say what the server supports and what the client may do.

docs.title: Before the day
docs.text:
• Read the Candidate Handbook and Important Instructions
  • Run the system compatibility check on the exact machine and network you will use
  • Have valid government-issued photo ID ready
  • Confirm your appointment time and time zone

docs.title: On the day
docs.text:
• Clear desk, no notes, no phone within reach, no second monitor
  • Private, quiet, well-lit room with nobody entering
  • Close every other application and disable notifications
  • Laptop on power, wired network if possible
  • Log in early, since check-in takes time

Proctoring is strict

Looking away from the screen repeatedly, reading questions aloud, or another person entering the room can end the session. Keep your face in frame.

docs.title: Time budget
docs.text:
90 minutes. The question count is not published. If it is around 60, that gives you 90 seconds per question, which is comfortable for recognition questions and tight for message-flow scenarios.

Pass Time What to do 1 ~55 min Answer everything you can in under a minute. Flag anything slower. 2 ~25 min Work the flagged questions properly. Sketch message flows on the whiteboard if one is provided. 3 ~10 min Check nothing is blank. There is no penalty for guessing.

docs.title: Question types and how to attack them
docs.text:
Recognition. “Which method must every server implement?” Either you know it or you don’t. Answer fast and bank the time.

Direction and sequence. “A server needs user confirmation during a tool call. What happens next?” Picture the messages. Who sends what, with which id, and what does the result contain? Eliminate any option in which the server sends a request to the client: that is legacy behavior.

MUST vs. SHOULD. “Which is REQUIRED of a client that receives an InputRequiredResult containing requestState?” The exact keyword matters. Echoing requestState is a MUST; logging it is not mentioned at all.

Security judgement. “A remote server receives a token issued for a different API. What should it do?” Find the violated boundary first (audience, consent, trust), then pick the option that enforces it at the server, not the one that hopes the client behaves.

Primitive selection. “A server wants users to trigger a code review workflow via a slash command.” Map to the control model: user-controlled means prompt, application-controlled means resource, model-controlled means tool.

docs.title: Traps specific to this exam
docs.text:
Legacy answers

Distractors will describe the pre-2026 protocol as if it were current: - “The client sends initialize and the server returns its capabilities” - “The server sends sampling/createMessage to the client” - “The client uses Mcp-Session-Id to resume its session” - “The client sends ping to keep the connection alive” - “Resource not found returns -32002“

All of these were true once. None are current behavior in 2026-07-28.

Deprecated is not removed

Sampling, Roots and Logging are deprecated, not removed. They still work and are still in the spec. An option saying “sampling is no longer supported” is wrong; one saying “new implementations should not adopt sampling” is right.

Protocol can’t enforce consent

The spec says plainly that MCP cannot enforce its security principles at the protocol level. Consent, confirmation and access control are implementor responsibilities, mostly the host’s. Options claiming “the protocol prevents the server from…” are usually wrong.

docs.title: The reflexes that earn the most points
docs.text:
1. Server needs input mid-request → InputRequiredResult, client retries with inputResponses and requestState, new id.
  2. Secrets or credentials from the user → URL mode elicitation, never form mode.
  3. Token not issued for this server → reject it. Never pass it through.
  4. Local single-user integration → stdio; credentials from the environment, not OAuth.
  5. Remote multi-user server → Streamable HTTP + OAuth 2.1 with PKCE and resource indicators.
  6. Server needs state across calls → explicit handle as a tool argument, bound server-side to the authenticated user.
  7. Tool failed because of bad input the model can fix → result with isError: true, not a JSON-RPC error.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Terms and method names you should recognize on sight. Items marked 2026 are new or changed in 2026-07-28.

docs.title: Participants and architecture
docs.text: Host The AI application the user interacts with (Claude Desktop, VS Code, an agent). Creates and   manages clients, enforces consent and security policy, and coordinates the LLM. Client A protocol component inside the host that talks to exactly one server. Server A program that exposes tools, resources and prompts. Local (usually stdio) or remote (usually   Streamable HTTP). Local server A server running on the user’s machine, typically launched by the client as a subprocess over stdio. Remote server A server reached over the network, typically via Streamable HTTP, usually serving many clients. Data layer The JSON-RPC protocol: discovery, primitives, notifications. Transport layer How messages move: connection setup, framing, authorization. stdio or Streamable HTTP.

docs.title: Base protocol
docs.text: JSON-RPC 2.0 The message format. Requests, responses (result or error) and notifications. Request A message with a non-null id that expects a response. In MCP only clients send requests. Notification A message with no id. The receiver MUST NOT respond. _meta Reserved metadata field on params and results. Holds protocol-level keys under the io.modelcontextprotocol/ prefix. Stateless 2026 Each request carries everything needed to process it. No state may be inferred from earlier requests on the same connection. io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion 2026 Required on every request. The protocol version the request uses. io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities 2026 Required on every request. What the client supports for this request. io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo / serverInfo 2026 Self-reported, unverified identity. For display, logging and debugging, not security decisions. resultType 2026 Required on every result. "complete" or "input_required" (extensions may add more). Missing means "complete"; unrecognized means invalid. Capabilities Declared feature support. Client capabilities go in each request’s _meta; server capabilities are returned by server/discover. Extension Optional, opt-in addition to the core protocol, negotiated via the extensions capability map. Identifiers look like io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks. Protocol version A date string YYYY-MM-DD, the last date backward-incompatible changes were made. Modern / Legacy / Dual-era 2026 Modern = 2026-07-28+ (per-request metadata). Legacy = 2025-11-25 and earlier (initialize handshake). Dual-era = supports both.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: Method Direction Purpose server/discover 2026 C→S Supported versions, capabilities, identity, instructions. Servers MUST implement tools/list C→S List tools (paginated, cacheable) tools/call C→S Invoke a tool (MRTR-capable) resources/list C→S List direct resources resources/templates/list C→S List resource templates resources/read C→S Read resource contents (MRTR-capable, cacheable) prompts/list C→S List prompts prompts/get C→S Get a prompt with arguments filled in (MRTR-capable) completion/complete C→S Argument autocompletion for prompts and resource templates subscriptions/listen 2026 C→S Open a long-lived stream of opted-in change notifications elicitation/create inside inputRequests Ask the user for input (form or URL mode) sampling/createMessage inside inputRequests Deprecated. Ask the client’s LLM for a completion roots/list inside inputRequests Deprecated. Ask the client for filesystem roots Notification Direction Purpose notifications/subscriptions/acknowledged 2026 S→C First message on a listen stream; which filters are honored notifications/tools/list_changed S→C Tool list changed (on a listen stream) notifications/prompts/list_changed S→C Prompt list changed notifications/resources/list_changed S→C Resource list changed notifications/resources/updated S→C A subscribed resource changed notifications/progress S→C Progress on an in-flight request (request-scoped) notifications/message S→C Deprecated. Log message (request-scoped, only if logLevel was set) notifications/cancelled C→S (stdio) Cancel an in-flight request. Servers send it only to end a listen stream

docs.title: Interaction patterns
