docs.text: Request and response Client sends a request, server returns a result or error, optionally preceded by request-scoped notifications. Multi Round-Trip Requests (MRTR) 2026 Server returns InputRequiredResult; client gathers input and retries the original request. InputRequiredResult 2026 Result with resultType: "input_required", carrying inputRequests and/or requestState. inputRequests / inputResponses 2026 Maps keyed by server-chosen strings. Requests (elicitation, sampling, roots) and the client’s answers. requestState 2026 Opaque server string the client must echo exactly. Attacker-controlled from the server’s view. Subscribe and notify 2026 subscriptions/listen opens a stream; notifications carry io.modelcontextprotocol/subscriptionId.

docs.title: Server features
docs.text: Tool A function the model can invoke. Model-controlled. Resource Data identified by a URI, provided as context. Application-controlled. Resource template A parameterized resource URI (RFC 6570), e.g. file:///{path}. Prompt A server-defined message template the user selects. User-controlled. inputSchema / outputSchema JSON Schema (default 2020-12) for tool arguments and structured results. structuredContent Machine-readable tool result (any JSON value), validated against outputSchema if present. isError true on a tool result means a tool execution error, reported to the model so it can self-correct. Tool annotations Hints like readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, openWorldHint. Untrusted unless the server is trusted. x-mcp-header 2026 Schema annotation that mirrors a tool parameter into an Mcp-Param-{Name} HTTP header. Content annotations audience (user/assistant), priority (0–1), lastModified. Resource link vs. embedded resource A resource_link points to a URI; a resource content block includes the contents inline.

docs.title: Client features
docs.text: Elicitation Server asks the user for input via the client. Form mode collects structured, non-sensitive data. URL mode sends the user to a URL for sensitive interactions that must not pass through the client. Elicitation actions accept (submitted), decline (explicitly refused), cancel (dismissed without choosing). Sampling (deprecated) Server asks the client’s LLM for a completion. Roots (deprecated) Client tells the server which file:// directories are relevant. Advisory, not enforced.

docs.title: Utilities
docs.text: Caching 2026 ttlMs (freshness hint in ms) and cacheScope (public or private) on cacheable results. Pagination Opaque cursor / nextCursor. Server chooses page size. An empty string cursor is still a cursor. Progress Client puts progressToken in _meta; server sends increasing notifications/progress. Cancellation stdio: notifications/cancelled. Streamable HTTP: close the SSE response stream. Completion completion/complete with ref/prompt or ref/resource; up to 100 values.

docs.title: Transports
docs.text: stdio Client launches server as subprocess. Newline-delimited JSON-RPC on stdin/stdout. Logs to stderr. Streamable HTTP One MCP endpoint. Every client message is a POST. Reply is JSON or a request-scoped SSE stream. MCP-Protocol-Version, Mcp-Method, Mcp-Name 2026 Required HTTP headers mirroring body fields so intermediaries can route without parsing JSON. HTTP+SSE (deprecated) The 2024-11-05 two-endpoint transport, replaced by Streamable HTTP. DNS rebinding Attack in which a website reaches a local server. Mitigated by validating Origin and binding to 127.0.0.1.

docs.title: Authorization
docs.text: Resource server A protected MCP server, in OAuth terms. Authorization server (AS) Issues access tokens. May be separate from the MCP server. Protected Resource Metadata (PRM) RFC 9728 document at /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource, listing authorization_servers. MCP servers MUST implement it. WWW-Authenticate Header on a 401/403 carrying resource_metadata and optionally scope / error="insufficient_scope". PKCE Proof Key for Code Exchange. MUST, with S256. Clients must refuse to proceed if the AS doesn’t advertise support. Resource indicator (resource parameter) RFC 8707. MUST be sent in authorization and token requests, set to the MCP server’s canonical URI. Audience validation Server MUST only accept tokens issued for itself. Token passthrough Forbidden anti-pattern: forwarding a client’s token to an upstream API. Client ID Metadata Document (CIMD) Client uses an HTTPS URL as its client_id, pointing to a JSON metadata document. The preferred registration method. Dynamic Client Registration (DCR) (deprecated) RFC 7591 POST /register to obtain a client ID. Step-up authorization Re-authorizing with the union of previous and newly challenged scopes after insufficient_scope. iss validation RFC 9207 check that the authorization response came from the expected AS, preventing mix-up attacks.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: Confused deputy A privileged intermediary (an MCP proxy) is tricked into using its authority for an attacker. SSRF Server-side request forgery. A malicious server supplies URLs that make a client fetch internal resources. State handle hijacking 2026 Guessing or stealing another user’s explicit state handle. Mitigated by binding handles to the authenticated user. Tool poisoning Hidden instructions in tool descriptions or metadata, aimed at the model. Rug pull A server silently changes a tool’s definition after the user approved it.

docs.title: How to study a protocol
docs.text:
Read messages, not just prose

For every mechanism, be able to write the JSON from memory: a tools/call request with its _meta, an InputRequiredResult, the retry with inputResponses, a subscriptions/listen acknowledgment. If you can write the message, you understand the mechanism well enough to reject the distractors.

Always ask: who sends this, and in which direction?

A large share of MCP questions reduces to direction. Clients send requests and notifications. Servers send responses and notifications, never requests. A question that has the server initiating a request is either describing the legacy protocol or is wrong.

Learn the MUSTs

The specification uses RFC 2119 keywords deliberately. Exam questions distinguish MUST from SHOULD from MAY. Where this course says MUST, the spec says MUST.

docs.title: What Changed in 2026-07-28
docs.text:
The exam references specification revision 2026-07-28. It is the most significant redesign MCP has had since its launch in November 2024. This page explains what changed, why, and how to tell legacy from modern behavior in a question.

Read it even if you already build with MCP. The changes are not cosmetic. Several of them reverse things that were true for the protocol’s first eighteen months, and much of the material you will find online still describes the old design.

docs.title: 1. The big idea: MCP became stateless
What MCP used to look like
docs.text:
Until 2025-11-25, every MCP connection started with a handshake:

sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant Server
    Client->>Server: initialize (protocolVersion, capabilities, clientInfo)
    Server-->>Client: InitializeResult (protocolVersion, capabilities, serverInfo)
    Client->>Server: notifications/initialized
    Note over Client,Server: Session established. Everything after this<br/>relies on what was negotiated here.
    Client->>Server: tools/list
    Client->>Server: tools/call

The negotiated version and capabilities were remembered by the connection. Over HTTP, the server could also mint a session ID (Mcp-Session-Id header), and every later request carried it so the server could find the session state again.

That design works fine for a local server launched as a subprocess: one client, one process, one long-lived connection. It works badly for a remote server behind a load balancer. Consider what happens when:

  • Request 1 (initialize) lands on server instance A.
  • Request 2 (tools/call) lands on instance B.

Instance B has never heard of this session. You need sticky sessions (always route this client to A) or a shared session store (Redis, a database) that every instance consults. Both are operational pain. Sticky sessions break autoscaling and failover. A shared store is a new dependency on every request’s path.

SEP-2575 (“Make MCP Stateless”), which drove the redesign, names three problems: scalability (a plain round-robin load balancer can’t be used, forcing sticky sessions), resilience (if the instance holding a session fails, the session is lost and the handshake must be redone), and implementation complexity (servers must create, manage and garbage-collect per-client session state, a common source of bugs and memory leaks).

docs.title: What MCP looks like now
docs.text:
In 2026-07-28 there is no handshake. Every request is self-contained:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 3,
  "method": "tools/call",
  "params": {
    "name": "get_weather",
    "arguments": { "location": "Seattle, WA" },
    "_meta": {
      "io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion": "2026-07-28",
      "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities": { "elicitation": {} },
      "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo": { "name": "ExampleClient", "version": "1.0.0" }
    }
  }
}

The three fields that the handshake used to establish once now travel on every request:

Field Required? Replaces io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion Yes protocolVersion in initialize io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities Yes capabilities in initialize io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo SHOULD clientInfo in initialize

The server’s identity travels the other way, in each result’s _meta as io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo.

Now any instance can serve any request, because everything it needs is in the request. Load balancing is plain round-robin. Instances can come and go freely.

The rule the spec states explicitly

Servers MUST NOT rely on prior requests over the same connection to establish context. An open connection (including a stdio process) is not a conversation or a session. A client may interleave unrelated requests on it.

A request missing a required _meta field is malformed. The server MUST reject it with -32602 (Invalid params), and on HTTP with 400 Bad Request.

docs.title: How servers still keep state
docs.text:
Some things genuinely need state: a shopping cart, an open browser session, a database transaction. Statelessness does not forbid state. It forbids implicit, connection-bound state.

The pattern is an explicit handle. A creation tool returns an ID, and later calls pass it back as an ordinary argument:

// → tools/call  create_basket  {}
// ← result      { "structuredContent": { "basket_id": "bsk_a1b2c3" } }

// → tools/call  add_item  { "basket_id": "bsk_a1b2c3", "sku": "..." }

The model carries basket_id forward. The server stores the cart under that key. This creates a new security concern, state handle hijacking, covered in Attacks & Mitigations.

docs.title: 2. server/discover replaces the handshake’s discovery role
docs.text:
Without initialize, how does a client learn what a server supports?

server/discover is a new RPC that every server MUST implement. It returns the server’s supported versions, capabilities, identity and optional instructions:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": "discover-1",
  "result": {
    "resultType": "complete",
    "supportedVersions": ["2026-07-28"],
    "capabilities": { "tools": {}, "resources": {} },
    "_meta": {
      "io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo": { "name": "ExampleServer", "version": "1.0.0" }
    },
    "instructions": "This server provides weather and resource utilities.",
    "ttlMs": 3600000,
    "cacheScope": "public"
  }
}

The crucial difference from initialize: calling server/discover is optional. Servers must implement it, but clients may skip it. A client can send tools/call directly and handle an error if the version is wrong.

Version negotiation is now per request. If the server does not support the version a request declares, it returns an UnsupportedProtocolVersionError (-32022) listing the versions it does support, and the client retries with one of them.

Exam distinction

  • initialize (legacy): mandatory first message, establishes a session.
  • server/discover (modern): mandatory for servers to implement, optional for clients to call, establishes nothing. Its result is cacheable.

docs.title: 3. Servers no longer send requests: Multi Round-Trip Requests
docs.text: This is the change most likely to trip up experienced MCP users.

docs.title: The old way
docs.text:
Previously a server could send its own JSON-RPC request to the client, in the middle of handling the client’s request:

sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant Server
    Client->>Server: tools/call (id: 1)
    Server->>Client: elicitation/create (id: 99)   ← server-initiated request
    Client-->>Server: result for id 99
    Server-->>Client: result for id 1

For the server to do this, it had to suspend the tool call while waiting, remember it, and then resume it when the answer arrived. That is state held on a specific server instance for an unknown amount of time, exactly what breaks horizontal scaling. It also needed a channel for server-to-client requests. On HTTP that meant either a long-lived SSE stream or a separate GET endpoint.

docs.title: The new way
docs.text:
Now the server returns instead of asking. It answers the tool call with an InputRequiredResult describing what it needs, and the client retries the whole request with the answers attached:

sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant Client
    participant Server
    Client->>Server: tools/call (id: 1)
    Server-->>Client: result: resultType "input_required"<br/>inputRequests + requestState
    Note over Client,Server: Request 1 is finished.
    Client->>User: ask for the input
    User-->>Client: answer
    Client->>Server: tools/call (id: 2)<br/>same params + inputResponses + requestState
    Server-->>Client: result: resultType "complete"

Request 1 is over when the server returns. Nothing is suspended. Anything the server needs to remember goes into requestState, an opaque string the client must echo back unchanged. The retry can land on a completely different server instance, and that instance can finish the job from what is in the retry alone.

The rules to memorize

  • Servers MUST NOT initiate JSON-RPC requests. Clients do not send JSON-RPC responses.
  • Only tools/call, resources/read and prompts/get may return InputRequiredResult.
  • The retry MUST use a new JSON-RPC id.
  • The client MUST echo requestState exactly, and MUST NOT inspect or modify it.
  • The server MUST treat requestState as attacker-controlled, and protect its integrity (HMAC or AEAD) whenever it influences authorization or business logic.

This is the subject of a full chapter: Multi Round-Trip Requests & Elicitation.

docs.title: 4. Every result now has a resultType
docs.text:
Because a request can now end in two different ways (finished, or needs input), results are polymorphic. Every result MUST carry resultType:

resultType Meaning "complete" The request finished; the result holds the final content "input_required" The request needs more input; the result is an InputRequiredResult (extension values) Extensions may add types, e.g. the Tasks extension’s "task"

Two compatibility rules:

  • A client that receives a resultType it does not recognize MUST treat the result as invalid.
  • A result with no resultType (from a legacy server) MUST be treated as "complete".

docs.title: 5. Subscriptions replaced the GET stream and resources/subscribe
docs.text:
Change notifications (“the tool list changed”, “this resource was updated”) need a way to reach the client without the client asking.

Before: the client opened a standalone SSE stream with HTTP GET, and subscribed to individual resources with resources/subscribe / resources/unsubscribe.

Now: one mechanism, subscriptions/listen. It is an ordinary request whose response is a long-lived stream. The client names exactly what it wants:

{
  "method": "subscriptions/listen",
  "params": {
    "notifications": {
      "toolsListChanged": true,
      "resourceSubscriptions": ["file:///project/config.json"]
    }
  }
}

The server first sends notifications/subscriptions/acknowledged (saying which of those it will honor), then the matching notifications. Every one of them carries io.modelcontextprotocol/subscriptionId, whose value is the JSON-RPC id of the listen request.

Request-scoped notifications do not move

notifications/progress and notifications/message still travel on the response stream of the request they relate to, never on the subscriptions/listen stream.

docs.title: 6. Things that were removed outright
docs.text:
Removed What replaces it initialize / notifications/initialized Per-request _meta + optional server/discover Protocol-level sessions, Mcp-Session-Id header Stateless requests; explicit handles as tool arguments HTTP GET stream endpoint subscriptions/listen resources/subscribe, resources/unsubscribe subscriptions/listen with resourceSubscriptions Server-initiated JSON-RPC requests InputRequiredResult + client retry (MRTR) ping Nothing. Stateless requests have no connection to keep alive logging/setLevel Per-request io.modelcontextprotocol/logLevel in _meta notifications/roots/list_changed Nothing. Servers request roots when they need them SSE resumability (Last-Event-ID, event IDs) A broken stream loses the request; the client re-issues it with a new id notifications/elicitation/complete, elicitationId The client learns the outcome by retrying; servers correlate via requestState Tasks in the core protocol The io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks extension

A server that speaks only 2026-07-28 and receives legacy HTTP traffic SHOULD answer GET or DELETE on the endpoint with 405 Method Not Allowed, and ignore any Mcp-Session-Id or Last-Event-ID header.

docs.title: 7. Things that were deprecated
docs.text:
Deprecated means the feature still works and remains in the spec, but new implementations SHOULD NOT adopt it. Under the new feature lifecycle policy, a deprecated feature stays for at least twelve months before it becomes eligible for removal (ninety days under an expedited exception).

Deprecated feature Migration path Earliest removal Sampling Integrate directly with LLM provider APIs First revision on or after 2027-07-28 Roots Pass directories/files via tool parameters, resource URIs or server configuration First revision on or after 2027-07-28 Logging Log to stderr (stdio) or use OpenTelemetry First revision on or after 2027-07-28 Dynamic Client Registration (RFC 7591) Client ID Metadata Documents First revision on or after 2027-07-28 includeContext: "thisServer" / "allServers" Omit it, or use "none" No later than Sampling itself HTTP+SSE transport (from 2024-11-05) Streamable HTTP Three months after SEP-2596 is Final

Why deprecate sampling, roots and logging? SEP-2577 gives the criteria: the specification “aims to remain minimal and focused”, and these features showed low adoption, overlap with existing alternatives, or disproportionate implementation burden. Specifically:

  • Sampling is complex to implement correctly (human review, model selection, tool loops), few clients support it, and servers can call LLM provider APIs directly.
  • Roots have vague, advisory semantics that servers need not respect, low adoption, and more explicit alternatives (tool parameters, resource URIs, configuration).
  • Logging duplicates mature infrastructure (stderr, OpenTelemetry) at a cost in implementation surface.

The details are in Deprecated Features.

docs.title: 8. New and changed details worth knowing
docs.text:
Error codes were partitioned. The JSON-RPC server-error range is now split:

  • -32000 to -32019: legacy, implementation-defined. New codes must not be allocated here.
  • -32020 to -32099: reserved for the MCP specification.

The spec-defined codes are -32020 HeaderMismatch, -32021 MissingRequiredClientCapability and -32022 UnsupportedProtocolVersion.

Resource-not-found changed from -32002 to -32602 (Invalid params). Clients SHOULD still accept -32002 from older servers.

Caching hints are mandatory on server/discover, tools/list, prompts/list, resources/list, resources/templates/list and resources/read: every complete result carries ttlMs and cacheScope ("public" or "private").

Streamable HTTP now mirrors metadata into headers. Every POST carries MCP-Protocol-Version and Mcp-Method. tools/call, resources/read and prompts/get also carry Mcp-Name. Tool parameters can be mirrored as Mcp-Param-{Name} via the x-mcp-header schema annotation. Servers must reject mismatches between headers and body with -32020.

Tool lists should be deterministic. Servers SHOULD return tools/list in a stable order, which enables caching and improves LLM prompt-cache hit rates.

List results must not vary per connection. They MAY vary by the authorization on the request, because credentials are per-request input, not connection state.

Schemas were loosened. inputSchema and outputSchema may use any JSON Schema 2020-12 keywords, and structuredContent may be any JSON value, not just an object.

OpenTelemetry trace context (traceparent, tracestate, baggage) has reserved keys in _meta.

Extensions have a formal home. Both client and server capabilities have an extensions map, for example "io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks": {}.

Authorization hardening. Clients MUST validate the iss parameter in authorization responses (RFC 9207) to stop mix-up attacks; must set application_type in dynamic registration; and must key stored client credentials by authorization-server issuer.

docs.title: 9. Legacy vs. modern at a glance
docs.text:
Use this table to classify a question stem. If the stem mentions anything in the left column as current behavior, it is describing the old protocol.

Legacy (2025-11-25 and earlier) Modern (2026-07-28) initialize handshake, then notifications/initialized No handshake; per-request _meta Session per connection; Mcp-Session-Id Stateless; explicit handles if state is needed Server sends sampling/createMessage etc. as requests Server returns InputRequiredResult; client retries Results have no resultType Every result has resultType GET SSE stream, resources/subscribe subscriptions/listen ping keep-alive Removed logging/setLevel io.modelcontextprotocol/logLevel per request Resumable SSE via Last-Event-ID Not resumable; re-issue with a new id Tasks in core (tasks/result, tasks/list) Tasks extension (tasks/get polling, tasks/update) Resource not found = -32002 Resource not found = -32602 Dynamic Client Registration as a normal option DCR deprecated; Client ID Metadata Documents preferred

docs.title: Backward compatibility, briefly
docs.text:
Implementations that support both eras are called dual-era.

  • On stdio, a dual-era client probes with server/discover first. A DiscoverResult or a recognized modern error means a modern server. Any other error, or a timeout, means legacy: fall back to initialize.
  • On Streamable HTTP, a dual-era client sends a modern request and, on 400 Bad Request, inspects the body. A recognized modern JSON-RPC error means modern. An empty or unrecognized body means legacy.

A legacy client cannot talk to a modern-only server. Legacy clients have no fall-forward mechanism. A modern-only server therefore SHOULD name its supported versions in whatever error it returns to an initialize request, since that message may be the only diagnostic the user ever sees.

Full detail: Versioning & Discovery.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Stateless: no initialize, no sessions. Version and capabilities ride in every request’s _meta.
  • server/discover: servers must implement it, clients may call it, and its result is cacheable.
  • MRTR: servers never send requests. They return resultType: "input_required" with inputRequests and requestState, and the client retries with a new id.
  • subscriptions/listen replaces the GET stream and resources/subscribe.
  • Removed: ping, logging/setLevel, roots list_changed, SSE resumability, core Tasks.
  • Deprecated: Sampling, Roots, Logging, Dynamic Client Registration, HTTP+SSE.
  • New error codes: -32020 HeaderMismatch, -32021 MissingRequiredClientCapability, -32022 UnsupportedProtocolVersion; resource-not-found is now -32602.

docs.title: Hands-on Labs
docs.text:
The MCPA exam is multiple choice and does not ask you to write code. So why do labs?

Because most exam questions describe a situation, and it is much easier to reason about a situation you have already seen. Once you have watched a server reject a request with -32020, you do not need to memorise what HeaderMismatch means. The same goes for:

  • a requestState you tampered with getting refused,
  • a 401 that carries a resource_metadata URL,
  • a debug print that corrupts a stdio stream.

Every lab below was run against the official Python SDK mcp 2.2.0, which speaks protocol version 2026-07-28. Every output shown is real output, trimmed only for width.

docs.title: The labs
docs.text:
Lab You will Main exam domains 0. Environment Setup Install Python, the SDK and a working folder none 1. Speak MCP by Hand Send raw JSON-RPC to a server over stdio and read every field 2, 3 2. Build a Server Expose tools, resources and prompts; return proper errors; set cache hints 1, 3 3. Build a Client Discover a server’s features and map tools to an LLM’s function-calling format 2, 5 4. Streamable HTTP Drive a remote server with curl and trigger every header check 2, 3, 4 5. Elicitation & MRTR Watch a tool pause for user input across several rounds 3, 4 6. Security Hardening Protect a server with OAuth bearer tokens, scopes, audience checks and input policies 4

Labs 1 to 5 each build on the previous one’s files, so do them in order. Lab 6 stands on its own.

docs.title: How to use a lab
docs.text:
1. Predict before you run. Each lab has Predict boxes. Write your guess down before you run the code. A wrong prediction is where the learning happens.
  2. Type the code. Don’t copy and paste it. Typing makes you read every line.
  3. Break things on purpose. The Try it boxes suggest changes that make the code fail in instructive ways.
  4. Link it back. Each lab ends with What this showed you, which points to the study chapters the lab reinforces.

SDK behaviour is not the specification

An SDK is one implementation of the spec, and it sometimes differs from it. It may keep older behaviour for compatibility, or pick a default where the spec allows several. When the labs hit such a difference, they flag it in a box like this one.

The exam tests the specification, not the SDK. When they disagree, answer with the spec.

docs.title: Lab 0: Environment Setup
docs.text: Time: 10 minutes · Goal: a folder with a virtual environment and the MCP Python SDK installed.

docs.title: 1. Requirements
docs.text:
Tool Version used in these labs Check with Python 3.12 (3.10+ works) python3 --version curl any recent curl --version A terminal macOS, Linux or WSL

There is no need for an LLM API key. The labs play the part of the model themselves, so that you can see exactly what a host would send and receive.

docs.title: 2. Create the working folder
docs.text:
mkdir mcp-lab && cd mcp-lab
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

Every later command assumes you are inside mcp-lab with the virtual environment active.

docs.title: 3. Install the SDK
docs.text:
pip install "mcp==2.2.0"

The mcp package pulls in everything the labs need:

  • mcp-types: the Pydantic models for every protocol message
  • starlette and uvicorn: the HTTP server used for Streamable HTTP
  • httpx: the HTTP client
  • pydantic, jsonschema and cryptography: validation, and the sealing of requestState

Check the install:

python -c "import mcp, mcp_types.version as v; print(v.MODERN_PROTOCOL_VERSIONS)"

You should see a collection containing 2026-07-28.

Why pin the version

MCP changed a lot between 2025-11-25 and 2026-07-28. Sessions disappeared, MRTR arrived and the envelope moved into _meta. SDK releases track those changes. Pinning 2.2.0 keeps your output identical to the output shown in the labs.

docs.title: 4. Two SDK habits to learn now
docs.text:
The Python API uses snake_case; the wire uses camelCase. In Python the attributes are tool.input_schema, result.is_error, result.structured_content. On the wire the same fields are inputSchema, isError, structuredContent. To see the wire form of any model, dump it with aliases:

import json

def wire(model) -> str:
    return json.dumps(model.model_dump(by_alias=True, exclude_none=True, mode="json"))

stdio servers log to stderr. On stdio, stdout is the protocol channel. Lab 1 shows what happens when you forget that.

docs.title: 5. Optional: MCP Inspector
docs.text:
The MCP Inspector is the official visual debugging tool. It needs Node.js:

npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector

It is handy for clicking through a server’s tools. The labs use raw messages and code instead, because the exam asks about what is inside the messages.

docs.title: Lab 1: Speak MCP by Hand
docs.text:
Time: 40 minutes · Goal: talk to an MCP server with nothing but JSON lines, and understand every field that comes back.

SDKs hide the protocol, which is exactly why this lab avoids them on the client side. You will start a real server as a subprocess, write JSON-RPC messages to its stdin, and read its replies from stdout. This is what every host does underneath.

docs.title: 1. A minimal server
docs.text:
Create weather_server.py:

weather_server.py
import logging
from mcp.server import MCPServer

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)  # logging writes to stderr
log = logging.getLogger("weather")

mcp = MCPServer("weather", version="1.0.0", instructions="Use get_forecast for any weather question.")

FAKE = {"oslo": "4°C, snow", "rome": "24°C, sunny", "seattle": "12°C, rain"}

@mcp.tool()
def get_forecast(city: str) -> str:
    """Get today's forecast for a city.

    Args:
        city: City name, e.g. "Oslo"
    """
    log.info("forecast requested for %s", city)
    return FAKE.get(city.lower(), f"No data for {city}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run(transport="stdio")

Three things to notice:

  • instructions: free text the server gives the host, typically added to the model’s system prompt.
  • The docstring and type hints: the SDK turns them into the tool’s description and inputSchema. A missing docstring means a model that can’t tell what the tool is for.
  • logging goes to stderr, which the stdio transport leaves free for logs.

docs.title: 2. The raw client
docs.text:
Create send_raw.py. It starts the server, then writes six requests and reads one reply line for each:

send_raw.py
import json, subprocess, sys

META = {
    "io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion": "2026-07-28",
    "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities": {},
    "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo": {"name": "raw-lab", "version": "0.1"},
}

messages = [
    {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "server/discover", "params": {"_meta": META}},
    {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 2, "method": "tools/list", "params": {"_meta": META}},
    {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 3, "method": "tools/call",
     "params": {"name": "get_forecast", "arguments": {"city": "Oslo"}, "_meta": META}},
    {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 4, "method": "tools/call",
     "params": {"name": "no_such_tool", "arguments": {}, "_meta": META}},
    {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 5, "method": "tools/list", "params": {}},
    {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 6, "method": "tools/list",
     "params": {"_meta": {**META, "io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion": "1900-01-01"}}},
]

proc = subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, "weather_server.py"], stdin=subprocess.PIPE,
                        stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.PIPE, text=True)
for m in messages:
    line = json.dumps(m)
    print(">>>", line)
    proc.stdin.write(line + "\n"); proc.stdin.flush()
    print("<<<", proc.stdout.readline().strip(), "\n")
proc.stdin.close()
proc.wait(timeout=5)
print("--- stderr ---")
print(proc.stderr.read())

Predict

Before running it, write down your answers:

  1. Is there an initialize request before server/discover? Should there be?
  2. What will message 4 (unknown tool) return: a JSON-RPC error or a result?
  3. What will message 5 (no _meta) return?
  4. What will message 6 (version 1900-01-01) return, and which error code?

Run it:

python send_raw.py

docs.title: Message 1: server/discover
docs.text:
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"result":{
  "cacheScope":"private",
  "capabilities":{"prompts":{"listChanged":true},
                  "resources":{"listChanged":true,"subscribe":true},
                  "tools":{"listChanged":true}},
  "instructions":"Use get_forecast for any weather question.",
  "resultType":"complete",
  "supportedVersions":["2026-07-28"],
  "ttlMs":0,
  "_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo":{"name":"weather","version":"1.0.0"}}}}

There was no handshake. In 2026-07-28 the protocol is stateless: every request carries its own version and capabilities in params._meta, so the client can call tools/list first if it likes.

server/discover is still worth calling because it answers several questions at once:

Field Meaning supportedVersions Versions the server speaks. The client picks one it also supports. capabilities Features the server offers, so the client knows what to ask for. instructions Usage guidance for the host or model. resultType: "complete" Required on every result in 2026-07-28. The other value, input_required, appears in Lab 5. ttlMs / cacheScope Cache hints: how long the client may reuse this answer, and whether it may share it across users (public) or only within one user’s context (private). _meta.serverInfo Who answered. It lives in _meta because there is no handshake to carry it.

docs.title: Message 2: tools/list
docs.text:
{"name":"get_forecast",
 "description":"Get today's forecast for a city.\n\n    Args:\n        city: City name, e.g. \"Oslo\"\n    ",
 "inputSchema":{"type":"object","properties":{"city":{"title":"City","type":"string"}},
                "required":["city"],"title":"get_forecastArguments"},
 "outputSchema":{"properties":{"result":{"title":"Result","type":"string"}},
                 "required":["result"],"title":"get_forecastOutput","type":"object"}}

The SDK built a JSON Schema from city: str. It also generated an outputSchema, because the function declares a return type. A tool’s result must be an object, so a plain str return gets wrapped as {"result": ...}.

docs.title: Message 3: tools/call
docs.text:
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"result":{
  "content":[{"text":"4°C, snow","type":"text"}],
  "isError":false,
  "resultType":"complete",
  "structuredContent":{"result":"4°C, snow"}, ...}}

The result carries two views of the same data:

  • content is unstructured and meant for the model.
  • structuredContent matches the outputSchema and is meant for programs.

The spec says a tool that returns structured content SHOULD also return its serialised JSON as a text block, for clients that ignore structured output. That is why the text appears in both.

docs.title: Message 4: unknown tool
docs.text:
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":4,"result":{
  "content":[{"text":"Unknown tool: no_such_tool","type":"text"}],
  "isError":true,"resultType":"complete", ...}}

SDK behaviour is not the specification

The specification lists “unknown tool” among the protocol errors, which should be a JSON-RPC error with code -32602 (Invalid params). The Python SDK returns a tool execution error instead: a normal result with isError: true.

For the exam, go with the spec: an unknown tool name is a protocol error, -32602. Keep isError for failures inside a tool that the model could fix, such as a bad date format or an API rate limit.

docs.title: Message 5: missing _meta
docs.text:
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":5,"error":{"code":-32602,
  "message":"params._meta must be an object carrying the required 'io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion' and 'io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities' envelope keys"}}

Without a handshake, the server cannot learn the client’s version from anywhere else, so these two keys are required on every request. clientInfo is only a SHOULD, which is why the error message doesn’t mention it.

docs.title: Message 6: unsupported version
docs.text:
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":6,"error":{"code":-32022,"message":"Unsupported protocol version",
  "data":{"supported":["2026-07-28"],"requested":"1900-01-01"}}}

-32022 UnsupportedProtocolVersion includes data.supported, so a client can pick a version from the list and retry straight away, with no extra discovery round.

docs.title: stderr
docs.text:
INFO:weather:forecast requested for Oslo
INFO:mcp.server.mcpserver.server:Tool 'no_such_tool' failed: 'Unknown tool: no_such_tool'

The logs never touched the protocol stream.

docs.title: 4. The stdout trap
docs.text:
What happens if a server writes something that isn’t JSON-RPC to stdout? The SDK protects you: while it serves stdio it redirects print() to stderr. To see the real failure, use a tiny hand-written server without the SDK.

handrolled_server.py
"""Lab 1: a deliberately tiny stdio 'server' written without the SDK, with a stdout bug."""
import json
import sys

for raw in sys.stdin:
    msg = json.loads(raw)
    print(f"DEBUG got {msg['method']}")                     # BUG: this goes to stdout
    # print(f"DEBUG got {msg['method']}", file=sys.stderr)  # FIX: log to stderr
    reply = {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": msg["id"], "result": {"resultType": "complete", "tools": []}}
    sys.stdout.write(json.dumps(reply) + "\n")
    sys.stdout.flush()
send_handrolled.py
import json, subprocess, sys

p = subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, "handrolled_server.py"], stdin=subprocess.PIPE,
                     stdout=subprocess.PIPE, text=True)
req = {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "tools/list", "params": {}}
out, _ = p.communicate(json.dumps(req) + "\n", timeout=5)
for line in out.splitlines():
    try:
        json.loads(line)
        print("valid JSON-RPC ->", line)
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        print("NOT JSON       ->", repr(line))

NOT JSON       -> 'DEBUG got tools/list'
valid JSON-RPC -> {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "result": {"resultType": "complete", "tools": []}}

A real client reading line by line would try to parse DEBUG got tools/list as a message and fail. Depending on the client, that means a dropped connection or a “server disconnected” error in the host.

The stdio rules in the spec exist for exactly this reason:

  • The server MUST NOT write anything to stdout that is not a valid MCP message.
  • The client MUST NOT write anything to the server’s stdin that is not a valid MCP message.
  • Messages are newline-delimited and MUST NOT contain embedded newlines.
  • The server MAY write any logging to stderr, and the client should not treat stderr output as an error.

Try it

Swap the two print lines in handrolled_server.py so the debug output goes to stderr, then run send_handrolled.py again. Only the valid line remains.

docs.title: 5. Bonus: an old client meets a new server
docs.text:
A 2025-11-25 client opens with initialize. What does a 2026-07-28 SDK server do with that?

legacy_probe.py
import json, subprocess, sys
proc = subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, "weather_server.py"], stdin=subprocess.PIPE,
                        stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL, text=True)
legacy = {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "initialize",
          "params": {"protocolVersion": "2025-11-25", "capabilities": {},
                     "clientInfo": {"name": "old-client", "version": "1.0"}}}
print(">>>", json.dumps(legacy)); proc.stdin.write(json.dumps(legacy) + "\n"); proc.stdin.flush()
print("<<<", proc.stdout.readline().strip())
proc.stdin.close(); proc.wait(timeout=5)

<<< {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"result":{"capabilities":{...},
     "instructions":"Use get_forecast for any weather question.",
     "protocolVersion":"2025-11-25","serverInfo":{"name":"weather","version":"1.0.0"}}}

The server answers in the old style: an InitializeResult, no resultType, and serverInfo at the top level rather than in _meta. The SDK server is dual-era, which the spec allows: a server MAY implement both behaviours. This is how the ecosystem migrates without a flag day.

The spec’s compatibility matrix gives the rest of the picture:

Client Server Outcome Legacy Dual-era Works; the server answers initialize (what you just saw). Legacy Modern-only Fails: initialize is rejected. The error SHOULD name the supported versions, because a legacy client has no way to move forward. Dual-era Legacy Works. On stdio the client probes with server/discover, gets a non-modern error or no reply, and falls back to initialize. Modern-only Legacy Fails. Probing first makes the failure deterministic.

On stdio, a dual-era client MUST NOT base the fallback on one specific error code, because legacy servers answer unknown methods in different ways. A recognised modern error such as -32022 means “modern server, wrong version”: the client retries with a supported version and does not fall back.

docs.title: What this showed you
docs.text: You saw Study chapter No handshake; _meta on every request Versioning & Discovery JSON-RPC shape, ids, resultType Messages inputSchema, outputSchema, structuredContent Tools & the Invocation Lifecycle -32602 vs isError, -32022 Error Handling stdout is the channel, stderr is for logs Transports Cache hints on discovery results Caching, Pagination & Completion

docs.title: Lab 2: Build a Server
docs.text: Time: 60 minutes · Goal: build a server that exposes all three server primitives (tools, resources and prompts), reports errors the right way, keeps state without sessions, and sends cache hints.

docs.title: 1. Choosing the right primitive
docs.text:
Before writing any code, decide who should be in control of each feature. This is the question the exam asks most often about primitives:

Primitive Controlled by Use it when In this lab Tool The model decides when to call it An action, or a lookup the model should decide to do search_notes, create_note, drafts Resource The application decides what to attach Context data the host or user picks notes://index, notes://{note_id} Prompt The user picks it, e.g. from a slash menu A reusable, parameterised message template summarize_note

docs.title: 2. The server
docs.text:
Create notes_server.py. It is a single file, so each section is explained below the code.

notes_server.py
"""Lab 2: a small notes server exposing tools, resources and prompts."""
import logging
import secrets
from datetime import datetime, timezone

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from mcp.server import MCPServer
from mcp.server.caching import CacheHint
from mcp.server.mcpserver.exceptions import ResourceNotFoundError, ToolError
from mcp.types import ToolAnnotations

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
log = logging.getLogger("notes")

mcp = MCPServer(
    "notes",
    version="1.0.0",
    instructions="Search notes before creating a new one to avoid duplicates.",
    # Caching hints: the tool and prompt lists are the same for everyone and change rarely.
    cache_hints={
        "tools/list": CacheHint(ttl_ms=300_000, scope="public"),
        "prompts/list": CacheHint(ttl_ms=300_000, scope="public"),
    },
)

NOTES: dict[str, dict] = {
    "n1": {"title": "MCP transports", "body": "stdio for local, Streamable HTTP for remote."},
    "n2": {"title": "MRTR", "body": "Servers return input_required; clients retry with a new id."},
}


class Note(BaseModel):
    id: str
    title: str
    body: str


# ---------- Tools ----------

@mcp.tool(annotations=ToolAnnotations(readOnlyHint=True, openWorldHint=False))
def search_notes(query: str) -> list[Note]:
    """Search notes by a word in the title or body.

    Args:
        query: A word to look for, case-insensitive.
    """
    q = query.lower()
    return [Note(id=k, **v) for k, v in NOTES.items() if q in (v["title"] + v["body"]).lower()]


@mcp.tool(annotations=ToolAnnotations(readOnlyHint=False, destructiveHint=False, idempotentHint=False))
def create_note(title: str, body: str = Field(description="Markdown body, at most 2000 characters")) -> Note:
    """Create a new note and return it."""
    if len(body) > 2000:
        # ToolError becomes a tool execution error (isError: true) whose message the model can read.
        raise ToolError(f"Body is {len(body)} characters; the maximum is 2000. Shorten it and retry.")
    note_id = f"n{len(NOTES) + 1}"
    NOTES[note_id] = {"title": title, "body": body}
    log.info("created %s", note_id)
    return Note(id=note_id, title=title, body=body)


# ---------- Stateful handles (explicit state, no sessions) ----------

DRAFTS: dict[str, dict] = {}

class Draft(BaseModel):
    draft_id: str

@mcp.tool()
def start_draft(title: str) -> Draft:
    """Start a draft note. Returns a draft_id to pass to append_to_draft. Drafts expire after 1 hour."""
    draft_id = "dft_" + secrets.token_urlsafe(12)      # unguessable handle, not dft_1, dft_2...
    DRAFTS[draft_id] = {"title": title, "lines": [], "created": datetime.now(timezone.utc)}
    return Draft(draft_id=draft_id)

@mcp.tool()
def append_to_draft(draft_id: str, line: str) -> str:
    """Append a line to a draft started with start_draft."""
    draft = DRAFTS.get(draft_id)
    if draft is None:
        raise ToolError("Unknown or expired draft_id. Call start_draft to create a new draft.")
    draft["lines"].append(line)
    return f"Draft now has {len(draft['lines'])} line(s)."


# ---------- Resources ----------

@mcp.resource("notes://index", mime_type="text/markdown", description="Index of all notes")
def notes_index() -> str:
    return "\n".join(f"- {k}: {v['title']}" for k, v in NOTES.items())

@mcp.resource("notes://{note_id}", mime_type="text/markdown", description="A single note by id")
def note_by_id(note_id: str) -> str:
    note = NOTES.get(note_id)
    if note is None:
        raise ResourceNotFoundError(f"Note {note_id} not found")   # -> JSON-RPC -32602
    return f"# {note['title']}\n\n{note['body']}"


# ---------- Prompts ----------

@mcp.prompt(title="Summarize a note")
def summarize_note(note_id: str, audience: str = "engineer") -> str:
    """Ask the model to summarize a note for a given audience."""
    note = NOTES.get(note_id, {"title": "?", "body": "(missing)"})
    return f"Summarize this note for a {audience} in three bullet points:\n\n# {note['title']}\n{note['body']}"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run(transport="stdio")

docs.title: Tool annotations are hints, not guarantees
docs.text:
readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint and openWorldHint help a host decide how carefully to treat a tool. For example, it might skip the confirmation dialog for a read-only lookup.

The spec is explicit that clients MUST treat annotations as untrusted unless the server itself is trusted. A malicious server can label delete_everything as readOnlyHint: true. Annotations help UX; they are not a security boundary.

docs.title: Return a model, get structured output
docs.text:
search_notes returns list[Note], and start_draft returns Draft. With a Pydantic model or typed return value, the SDK does two things:

  1. It publishes an outputSchema in tools/list.
  2. It fills structuredContent in every result, and the client can validate it against that schema.

Try it

Change start_draft to return a plain dict. tools/list no longer shows a useful outputSchema, and result.structured_content becomes None. A client that relies on structured output then has nothing to validate against.

docs.title: Two kinds of error
docs.text:
Situation What to raise What the client receives Who handles it The model sent a body that is too long ToolError("... Shorten it and retry.") result with isError: true and your message The model, which can correct itself A resource id doesn’t exist ResourceNotFoundError JSON-RPC error, code -32602 The client application A bug in your code (e.g. KeyError) Nothing: it escapes isError: true with a generic message, so internals are not leaked You, from the logs

The spec draws the same line. Tool execution errors go back to the model in the result so it can recover. Protocol errors are problems with the request itself, and the application handles them.

Try it

Replace ToolError with ValueError in create_note. The model now sees only a generic Error executing tool create_note, with no hint about the 2000-character limit, so it cannot fix its call. A good tool error tells the model what to do next.

docs.title: Stateful work without sessions
docs.text:
The 2026-07-28 protocol has no sessions: no Mcp-Session-Id, no connection-scoped memory. So how does a multi-step workflow like a draft keep its state? It does what start_draft does: the server returns an explicit handle (draft_id), and the model passes it back on later calls.

Rules for handles, all visible in the code:

  • Unguessable. secrets.token_urlsafe, never dft_1, dft_2. If handles are guessable, one user can reach another user’s state. The spec calls this state handle hijacking, and it is covered in Attacks & Mitigations.
  • Documented. The description tells the model where the handle comes from and how long it lives.
  • Expiring, with an actionable error when an expired or unknown handle comes back.
  • In a multi-user deployment, also bound to the authenticated user. Check the owner on every use, not just that the handle exists.

docs.title: Resources and templates
docs.text:
notes://index is a direct resource, listed by resources/list. notes://{note_id} is a resource template (RFC 6570), listed by resources/templates/list. The host fills in the template to build concrete URIs.

For a URI that doesn’t exist, 2026-07-28 uses -32602 Invalid params. The old -32002 “resource not found” code is retired.

docs.title: Cache hints
docs.text:
Every list and discovery result carries ttlMs and cacheScope. By default the SDK sends ttlMs: 0, cacheScope: "private", meaning “don’t reuse this”. This server overrides the default for tools/list and prompts/list, which are identical for every user and change rarely: scope="public" lets a shared cache reuse them for five minutes.

Choosing a scope

public means the result is the same for every caller. If tools/list depended on the user’s permissions, it would have to be private. Otherwise one user’s tool list could be served to another user.

docs.title: 4. Test it in memory
docs.text:
The SDK Client can connect directly to an MCPServer object, with no subprocess. That makes it great for tests. Create test_notes.py:

test_notes.py
import anyio, json
from mcp import Client
from notes_server import mcp

def wire(model):
    """Show a result the way it looks on the wire (camelCase JSON)."""
    return json.dumps(model.model_dump(by_alias=True, exclude_none=True, mode="json"))

async def main():
    async with Client(mcp) as client:
        print("protocol:", client.protocol_version)
        r = await client.call_tool("search_notes", {"query": "mrtr"})
        print("search ->", wire(r))
        r = await client.call_tool("create_note", {"title": "big", "body": "x" * 2500})
        print("oversize ->", wire(r))
        d = await client.call_tool("start_draft", {"title": "t"})
        print("draft ->", d.structured_content)
        bad = await client.call_tool("append_to_draft", {"draft_id": "dft_guess", "line": "x"})
        print("bad handle ->", wire(bad))
        print("templates ->", wire(await client.list_resource_templates()))
        print("read n2 ->", wire(await client.read_resource("notes://n2")))
        try:
            await client.read_resource("notes://n99")
        except Exception as e:
            print("read n99 ->", type(e).__name__, getattr(e, "error", e))
        print("prompts ->", wire(await client.list_prompts()))
        print("get_prompt ->", wire(await client.get_prompt("summarize_note", {"note_id": "n1"})))

anyio.run(main)

python test_notes.py 2>/dev/null

Output, with _meta.serverInfo removed for readability:

protocol: 2026-07-28
search -> {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": "{\n  \"id\": \"n2\",\n  \"title\": \"MRTR\", ...}"}],
           "structuredContent": {"result": [{"id": "n2", "title": "MRTR",
             "body": "Servers return input_required; clients retry with a new id."}]},
           "isError": false, "resultType": "complete"}
oversize -> {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Error executing tool create_note: Body is 2500
             characters; the maximum is 2000. Shorten it and retry."}], "isError": true, "resultType": "complete"}
draft -> {'draft_id': 'dft_FvDeigN2YQh7qcgT'}
bad handle -> {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Error executing tool append_to_draft: Unknown or
             expired draft_id. Call start_draft to create a new draft."}], "isError": true, ...}
templates -> {"ttlMs": 0, "cacheScope": "private", "resourceTemplates": [{"name": "note_by_id",
             "uriTemplate": "notes://{note_id}", "description": "A single note by id",
             "mimeType": "text/markdown"}], "resultType": "complete"}
read n2 -> {"ttlMs": 0, "cacheScope": "private", "contents": [{"uri": "notes://n2",
             "mimeType": "text/markdown", "text": "# MRTR\n\nServers return input_required; ..."}], ...}
read n99 -> MCPError code=-32602 message='Note n99 not found' data={'uri': 'notes://n99'}
prompts -> {"ttlMs": 300000, "cacheScope": "public", "prompts": [{"name": "summarize_note",
             "title": "Summarize a note", "arguments": [{"name": "note_id", "required": true},
             {"name": "audience", "required": false}]}], "resultType": "complete"}
get_prompt -> {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": {"type": "text", "text": "Summarize this
             note for a engineer in three bullet points: ..."}}], "resultType": "complete"}

Check yourself

  1. Why does prompts/list show ttlMs: 300000, cacheScope: "public" while resources/templates/list shows 0 and private?
  2. The model called append_to_draft with a made-up id. Is that a protocol error or a tool execution error, and why is that the right choice here?
  3. The prompt argument audience has required: false. Where did that come from?
Answers
  1. Only tools/list and prompts/list got a CacheHint. Everything else uses the SDK’s conservative default.
  2. A tool execution error (isError: true). The request itself was valid; the failure is in the tool’s domain, and the model can recover by calling start_draft.
  3. The Python default value audience: str = "engineer".

docs.title: Lab 3: Build a Client
docs.text: Time: 45 minutes · Goal: write the client side of a host. Launch a server, find out what it offers, show its tools to a model in function-calling format, and send the model’s choices back as MCP calls.

docs.title: 1. What a host actually does
docs.text:
When a user types a question into an AI application, the host runs this loop:

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant H as Host (+ MCP client)
    participant L as LLM
    participant S as MCP server
    H->>S: tools/list (and resources, prompts)
    S-->>H: Tool definitions
    U->>H: "Find my notes about MCP"
    H->>L: user message + tools converted to LLM format
    L-->>H: tool_use: search_notes {"query": "mcp"}
    H->>H: policy check / user confirmation
    H->>S: tools/call search_notes
    S-->>H: CallToolResult
    H->>L: tool_result (text or structured)
    L-->>H: final answer
    H-->>U: answer

Notice that the model never talks to the server. The host sits in the middle and decides:

  • which tools the model gets to see,
  • whether a call needs the user’s confirmation,
  • what goes back into the model’s context.

This is the trust boundary from Hosts, Clients & Servers turned into code.

docs.title: 2. The client
docs.text:
This client launches notes_server.py from Lab 2 as a subprocess. Create notes_client.py next to it:

notes_client.py
"""Lab 3: a minimal host-side client for the notes server."""
import json
import sys

import anyio
from mcp import Client
from mcp.client.stdio import StdioServerParameters
from mcp.types import Implementation, TextContent

SERVER = StdioServerParameters(command=sys.executable, args=["notes_server.py"])


def to_llm_tool(tool) -> dict:
    """Map an MCP Tool to the function-calling format most LLM APIs accept."""
    return {
        "name": tool.name,
        "description": tool.description or "",
        "input_schema": tool.input_schema,   # snake_case attribute; "inputSchema" on the wire
    }


def result_for_model(result) -> str:
    """Flatten a CallToolResult into the text a model would see."""
    if result.structured_content is not None:
        body = json.dumps(result.structured_content)
    else:
        body = "\n".join(c.text for c in result.content if isinstance(c, TextContent))
    return ("ERROR: " if result.is_error else "") + body


async def main() -> None:
    async with Client(SERVER, client_info=Implementation(name="lab-host", version="0.1.0")) as client:
        print("protocol    :", client.protocol_version)
        print("server      :", client.server_info.name, client.server_info.version)
        print("instructions:", client.instructions)
        caps = client.server_capabilities
        print("capabilities:", [k for k in ("tools", "resources", "prompts") if getattr(caps, k)])

        tools = await client.list_tools()
        llm_tools = [to_llm_tool(t) for t in tools.tools]
        print("\nTools offered to the model:")
        print(json.dumps(llm_tools[0], indent=2))
        print("...and", len(llm_tools) - 1, "more")

        # Pretend the model decided to call search_notes.
        call = {"name": "search_notes", "arguments": {"query": "mcp"}}
        result = await client.call_tool(call["name"], call["arguments"])
        print("\nsearch_notes ->", result_for_model(result))

        bad = await client.call_tool("create_note", {"title": "x", "body": "y" * 2500})
        print("create_note (too long) ->", result_for_model(bad))

        resources = await client.list_resources()
        templates = await client.list_resource_templates()
        print("\nresources :", [r.uri for r in resources.resources])
        print("templates :", [t.uri_template for t in templates.resource_templates])
        index = await client.read_resource("notes://index")
        print("notes://index ->", index.contents[0].text[:80])

        prompts = await client.list_prompts()
        print("\nprompts   :", [p.name for p in prompts.prompts])
        p = await client.get_prompt("summarize_note", {"note_id": "n1"})
        print("prompt msg:", p.messages[0].role, "|", p.messages[0].content.text[:80])


anyio.run(main)

python notes_client.py 2>/dev/null

Predict

Client(...) uses mode="auto" by default. What will its first message to the server be?

Answer

server/discover. In auto mode, a dual-era client probes with discovery and only falls back to initialize if the server turns out to be legacy. This is the stdio backward-compatibility procedure from the spec, done for you.

docs.title: 3. The output
docs.text:
protocol    : 2026-07-28
server      : notes 1.0.0
instructions: Search notes before creating a new one to avoid duplicates.
capabilities: ['tools', 'resources', 'prompts']

Tools offered to the model:
{
  "name": "search_notes",
  "description": "Search notes by a word in the title or body.\n\n    Args:\n        query: A word to look for, case-insensitive.\n    ",
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "query": {
        "title": "Query",
        "type": "string"
      }
    },
    "required": [
      "query"
    ],
    "title": "search_notesArguments"
  }
}
...and 3 more

search_notes -> {"result": [{"id": "n1", "title": "MCP transports", "body": "stdio for local, Streamable HTTP for remote."}]}
create_note (too long) -> ERROR: Error executing tool create_note: Body is 2500 characters; the maximum is 2000. Shorten it and retry.

resources : ['notes://index']
templates : ['notes://{note_id}']
notes://index -> - n1: MCP transports
- n2: MRTR

prompts   : ['summarize_note']
prompt msg: user | Summarize this note for a engineer in three bullet points:

docs.title: 4. What the client had to decide
Capabilities first
docs.text: The client checked server_capabilities before listing anything. On a server without resources, calling resources/list would fail. Discovery tells the client what it may ask for.

docs.title: Mapping tools is almost free
docs.text: An MCP Tool already has a name, a description and a JSON Schema for its input, which is exactly what LLM function-calling APIs want. That is no accident: it is why a server written once works with any model vendor. Portability is the heart of Domain 1’s interoperability story.

docs.title: Errors go back to the model
docs.text: result_for_model sends a tool execution error back as text, marked as an error, rather than raising an exception. The model reads “maximum is 2000. Shorten it and retry.” and can try again. If the client threw instead, the conversation would simply stop.

docs.title: Resources and prompts are not given to the model as tools
docs.text: The host lists them and decides what to do with them itself. Typically it offers resources in an “attach context” picker and prompts in a slash-command menu. That matches their control model: resources are application-controlled and prompts are user-controlled.

docs.title: 5. Extending the host
docs.text:
These exercises have no single answer. Each one practises a decision that comes up on the exam.

Try it: several servers

Connect to both weather_server.py (Lab 1) and notes_server.py at once. What if two servers both had a tool called search? A common host approach is to namespace names before showing them to the model, e.g. notes__search, and keep a map back to (server, original name).

Try it: human in the loop

Before call_tool, print the tool name and arguments and ask Run this? [y/N]. Skip the prompt for tools annotated readOnlyHint: true. Then think about why that shortcut is only safe for servers you trust. (The spec says annotations from untrusted servers are untrusted.)

Try it: caching

Call client.list_tools() and client.list_resources() three times each, and count the requests that actually reach the server (for example by wrapping client.session.list_tools). When we ran it:

wire requests after 3 calls each: {'tools/list': 1, 'resources/list': 3}

tools/list carries Lab 2’s 5-minute hint, so the SDK’s default CacheConfig answers the repeat calls from its cache. resources/list carries ttlMs: 0, so every call goes to the server.

docs.text: You saw Study chapter Host-mediated model ↔ server interaction Interaction Flow Discovery before use; capabilities Versioning & Discovery Tools → LLM function calling, vendor-neutral Interoperability Host roles and control points Hosts, Clients & Servers Confirmation and trust decisions Permissions & Consent

docs.title: Lab 4: Streamable HTTP
docs.text: Time: 50 minutes · Goal: serve the Lab 2 server over HTTP, drive it with plain curl, and set off every check the transport defines: header mirroring, version errors, Origin validation, and the removed session-era methods.

docs.title: 1. Why a second transport
docs.text:
stdio is ideal when the host launches the server as a local process: there is no network, no port and no authentication. It cannot serve a remote team, a SaaS integration, or a server that runs once for thousands of users.

Streamable HTTP is the standard transport for remote servers. In 2026-07-28 it is simple:

  • One endpoint (here /mcp) and one method, POST. Every JSON-RPC message is its own POST.
  • The response is either a single JSON object (application/json) or an SSE stream (text/event-stream) for that one request, e.g. to send progress before the result.
  • No sessions: no Mcp-Session-Id, no GET stream, no resumability.
  • Key body fields are mirrored into HTTP headers, so load balancers and gateways can route requests without parsing JSON.

docs.title: 2. Start the server
docs.text:
Create notes_http.py next to notes_server.py:

notes_http.py
"""Lab 4: serve the notes server over Streamable HTTP."""
from notes_server import mcp

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run(transport="streamable-http", host="127.0.0.1", port=8799)   # endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8799/mcp

Run it in its own terminal and leave it running:

python notes_http.py

If port 8799 is already taken, change it here and in the commands below.

Bind to 127.0.0.1

The spec says local servers SHOULD bind only to localhost, not 0.0.0.0. The SDK defaults to 127.0.0.1 for this reason.

docs.title: 3. Set up shell variables
docs.text:
In a second terminal, define the parts that repeat:

U=http://127.0.0.1:8799/mcp
META='"_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion":"2026-07-28","io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities":{},"io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo":{"name":"curl","version":"1"}}'
H=(-H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" -H "MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28")

The client MUST send an Accept header listing both content types, because the server may choose either.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
curl -si $U "${H[@]}" -H "Mcp-Method: server/discover" \
  -d "{\"jsonrpc\":\"2.0\",\"id\":1,\"method\":\"server/discover\",\"params\":{$META}}"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
content-type: application/json

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"result":{"cacheScope":"private","capabilities":{...},
 "instructions":"Search notes before creating a new one to avoid duplicates.",
 "resultType":"complete","supportedVersions":["2026-07-28"],"ttlMs":0,...}}

docs.title: A tool call
docs.text:
curl -si $U "${H[@]}" -H "Mcp-Method: tools/call" -H "Mcp-Name: search_notes" \
  -d "{\"jsonrpc\":\"2.0\",\"id\":2,\"method\":\"tools/call\",\"params\":{\"name\":\"search_notes\",\"arguments\":{\"query\":\"mcp\"},$META}}"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
content-type: application/json

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"result":{"content":[...],"isError":false,"resultType":"complete",
 "structuredContent":{"result":[{"id":"n1","title":"MCP transports",...}]},...}}

The standard headers you just sent:

Header Mirrors Required on MCP-Protocol-Version params._meta["io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion"] Every POST Mcp-Method method All requests Mcp-Name params.name or params.uri tools/call, resources/read, prompts/get

Tools can also declare parameters to mirror as Mcp-Param-{Name} headers, using the x-mcp-header schema extension. A gateway can then, for example, route by a region argument.

docs.title: 5. Breaking it on purpose
docs.text:
Predict

For each request below, predict the HTTP status and the JSON-RPC error code before you run it.

docs.title: 5.1 A header that disagrees with the body
docs.text:
The header says tools/list, but the body says tools/call:

curl -si $U "${H[@]}" -H "Mcp-Method: tools/list" -H "Mcp-Name: search_notes" \
  -d "{\"jsonrpc\":\"2.0\",\"id\":3,\"method\":\"tools/call\",\"params\":{\"name\":\"search_notes\",\"arguments\":{\"query\":\"mcp\"},$META}}"

HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"error":{"code":-32020,"message":"mcp-method header does not match the request body's method"}}

Why this rule exists. Picture a gateway that allows tools/list for everyone but restricts tools/call. It checks the header. The MCP server executes the body. If they could disagree, an attacker would put tools/list in the header and tools/call in the body and walk straight past the policy. So servers MUST reject any mismatch with 400 and -32020 HeaderMismatch.

docs.title: 5.2 A missing required header
docs.text:
The same thing without Mcp-Name:

curl -si $U "${H[@]}" -H "Mcp-Method: tools/call" \
  -d "{\"jsonrpc\":\"2.0\",\"id\":4,\"method\":\"tools/call\",\"params\":{\"name\":\"search_notes\",\"arguments\":{\"query\":\"x\"},$META}}"

HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":4,"error":{"code":-32020,"message":"mcp-name header does not match the request body's 'name' parameter"}}

The spec counts a missing required header as a validation failure too, with the same code, -32020. The Mcp-Name mismatch (header create_note, body search_notes) gives the same result.

docs.title: 5.3 A version header that disagrees with _meta
docs.text:
curl -s $U -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  -H "MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28" -H "Mcp-Method: tools/list" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":5,"method":"tools/list","params":{"_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion":"2025-11-25","io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities":{}}}}'

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":5,"error":{"code":-32020,"message":"mcp-protocol-version header does not match the request envelope's protocol version"}}

docs.title: 5.4 A version the server doesn’t support
docs.text:
Both the header and _meta say 2027-01-01:

curl -si $U -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  -H "MCP-Protocol-Version: 2027-01-01" -H "Mcp-Method: tools/list" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":6,"method":"tools/list","params":{"_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion":"2027-01-01","io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities":{}}}}'

HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":6,"error":{"code":-32022,"message":"Unsupported protocol version",
 "data":{"supported":["2026-07-28"],"requested":"2027-01-01"}}}

Compare this with 5.3. There the request contradicted itself, so it got -32020. Here it is consistent but unsupported, so it gets -32022, and data.supported tells the client what to use instead.

docs.title: 5.5 A method the server doesn’t implement
docs.text:
curl -si $U "${H[@]}" -H "Mcp-Method: tools/frobnicate" \
  -d "{\"jsonrpc\":\"2.0\",\"id\":7,\"method\":\"tools/frobnicate\",\"params\":{$META}}"

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":7,"error":{"code":-32601,"message":"Method not found","data":"tools/frobnicate"}}

The spec requires 404 with a JSON-RPC -32601 body. The body is what tells this apart from the bare 404 of an old HTTP+SSE server that has no modern endpoint.

docs.title: 5.6 A hostile Origin
docs.text:
A web page on evil.example tries to reach your local server through the browser:

curl -si $U "${H[@]}" -H "Mcp-Method: tools/list" -H "Origin: https://evil.example" \
  -d "{\"jsonrpc\":\"2.0\",\"id\":8,\"method\":\"tools/list\",\"params\":{$META}}"

HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden

Invalid Origin header

This is the DNS rebinding defence. A malicious site points its own hostname at 127.0.0.1. The browser then treats requests to your local server as same-site, and the page can drive your tools. The browser always sends the page’s real Origin, so the server MUST validate it. If it is present and not allowed, the answer MUST be 403. Lab 6 adds the matching Host header check.

docs.title: 5.7 Session-era traffic
docs.text:
An older client may still try a GET stream or a DELETE to end its session:

curl -si $U -H "Accept: text/event-stream" -H "MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28"
curl -si -X DELETE $U -H "MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28"

HTTP/1.1 405 Method Not Allowed
allow: POST

Both give the same answer. The spec says a server that only speaks this revision SHOULD answer GET and DELETE with 405, ignore any Mcp-Session-Id header, and ignore Last-Event-ID.

docs.title: 5.8 A notification
docs.text:
curl -si $U "${H[@]}" -H "Mcp-Method: notifications/cancelled" \
  -d "{\"jsonrpc\":\"2.0\",\"method\":\"notifications/cancelled\",\"params\":{\"requestId\":99,$META}}"

HTTP/1.1 202 Accepted
content-length: 0

A notification has no id, so there is no response to send back. A server that accepts one MUST return 202 Accepted with an empty body.

Trap: cancellation on HTTP

This request only demonstrates the 202 mechanics. On Streamable HTTP, clients don’t send notifications/cancelled. Closing the response stream is the cancellation, and the server MUST treat it that way. notifications/cancelled is only used on stdio, where there is no per-request connection to close.

docs.title: 6. Legacy traffic on the same endpoint
docs.text:
Send an old-style initialize with no version header:

curl -si $U -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":9,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-11-25","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"old","version":"1"}}}'

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
content-type: text/event-stream
mcp-session-id: 2e7befc699884d22b0b09017d6cf99c0

event: message
data: {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":9,"result":{...,"protocolVersion":"2025-11-25","serverInfo":{"name":"notes","version":"1.0.0"}}}

The SDK server is dual-era here as well. It detects a legacy client and falls back to the 2025-11-25 transport, including a session id. A server that supports only 2026-07-28 would reject this request instead.

The reverse also happens. Earlier, a request with a missing or old MCP-Protocol-Version header fell into this legacy path and got -32600 "Bad Request: Missing session ID" rather than a modern error. That is how a dual-era client tells the two eras apart: a recognised modern error in a 400 body means “modern server, fix your request”. Anything else means “legacy server, fall back to initialize”.

docs.title: 7. The same thing, with the SDK
docs.text:
The high-level Client from Lab 3 accepts a URL too:

http_client.py
"""Lab 4: the same Client, pointed at a URL instead of a subprocess."""
import anyio
from mcp import Client


async def main() -> None:
    async with Client("http://127.0.0.1:8799/mcp") as client:
        print("protocol:", client.protocol_version)
        tools = await client.list_tools()
        print("tools   :", [t.name for t in tools.tools])
        result = await client.call_tool("search_notes", {"query": "mrtr"})
        print("call    :", result.structured_content)


anyio.run(main)

protocol: 2026-07-28
tools   : ['search_notes', 'create_note', 'start_draft', 'append_to_draft']
call    : {'result': [{'id': 'n2', 'title': 'MRTR', 'body': 'Servers return input_required; clients retry with a new id.'}]}

The application code is identical to the stdio version; only the connection target changed. Transport independence is a design goal: the data layer (JSON-RPC messages and primitives) knows nothing about the transport layer.
